outline.title: Randomised or as-if randomised
outline.one_liner: People were assigned by chance, or as good as chance.

outline.title: Adjust for background differences
outline.one_liner: Treatment was not random; we can measure the things that made people get it.

outline.title: Policy rolled out over time
outline.one_liner: Some places or groups got it earlier than others.

outline.title: A cutoff decided eligibility
outline.one_liner: Crossing a score, age, or border switched the programme on.

outline.title: Something else pushed people in
outline.one_liner: An instrument or encouragement changed treatment, not the outcome directly.

outline.title: One place, constructed twin
outline.one_liner: One treated unit; build a comparison from a donor pool.

outline.title: A shock in a single series
outline.one_liner: Before versus after an interruption; maybe a control series.

outline.title: How it worked (pathways)
outline.one_liner: We care about a mediator, not only the total effect.

outline.title: Treatment that changes over time
outline.one_liner: The same person is treated, untreated, treated again; confounders also move.

outline.title: Manski bounds
outline.one_liner: Report the range the effect must lie in given only what the data can support, without assuming away the missing counterfactual.

outline.title: Imputation (Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess)
outline.one_liner: Learn what untreated life looks like from untreated cells only, then ask how far each treated cell landed from it.

outline.title: Callaway & Sant'Anna group-time effects
outline.one_liner: Estimate one clean before-and-after for every adoption cohort, then say out loud how you averaged them.

outline.title: de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille
outline.one_liner: An estimator built for panels where treatment switches on and off, which the imputation and cohort estimators assume never happens.

outline.title: Doubly robust DiD
outline.one_liner: One before-and-after with covariates, using an outcome model and a comparison-group model together so either one can carry it.

outline.title: Event study (leads and lags)
outline.one_liner: Plot the effect period by period around adoption, so you can see whether the gap opened when the policy arrived or long before it.

outline.title: Two-stage DiD (Gardner / Wooldridge-Mundlak)
outline.one_liner: Strip out unit and period effects using untreated cells only, then regress what is left on the policy.

outline.title: Goodman-Bacon decomposition
outline.one_liner: Open up a two-way fixed effects estimate and show every two-group comparison inside it, with the weight each one carries -- including the ones that use already-treated units as controls.

outline.title: Matched difference-in-differences
outline.one_liner: Match treated to comparison units on pre-period characteristics first, then difference.

outline.title: Sun & Abraham event study
outline.one_liner: Give every cohort its own event-study path, then average the paths by cohort size instead of letting the regression choose the weights.

outline.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences (synthdid)
outline.one_liner: Weight both units and periods, then take a difference-in-differences -- halfway between synthetic control and DiD.

outline.title: Triple differences
outline.one_liner: Compare the treated-versus-comparison difference for the group the policy could reach with the same difference for a group inside the same units that it could not.

outline.title: Two-way fixed effects
outline.one_liner: One regression with unit and period fixed effects. Familiar, fast, and not an average treatment effect when units adopt at different dates.

outline.title: Difference-in-differences (2x2)
outline.one_liner: Two groups, two periods: compare how much the treated group changed with how much the comparison group changed over the same window.

outline.title: Structure learning (causal discovery)
outline.one_liner: Search for a graph consistent with the data. It does not recover the true causal structure from observational data without extra assumptions.

outline.title: Interference and spillovers
outline.one_liner: When one unit's treatment affects another's outcome, estimate the direct and spillover effects separately instead of pretending neither exists.

outline.title: ARIMA with an intervention
outline.one_liner: Model the memory in the series itself, then ask how big a step, pulse or ramp the data need at the intervention date.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Bayesian structural time series (CausalImpact)
outline.one_liner: Model the counterfactual series with a structural time-series model and control series, and report a posterior rather than an interval.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Controlled ITS
outline.one_liner: The same interruption, measured against a series the intervention did not touch, so a shock that hit everybody is not booked as your effect.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Segmented regression
outline.one_liner: Fit the trend before the interruption, project it forward, and measure the jump and the change of direction after it.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Two-stage least squares
outline.one_liner: Use only the part of the treatment that the instrument moved, and see what happened to the outcome.

outline.title: Two-step GMM
outline.one_liner: Weight the instruments by how informative each one actually is, using a weight matrix estimated from the data.

outline.title: LIML (and Fuller)
outline.one_liner: The maximum-likelihood cousin of two-stage least squares, which stays much better behaved when the instruments are weak.

outline.title: Marginal treatment effects
outline.one_liner: Trace the effect as a function of how reluctant a unit is to be treated, instead of reporting one local average.

outline.title: Shift-share (Bartik) instruments
outline.one_liner: Combine national shocks with local exposure shares to build an instrument for local changes.

outline.title: Weak-instrument-robust confidence set
outline.one_liner: Report the set of effects the data cannot reject, which stays honest however weak the instrument is.

outline.title: G-estimation of structural nested models
outline.one_liner: Estimate the effect of a treatment regime by finding the parameter that removes the association between treatment and the blipped-down outcome.

outline.title: Parametric g-formula
outline.one_liner: Model each period in turn, then simulate the world where everyone followed the strategy you name.

outline.title: Longitudinal modified treatment policies (lmtp)
outline.one_liner: Estimate the effect of shifting a continuous or multi-valued treatment, rather than of setting everyone to one value.

outline.title: Sequential doubly robust (ICE g-formula with augmentation)
outline.one_liner: Regress backwards from the final outcome, then correct with the treatment probabilities: right if either set of models is right.

outline.title: Longitudinal TMLE for survival outcomes
outline.one_liner: Time-to-event outcomes with time-varying treatment and censoring, targeted at each time.

outline.title: Marginal structural model (time-varying weights)
outline.one_liner: Reweight each person-period so the treated and untreated histories look alike, then fit one simple model to the reweighted data.

outline.title: Controlled direct effect
outline.one_liner: What the treatment would still do if the mediator were fixed at one value for everybody.

outline.title: Interventional direct and indirect effects
outline.one_liner: Shift the mediator to the distribution it would have in the population, rather than to each person's own unobservable counterfactual.

outline.title: Natural direct and indirect effects
outline.one_liner: Split the total effect into the part that travelled through the mediator and the part that did not.

outline.title: Honest causal forest
outline.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

outline.title: Double ML (interactive)
outline.one_liner: A separate outcome model for each arm plus a treatment model, combined in a doubly robust score: right if either side is right.

outline.title: Double ML (partially linear)
outline.one_liner: Predict the outcome and the treatment from the confounders, then regress what is left of one on what is left of the other.

outline.title: Meta-learner (T, S, X, DR)
outline.one_liner: Build the per-unit effect out of ordinary prediction models, four different ways, on the same cross-fitting.

outline.title: Policy tree (who should be treated)
outline.one_liner: Learn a short, readable rule for who to treat, then value that rule on data it never saw.
tags: Value of the policy the rule would implement

outline.title: Doubly robust (AIPW)
outline.one_liner: Use a treatment model and an outcome model together; it is right if either one is.

outline.title: Coarsened exact matching
outline.one_liner: Bin the covariates, then compare only inside bins that contain both arms.

outline.title: Genetic matching
outline.one_liner: Search over distance-metric weights until balance is as good as it can get, instead of trusting one metric.

outline.title: Nearest-neighbour matching
outline.one_liner: Pair each treated unit with the most similar untreated unit, then compare within pairs.

outline.title: Optimal and full matching
outline.one_liner: Choose the whole set of matches at once to minimise total distance, rather than greedily one treated unit at a time.

outline.title: Multiple imputation compatible with the analysis
outline.one_liner: Impute the missing values several times, run the analysis in each, and combine -- instead of dropping every row with a gap.

outline.title: Outcome regression (g-computation)
outline.one_liner: Model the outcome, then ask what would have happened if everyone had been treated, and if nobody had.

outline.title: Super Learner nuisance models
outline.one_liner: Combine several candidate learners by cross-validated weights instead of betting on one.

outline.title: Targeted maximum likelihood (TMLE)
outline.one_liner: Fit the outcome model, then nudge it once in the direction the treatment model says it is wrong.

outline.title: Covariate balancing propensity score
outline.one_liner: Fit the treatment model so that it balances covariates, rather than fitting it to predict treatment and hoping balance follows.

outline.title: Entropy balancing
outline.one_liner: Find the weights closest to equal that make the covariate means match exactly.

outline.title: Propensity weighting
outline.one_liner: Reweight the sample so the treated and untreated groups look alike on the measured confounders.

outline.title: Boosted propensity scores (twang)
outline.one_liner: Grow a boosted model for the propensity score, stopping at the iteration that balances covariates best.

outline.title: ITT and CACE (noncompliance)
outline.one_liner: Not everyone offered a programme takes it. Report what the offer did, and separately what taking it up did for the people it moved.

outline.title: Cluster-randomised trial
outline.one_liner: When whole schools, clinics or villages were assigned, the number of clusters is the sample size that matters.

outline.title: Difference in means
outline.one_liner: Compare the two arms as they were randomised, and let covariates sharpen the comparison without letting them change the question.

outline.title: Randomisation (Fisher) inference
outline.one_liner: Re-run the randomisation thousands of times with the outcomes held fixed, and see how unusual what actually happened really is.

outline.title: Blocked or stratified experiment
outline.one_liner: Estimate inside the blocks the randomisation was run in, then average them the way your estimand says to.

outline.title: Do the covariates jump at the cutoff too?
outline.one_liner: Run the same estimator on variables the programme cannot have changed; they should not step at the threshold.

outline.title: Did people sort across the cutoff?
outline.one_liner: Compare how many units sit just below the threshold with how many sit just above.

outline.title: Fuzzy RD (crossing the cutoff only nudged people in)
outline.one_liner: Divide the jump in the outcome by the jump in take-up: the effect for the people the cutoff actually moved.

outline.title: Regression kink (the rule bends, it does not switch)
outline.one_liner: Where a formula changes slope rather than switching on, measure the change in slope of the outcome.
tags: Change in slope at the cutoff

outline.title: Sharp RD at the cutoff
outline.one_liner: Fit a line either side of the threshold and measure the step between them.

outline.title: Local randomisation RD
outline.one_liner: Treat a narrow window around the cutoff as a small randomised experiment rather than fitting a curve through it.

outline.title: Multi-cutoff and geographic RD
outline.one_liner: Several thresholds, or a boundary on a map, pooled into one design.

outline.title: Synthetic control
outline.one_liner: Build a weighted copy of the treated place out of untreated places that looked like it beforehand, then watch the two lines separate.

outline.title: Augmented synthetic control
outline.one_liner: When no weighted average of the donors can match the treated place, correct the leftover bias with a ridge model and show the size of the correction.

outline.title: Matrix completion
outline.one_liner: Treat the missing treated-period outcomes as holes in a panel and fill them in with a low-rank model of what the panel would have done.

outline.title: Microsynth (many treated units)
outline.one_liner: Synthetic control when the treated unit is a neighbourhood or a small area and there are many of them.

outline.title: Prediction intervals for synthetic control (scpi)
outline.one_liner: Confidence intervals for a synthetic control that come from a model of the prediction error rather than from permutation.

outline.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences
outline.one_liner: Weight the comparison units and the pre-treatment periods, then run a difference in differences on the result - a level gap is allowed, a trend gap is not.

outline.title: Transportability and generalisability
outline.one_liner: Take an effect estimated in one population and ask what it would be in another with a different mix of characteristics.

outline.title: Unobserved confounder
outline.one_liner: Simulate a common cause of a stated strength and watch the estimate move; read off how strong one would have to be to explain the result away.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Specification curve
outline.one_liner: Run the grid of defensible specifications and sort the answers. The curve is the result, not the one you happened to run.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Cinelli-Hazlett sensitivity (partial R2)
outline.one_liner: How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be -- compared with the covariates you already have -- to explain the estimate away?

outline.title: E-value
outline.one_liner: The smallest confounder-treatment and confounder-outcome association that could explain the result away.

outline.title: Honest DiD (Rambachan-Roth)
outline.one_liner: What survives when parallel trends is allowed to fail by a stated amount.

outline.title: Leave one out
outline.one_liner: Drop one cluster, cohort or donor at a time and see whether any single one is carrying the result.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Negative control
outline.one_liner: Estimate something that shares the confounding but not the causal path. A non-zero answer is bias you can see.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Oster coefficient stability
outline.one_liner: How important would unobserved variables have to be, relative to the controls you already have, to drive the coefficient to zero?

outline.title: Placebo outcome
outline.one_liner: Run the same analysis on something the treatment could not have changed. It should find nothing.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Placebo treatment
outline.one_liner: Move the policy date earlier, reshuffle who was treated, or swap in a variable that cannot cause the outcome.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Random common cause
outline.one_liner: Add a variable that causes nothing to the adjustment set. The estimate should barely move.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Rosenbaum bounds
outline.one_liner: How unequal could the odds of treatment be inside a matched pair before the conclusion stopped being clear?

outline.title: Subset stability
outline.one_liner: Re-estimate on random subsets. The answer should move about as much as losing that much data costs, and no more.
tags: A shock in a single series
Whichever effect the method it is applied to targets

outline.title: Trimming curve
outline.one_liner: Re-estimate across a grid of propensity-score trimming thresholds instead of picking one and hoping.

outline.title: Average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?

outline.title: Average treatment effect on the treated
outline.one_liner: For people who actually got it, what did it do?
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Average treatment effect on the controls
outline.one_liner: For people who didn't get it, what would it have done?

outline.title: Average treatment effect on the overlap population
outline.one_liner: For the people where treated and untreated genuinely overlap, what did it do?

outline.title: Local average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: For people who only got it because of the instrument or the cutoff, what did it do?

outline.title: Complier average causal effect
outline.one_liner: For the people who comply with what they were offered, what did it do?

outline.title: Local average treatment effect on the treated
outline.one_liner: For treated compliers, what did it do?

outline.title: Intention to treat
outline.one_liner: For everyone who was offered it, what did the offer do?

outline.title: Group-time average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: For each group that adopted it, what did their own rollout do?

outline.title: Conditional average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: How does the effect vary from person to person, or place to place?

outline.title: Group average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: How does the effect vary across pre-specified groups?

outline.title: Average dose-response function
outline.one_liner: If we changed the dose, how would the outcome change?

outline.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
outline.one_liner: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.

outline.title: Positivity / overlap
outline.one_liner: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.

outline.title: SUTVA / no interference
outline.one_liner: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
outline.one_liner: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Randomisation held
outline.one_liner: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.

outline.title: Parallel trends
outline.one_liner: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.

outline.title: No anticipation
outline.one_liner: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Exclusion restriction
outline.one_liner: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.

outline.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
outline.one_liner: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.

outline.title: Instrument relevance
outline.one_liner: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.

outline.title: No manipulation of the running variable
outline.one_liner: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.

outline.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
outline.one_liner: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.

outline.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
outline.one_liner: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.

outline.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
outline.one_liner: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.

outline.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
outline.one_liner: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
outline.one_liner: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Sequential ignorability
outline.one_liner: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.

outline.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
outline.one_liner: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.

outline.title: Adoption pattern
outline.one_liner: A grid of units by period, lit where treatment is on, sorted by when each unit adopted.

outline.title: Augmentation gap
outline.one_liner: The distance between the plain model-based estimate and the version with a correction term added.

outline.title: Goodman-Bacon decomposition
outline.one_liner: Every simple before-and-after comparison hidden inside a single fixed-effects coefficient, and how much weight each one carries.

outline.title: Bandwidth sensitivity path
outline.one_liner: The estimate recomputed using progressively wider and narrower windows around the cutoff.

outline.title: Baseline balance
outline.one_liner: In a randomised design, a check that the arms look alike on characteristics measured before assignment.

outline.title: Bias correction and robust interval
outline.one_liner: Fitting a curve over a window leaves a predictable error at the edge. This shows how much correcting for it moves the estimate and widens the interval.

outline.title: Block structure
outline.one_liner: When randomisation was done separately inside strata -- clinics, schools, waves -- this shows how big each block is and what share of it was treated.

outline.title: Block weights
outline.one_liner: Two ways of combining blocked results give two different numbers, and the difference is a difference in the question, not in the arithmetic.

outline.title: Bootstrap spread
outline.one_liner: The whole estimate recomputed on many resamples of the data, and whether those resamples behaved themselves.

outline.title: CATE calibration
outline.one_liner: Sort units by predicted effect, then check whether the groups you predicted would benefit most actually did.

outline.title: CATE distribution
outline.one_liner: The spread of the per-person effect estimates: how different the model thinks people are.

outline.title: Controlled direct effect across mediator levels
outline.one_liner: The direct effect computed with the mediator held at each of several values. There is one number per value, not one number.

outline.title: Cell means
outline.one_liner: The four averages -- treated and comparison, before and after -- that the headline difference is built from.

outline.title: Coarsened strata and common support
outline.one_liner: How many of the coarsened cells contain both treated and untreated units, and how many treated units had no comparable cell at all.

outline.title: Censoring weights
outline.one_liner: How people who left the study before the end are accounted for.

outline.title: Cluster structure
outline.one_liner: How many groups treatment was assigned to, how big they are, and how much of the sample the largest one holds.

outline.title: Cohort effects
outline.one_liner: One effect per group of units that adopted at the same date, instead of one number for all of them.

outline.title: Cohort-by-period interactions
outline.one_liner: The full set of coefficients, one for each cohort at each distance from its own adoption date, before they are averaged.

outline.title: Comparison group used
outline.one_liner: Which units are standing in for what would have happened without the policy, and how many of them there are.

outline.title: Compliance with assignment
outline.one_liner: How many people in each arm actually took the treatment, and what that implies about who the estimate is about.

outline.title: Complier share
outline.one_liner: An instrument only moves some people. The estimate describes those people, and this says roughly who and how many they are.

outline.title: Constant-effect assumption
outline.one_liner: Some estimators assume the treatment does the same thing to everybody. This says what that assumption buys and what it costs.

outline.title: Covariate balance
outline.one_liner: Run the same estimate on variables the programme cannot have changed. They should show no jump.

outline.title: Differential attrition
outline.one_liner: Whether the treated arm and the control arm lost rows at the same rate on the way from assignment to analysis.

outline.title: Moment balance
outline.one_liner: Whether the weighting actually achieved the balance it was asked for, and how far short it fell.

outline.title: Endogeneity test
outline.one_liner: The plain regression estimate next to the instrumented one, and what their difference does and does not tell you.

outline.title: Effective sample size
outline.one_liner: How many observations the weighted comparison is really worth, and how much of the total weight the single largest unit carries.

outline.title: E-value
outline.one_liner: The smallest strength of association -- with the treatment and with the outcome -- that an unmeasured variable would need to explain away the result.

outline.title: E-value scale
outline.one_liner: The E-value is defined for ratios of risks, so anything measured on another scale has to be converted first -- and the conversion is an approximation.

outline.title: Event study
outline.one_liner: One coefficient per period relative to treatment, with the period before treatment set to zero.

outline.title: Confounder strength needed to explain the estimate
outline.one_liner: Suppose a hidden variable explained everything left unexplained about who was treated. How much of the outcome would it still need to explain?

outline.title: First stage
outline.one_liner: How much the instrument actually moves the treatment, shown as a picture and as an F statistic.

outline.title: Stability across folds
outline.one_liner: The estimate computed within each cross-fitting fold. They should scatter around the overall estimate by roughly its standard error.

outline.title: Honest splitting scheme
outline.one_liner: Confirmation that each tree used one set of rows to decide where the subgroups are and a different set to estimate the effect inside them.

outline.title: Group-time effects
outline.one_liner: One effect for each adoption cohort in each period, which is the building block every modern staggered estimator aggregates.

outline.title: Honest DiD breakdown value
outline.one_liner: Rather than testing whether trends were parallel, this asks how far from parallel they could have been before your conclusion changes.

outline.title: Intra-cluster correlation and design effect
outline.one_liner: How alike people are inside the same cluster, and how many independent observations your rows are really worth once that similarity is counted.

outline.title: Untreated-cell model fit
outline.one_liner: How well the model of untreated behaviour describes the periods where nobody was treated, since everything else is built on it.

outline.title: Influence-function spread
outline.one_liner: Each unit's contribution to the estimate, and how much of the total the largest single contribution is.

outline.title: Residual autocorrelation
outline.one_liner: Whether the residuals of the segmented regression are still correlated over time. If they are, ordinary standard errors are far too small.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Control series at the interruption
outline.one_liner: A second series that the policy did not touch, to see whether the change happened everywhere.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Counterfactual projection
outline.one_liner: The line the series would have followed if the earlier pattern had simply continued, with a band around it.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Model choice
outline.one_liner: Which time-series model was fitted, what it was chosen against, and how close the runners-up were.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Pre-period length
outline.one_liner: How many periods there are before the change, and whether they are enough to establish what was going to happen anyway.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Seasonality
outline.one_liner: Whether a repeating annual or weekly cycle remains in the series after the model has done its work.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: The series and the interruption
outline.one_liner: The outcome plotted over time with a line at the date of the change. Read this before anything else.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Leave one unit out
outline.one_liner: Drop one unit -- or one cluster, or one donor -- at a time, refit, and see how far the estimate travels.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Level jump at a kink
outline.one_liner: A kink design assumes the rule changes the slope and not the level. This fits a step at the same threshold to check.

outline.title: Linearity of the outcome model
outline.one_liner: Whether the answer is being read off the data or produced by the shape the model was told to assume.

outline.title: Covariate balance (Love plot)
outline.one_liner: Absolute standardised differences for every covariate, before and after adjustment, on one axis.

outline.title: Density at the cutoff
outline.one_liner: Count how many units sit just below the threshold and just above it. A cliff between the two means somebody was steering.

outline.title: Total = direct + indirect
outline.one_liner: The total effect split into the part that runs through the mediator and the part that does not.

outline.title: Plug-in bias of the meta-learner
outline.one_liner: Averaging a machine-learning model's per-person predictions gives a different number from the headline estimate, and the headline is the one with an honest interval.

outline.title: How much the model is doing
outline.one_liner: A reminder that outcome regression extrapolates silently wherever the groups do not overlap.

outline.title: Multiple mediators
outline.one_liner: With more than one mediator, the separate pathway effects do not add up to the total, and the shortfall is meaningful.

outline.title: Match quality
outline.one_liner: How many treated units found a partner, how many comparison units were used, and how often the same one was reused.

outline.title: Natural-course calibration
outline.one_liner: Simulate the world as it actually was and check that the simulation reproduces the data it was built from.

outline.title: Negative control
outline.one_liner: An outcome the treatment cannot possibly have affected. Any effect found there is a measurement of your own bias.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Nuisance models by fold
outline.one_liner: How well the treatment and outcome models predicted on data they did not see, fold by fold.

outline.title: Oster's assumptions
outline.one_liner: The two assumptions behind the delta figure, stated plainly, because the number is meaningless without them.

outline.title: Oster delta
outline.one_liner: How much more important the things you did not measure would have to be than the things you did, to explain the result away.

outline.title: Outcome distribution
outline.one_liner: The shape of the outcome in each arm, before any model is fitted.

outline.title: Overidentification test
outline.one_liner: With more instruments than endogenous regressors, a check that they agree with each other.

outline.title: Overlap between the arms
outline.one_liner: The distribution of the estimated probability of treatment, drawn separately for the treated and the untreated. Where they do not overlap, there is no comparison to make.

outline.title: Matched-pair quality
outline.one_liner: How the matched pairs behind a sensitivity analysis were formed, and whether they are the same pairs the headline estimate used.

outline.title: Panel balance
outline.one_liner: Whether the same units are present in every period, and when the ones that come and go do so.

outline.title: Randomisation distribution
outline.one_liner: Reshuffle the treatment labels the way the study actually assigned them, thousands of times, and see how unusual the real result looks.

outline.title: Person-time and switching
outline.one_liner: How many people, over how many periods, following how many distinct treatment histories.

outline.title: Placebo outcome
outline.one_liner: Run the same analysis on an outcome the treatment should not move. Finding an effect means the design manufactures them.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Placebo reduced form
outline.one_liner: Check whether the instrument moves outcomes it has no business moving.

outline.title: Placebo treatment
outline.one_liner: Pretend the treatment happened to someone else, or at a date when nothing happened, and see whether the method still finds an effect.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Honest policy value
outline.one_liner: How much better off you would be following the model's recommendation about who to treat, valued on data the model never saw.

outline.title: Positivity by period
outline.one_liner: Whether, at every time point, people of every kind had a real chance of both receiving and not receiving the treatment.

outline.title: Size of the pre-trend
outline.one_liner: The size of the movements in the pre-treatment period, which is the yardstick the robustness bounds are measured against.

outline.title: Pre-trend test
outline.one_liner: A joint test that the pre-treatment coefficients are all zero. Useful, and much weaker evidence than it looks.

outline.title: Probe runs
outline.one_liner: How many of the re-runs a probe needed actually produced a number, and why the rest stopped.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Propensity clipping
outline.one_liner: How many units had an estimated chance of treatment so close to zero or one that the analysis had to trim it back before dividing by it.

outline.title: Treatment-model calibration
outline.one_liner: Within bands of predicted treatment probability, does the share actually treated match the prediction?

outline.title: Random common cause
outline.one_liner: Add a variable that is pure noise to the adjustment set. A well-behaved estimate should not move.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Rank-weighted average treatment effect
outline.one_liner: A single number for how much better you would do by treating people in the order the model recommends, rather than at random.

outline.title: Raw means by cohort and period
outline.one_liner: The average outcome for each group in each period, before any model is fitted.

outline.title: Binned scatter at the cutoff
outline.one_liner: Average outcomes in narrow bands of the score, either side of the threshold, with the fitted curve drawn through them.

outline.title: Reduced form
outline.one_liner: The direct relationship between the instrument and the outcome, before any division. It is the part of the design that rests on the least.

outline.title: Support for the intervention regime
outline.one_liner: How many people actually followed the treatment strategy you are asking about.

outline.title: Robustness value
outline.one_liner: A single number for how strongly an unmeasured variable would have to be related to both the treatment and the outcome to explain the result away.

outline.title: Rosenbaum bounds
outline.one_liner: For matched pairs: how unequal two apparently identical units' chances of treatment would have to be before the conclusion stops holding.

outline.title: Discreteness of the running variable
outline.one_liner: How many distinct values the score actually takes close to the threshold. A handful means this is a comparison of a few groups.

outline.title: Size of the augmentation correction
outline.one_liner: How far the correction for imperfect pre-treatment fit moved the answer.

outline.title: Treated unit inside the donor hull
outline.one_liner: Whether any blend of the comparison places could actually reproduce the treated place, or whether it sits outside their range entirely.

outline.title: Treated minus synthetic gap
outline.one_liner: The distance between the treated place and its synthetic twin, period by period. After the intervention, that distance is the estimate.

outline.title: Leave one donor out
outline.one_liner: Drop each contributing comparison place in turn and refit. The estimate should not depend on any single one.

outline.title: Matrix-completion rank
outline.one_liner: How flexible the fitted model of untreated behaviour was allowed to be.

outline.title: Placebo in space
outline.one_liner: Re-run the whole method pretending each comparison place was the treated one. If many of them show a gap as large, the real one is unremarkable.

outline.title: Placebo in time
outline.one_liner: Move the intervention to an earlier date when nothing happened, refit on the earlier data only, and see whether the method finds an effect anyway.

outline.title: Pre-treatment fit
outline.one_liner: How closely the weighted combination of comparison places tracked the treated place before the intervention. This is the whole basis of the method.

outline.title: Time weights
outline.one_liner: Which pre-treatment periods the fit was asked to match most closely.

outline.title: Donor weights
outline.one_liner: Which comparison places make up the synthetic twin, and how much of it each one is.

outline.title: Stability across seeds
outline.one_liner: Repeat the whole procedure with different random splits and see whether the answer stays put.

outline.title: Specification curve
outline.one_liner: Every defensible version of this analysis, sorted from smallest estimate to largest, with the one on your board marked.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Treatment strategies compared
outline.one_liner: The simulated outcome path under each strategy being compared, so you can see when and how they diverge.

outline.title: Pre-specified subgroups
outline.one_liner: Effects estimated inside named groups, with a reminder of how easily one of them looks impressive by chance.

outline.title: Stability on random subsets
outline.one_liner: Refit the analysis on random parts of the data and see whether the answer stays put.
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Temporal ordering of covariates
outline.one_liner: A check that every variable used to adjust a decision was measured before that decision was taken.

outline.title: Targeting step
outline.one_liner: How far the final correction moved the estimate away from the plain outcome model's answer, and whether the correction converged.

outline.title: Treatment-mediator interaction
outline.one_liner: Whether the mediator does the same work whether or not the treatment is on.

outline.title: What trimming costs
outline.one_liner: How many units a proposed trimming rule would drop, and who they are.

outline.title: Stability across trimming thresholds
outline.one_liner: The estimate recomputed at a range of trimming thresholds, so you can see whether the units in the tails are deciding it.

outline.title: Simulated unobserved confounder
outline.one_liner: Nobody can prove there is no missing common cause. This asks the answerable question instead: how strong would one have to be to overturn the finding?
tags: A shock in a single series

outline.title: Weak-instrument-robust set
outline.one_liner: A confidence set built by inverting a test that stays valid however weak the instrument is. It can be an interval, several intervals, or the whole line.

outline.title: Balance after weighting
outline.one_liner: Whether, after weighting, the treated and untreated person-periods look alike on the variables the weights were built from.

outline.title: Weights by period
outline.one_liner: How much of the sample survives, in effective terms, as the weights accumulate across periods.

outline.title: About Causal Capybara
outline.one_liner: A desktop studio for applied causal inference. Serious causal inference, casual to use.

outline.title: Caliper
outline.one_liner: The largest difference you are willing to tolerate inside a matched pair. Beyond it the treated unit is left unmatched rather than paired with somebody unlike them.

outline.title: Cluster-robust standard errors
outline.one_liner: A way of computing uncertainty that treats each group -- a school, a village, a clinic -- as one group's worth of independent evidence, rather than counting every row inside it separately.

outline.title: Clustering
outline.one_liner: When treatment was assigned to whole groups -- states, schools, clinics -- the number of independent observations is closer to the number of groups than the number of rows.

outline.title: Colliders and why adjusting can hurt
outline.one_liner: A variable that two arrows point into. Conditioning on it creates an association between its causes that was not there before.

outline.title: Complete-case analysis
outline.one_liner: Dropping every row that is missing any value the analysis needs and computing on what is left. Most software does this silently.

outline.title: Confounding
outline.one_liner: A common cause of both the treatment and the outcome makes the two look related even when the treatment does nothing.

outline.title: The sample flow
outline.one_liner: A step-by-step record of how the imported rows became the analysis sample, with a reason for every row that left.

outline.title: Cross-fitting
outline.one_liner: Fit the nuisance models on one part of the data and apply them to another, so a flexible learner cannot fit its own noise into the effect estimate.

outline.title: Cross-world assumptions
outline.one_liner: A condition relating outcomes under treatment and mediator values that no single person could ever experience together. Not testable, even in principle.

outline.title: The donor pool
outline.one_liner: The set of untreated places a synthetic comparison is allowed to be built from. Choosing it is a research decision, not a technical one.

outline.title: Effective sample size
outline.one_liner: How many observations your weighted comparison is really worth. Almost always smaller than the number of rows, sometimes dramatically.

outline.title: Estimand first, estimator second
outline.one_liner: Decide what number you want before deciding how to compute it. The estimator does not define the question; the question restricts the estimators.

outline.title: The forest plot, and why there is no headline number
outline.one_liner: One row per method, each with its interval. When several methods ran, the forest is the result -- not a single number chosen from it.

outline.title: Honest splitting
outline.one_liner: Use one half of the data to decide where the subgroups are and the other half to estimate their effects.

outline.title: Subgroups and multiplicity
outline.one_liner: Look at enough subgroups and one will look impressive. Pre-specify them, or report that you did not.

outline.title: Negative controls
outline.one_liner: A variable that shares your suspected confounding but cannot be affected by the treatment. An effect there is a measurement of your bias.

outline.title: Not-yet-treated comparisons
outline.one_liner: Units that do adopt the policy, but later. While they are still waiting they can serve as the comparison group for units that adopted earlier.

outline.title: Placebo tests
outline.one_liner: Run the same analysis somewhere the effect cannot exist. If you find one, the design is producing effects that are not there.

outline.title: Provisional results
outline.one_liner: A result the product does not think you should trust as it stands. It still computed it; it just will not let the flag disappear.

outline.title: Selection bias
outline.one_liner: Who ends up in your analysis sample can create an association all by itself, quite apart from confounding.

outline.title: Specification curve
outline.one_liner: Every defensible version of the analysis, sorted by estimate, so you can see the whole distribution instead of one draw from it.

outline.title: Staggered adoption
outline.one_liner: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.

outline.title: Standardised mean difference
outline.one_liner: The gap between groups on a covariate, divided by a pooled standard deviation, so covariates on different scales can be compared on one axis.

outline.title: The target trial
outline.one_liner: Write down the randomised experiment you would run if you could, then ask what your data lets you emulate.

outline.title: Time-varying confounding
outline.one_liner: A variable that is both a consequence of past treatment and a cause of future treatment. Ordinary regression cannot handle it; g-methods can.

outline.title: Two-way fixed effects
outline.one_liner: A regression that gives every unit its own baseline level and every period its own shift, so only change within a unit over time is compared. It is the workhorse behind difference-in-differences, and it misbehaves when units adopt at different dates.

outline.title: Bad controls
outline.one_liner: Anything measured after treatment, or caused by it, does not belong in the adjustment set. Adjusting for it blocks part of the effect you are trying to measure.

design:rct.title: Randomised or as-if randomised
design:rct.one_liner: People were assigned by chance, or as good as chance.
design:rct.plain_language: Assignment was by chance, so the arms are comparable on everything -- including the things nobody measured. That is the whole reason experiments are the benchmark.
design:rct.in_more_depth: What randomisation buys you is exchangeability for free. What it does not buy you is everything afterwards: people drop out, refuse the treatment, or take it when they were not offered it, and each of those can undo the comparison. So the questions this design asks are about implementation. Was assignment really random, or did someone with discretion do it? Did whole clusters get assigned together, in which case the number of independent observations is the number of clusters? Did everyone offered the programme take it, and if not, is the number you want the effect of the offer or the effect on the people it moved? Covariates are for precision here, not identification. Adjust for the ones you named before seeing the data.
design:rct.how_the_board_reads: Put the column that says who was offered the programme in Assignment, and what it was meant to change in Outcome. Blocks and clusters describe how the assignment was actually done, so they are facts about the study rather than choices you make here.

what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

assumption_notes: Randomisation held, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison
SUTVA -- one unit's assignment does not change another's outcome
Consistency -- the treatment is one well-defined thing

estimands.title: Average treatment effect
estimands.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?

estimands.title: Average treatment effect on the treated
estimands.one_liner: For people who actually got it, what did it do?

estimands.title: Intention to treat
estimands.one_liner: For everyone who was offered it, what did the offer do?

estimands.title: Complier average causal effect
estimands.one_liner: For the people who comply with what they were offered, what did it do?

estimands.title: Local average treatment effect
estimands.one_liner: For people who only got it because of the instrument or the cutoff, what did it do?

estimands.title: Conditional average treatment effect
estimands.one_liner: How does the effect vary from person to person, or place to place?

estimands.title: Group average treatment effect
estimands.one_liner: How does the effect vary across pre-specified groups?

default_estimand.title: Average treatment effect
default_estimand.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?

methods.title: Manski bounds
methods.one_liner: Report the range the effect must lie in given only what the data can support, without assuming away the missing counterfactual.

methods.title: Interference and spillovers
methods.one_liner: When one unit's treatment affects another's outcome, estimate the direct and spillover effects separately instead of pretending neither exists.

methods.title: ITT and CACE (noncompliance)
methods.one_liner: Not everyone offered a programme takes it. Report what the offer did, and separately what taking it up did for the people it moved.

methods.title: Cluster-randomised trial
methods.one_liner: When whole schools, clinics or villages were assigned, the number of clusters is the sample size that matters.

methods.title: Difference in means
methods.one_liner: Compare the two arms as they were randomised, and let covariates sharpen the comparison without letting them change the question.

methods.title: Randomisation (Fisher) inference
methods.one_liner: Re-run the randomisation thousands of times with the outcomes held fixed, and see how unusual what actually happened really is.

methods.title: Blocked or stratified experiment
methods.one_liner: Estimate inside the blocks the randomisation was run in, then average them the way your estimand says to.

methods.title: Transportability and generalisability
methods.one_liner: Take an effect estimated in one population and ask what it would be in another with a different mix of characteristics.

probes.title: Unobserved confounder
probes.one_liner: Simulate a common cause of a stated strength and watch the estimate move; read off how strong one would have to be to explain the result away.

probes.title: Specification curve
probes.one_liner: Run the grid of defensible specifications and sort the answers. The curve is the result, not the one you happened to run.

probes.title: Leave one out
probes.one_liner: Drop one cluster, cohort or donor at a time and see whether any single one is carrying the result.

probes.title: Negative control
probes.one_liner: Estimate something that shares the confounding but not the causal path. A non-zero answer is bias you can see.

probes.title: Placebo outcome
probes.one_liner: Run the same analysis on something the treatment could not have changed. It should find nothing.

probes.title: Placebo treatment
probes.one_liner: Move the policy date earlier, reshuffle who was treated, or swap in a variable that cannot cause the outcome.

probes.title: Random common cause
probes.one_liner: Add a variable that causes nothing to the adjustment set. The estimate should barely move.

probes.title: Subset stability
probes.one_liner: Re-estimate on random subsets. The answer should move about as much as losing that much data costs, and no more.

design:rct.common_mistake: Reporting the complier effect as the policy effect. A policy can offer a programme; it cannot make people take it.

design:observational.title: Adjust for background differences
design:observational.one_liner: Treatment was not random; we can measure the things that made people get it.
design:observational.plain_language: Treatment was not random, but you believe you measured the things that decided who got it. Everything then rests on that belief.
design:observational.in_more_depth: This is the workhorse and the hardest design to defend. The estimate is only as good as the adjustment set, and no diagnostic can tell you whether the set is complete -- balance plots only speak about the variables in it. Two things you can do. First, look at overlap: where the treated and untreated groups do not resemble each other at all, no method compares anything, it extrapolates. Second, ask the sensitivity question: how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be, relative to the ones you did measure, to overturn the finding? Be careful about what goes into the adjustment set. Variables measured after treatment, or caused by it, make things worse rather than better.
design:observational.how_the_board_reads: Every column you put in "measured confounders" is a claim that it was recorded before treatment was decided. Anything measured afterwards belongs in the box below it instead.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

assumption_notes: Exchangeability given the measured confounders -- untestable
Positivity -- visible in the overlap plot

methods.title: Manski bounds
methods.one_liner: Report the range the effect must lie in given only what the data can support, without assuming away the missing counterfactual.

methods.title: Structure learning (causal discovery)
methods.one_liner: Search for a graph consistent with the data. It does not recover the true causal structure from observational data without extra assumptions.

methods.title: Interference and spillovers
methods.one_liner: When one unit's treatment affects another's outcome, estimate the direct and spillover effects separately instead of pretending neither exists.

methods.title: Honest causal forest
methods.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

methods.title: Double ML (interactive)
methods.one_liner: A separate outcome model for each arm plus a treatment model, combined in a doubly robust score: right if either side is right.

methods.title: Double ML (partially linear)
methods.one_liner: Predict the outcome and the treatment from the confounders, then regress what is left of one on what is left of the other.

methods.title: Meta-learner (T, S, X, DR)
methods.one_liner: Build the per-unit effect out of ordinary prediction models, four different ways, on the same cross-fitting.

methods.title: Policy tree (who should be treated)
methods.one_liner: Learn a short, readable rule for who to treat, then value that rule on data it never saw.

methods.title: Doubly robust (AIPW)
methods.one_liner: Use a treatment model and an outcome model together; it is right if either one is.

methods.title: Coarsened exact matching
methods.one_liner: Bin the covariates, then compare only inside bins that contain both arms.

methods.title: Genetic matching
methods.one_liner: Search over distance-metric weights until balance is as good as it can get, instead of trusting one metric.

methods.title: Nearest-neighbour matching
methods.one_liner: Pair each treated unit with the most similar untreated unit, then compare within pairs.

methods.title: Optimal and full matching
methods.one_liner: Choose the whole set of matches at once to minimise total distance, rather than greedily one treated unit at a time.

methods.title: Multiple imputation compatible with the analysis
methods.one_liner: Impute the missing values several times, run the analysis in each, and combine -- instead of dropping every row with a gap.

methods.title: Outcome regression (g-computation)
methods.one_liner: Model the outcome, then ask what would have happened if everyone had been treated, and if nobody had.

methods.title: Super Learner nuisance models
methods.one_liner: Combine several candidate learners by cross-validated weights instead of betting on one.

methods.title: Targeted maximum likelihood (TMLE)
methods.one_liner: Fit the outcome model, then nudge it once in the direction the treatment model says it is wrong.

methods.title: Covariate balancing propensity score
methods.one_liner: Fit the treatment model so that it balances covariates, rather than fitting it to predict treatment and hoping balance follows.

methods.title: Entropy balancing
methods.one_liner: Find the weights closest to equal that make the covariate means match exactly.

methods.title: Propensity weighting
methods.one_liner: Reweight the sample so the treated and untreated groups look alike on the measured confounders.

methods.title: Boosted propensity scores (twang)
methods.one_liner: Grow a boosted model for the propensity score, stopping at the iteration that balances covariates best.

methods.title: Transportability and generalisability
methods.one_liner: Take an effect estimated in one population and ask what it would be in another with a different mix of characteristics.

probes.title: Unobserved confounder
probes.one_liner: Simulate a common cause of a stated strength and watch the estimate move; read off how strong one would have to be to explain the result away.

probes.title: Specification curve
probes.one_liner: Run the grid of defensible specifications and sort the answers. The curve is the result, not the one you happened to run.

probes.title: Cinelli-Hazlett sensitivity (partial R2)
probes.one_liner: How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be -- compared with the covariates you already have -- to explain the estimate away?

probes.title: E-value
probes.one_liner: The smallest confounder-treatment and confounder-outcome association that could explain the result away.

probes.title: Leave one out
probes.one_liner: Drop one cluster, cohort or donor at a time and see whether any single one is carrying the result.

probes.title: Negative control
probes.one_liner: Estimate something that shares the confounding but not the causal path. A non-zero answer is bias you can see.

probes.title: Oster coefficient stability
probes.one_liner: How important would unobserved variables have to be, relative to the controls you already have, to drive the coefficient to zero?

probes.title: Placebo outcome
probes.one_liner: Run the same analysis on something the treatment could not have changed. It should find nothing.

probes.title: Placebo treatment
probes.one_liner: Move the policy date earlier, reshuffle who was treated, or swap in a variable that cannot cause the outcome.

probes.title: Random common cause
probes.one_liner: Add a variable that causes nothing to the adjustment set. The estimate should barely move.

probes.title: Rosenbaum bounds
probes.one_liner: How unequal could the odds of treatment be inside a matched pair before the conclusion stopped being clear?

probes.title: Subset stability
probes.one_liner: Re-estimate on random subsets. The answer should move about as much as losing that much data costs, and no more.

probes.title: Trimming curve
probes.one_liner: Re-estimate across a grid of propensity-score trimming thresholds instead of picking one and hoping.

diagnostics.title: Confounder strength needed to explain the estimate
How much the model is doing

design:observational.common_mistake: Adding every available variable to the adjustment set. Post-treatment variables and colliders introduce bias that was not there before.
references: Hernán & Robins (2020)
Imbens & Rubin (2015)

see_also.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
see_also.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
see_also.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

see_also.title: Positivity / overlap
see_also.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
see_also.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

see_also.title: Bad controls
see_also.one_liner: Anything measured after treatment, or caused by it, does not belong in the adjustment set. Adjusting for it blocks part of the effect you are trying to measure.

see_also.title: Average treatment effect on the treated
see_also.one_liner: For people who actually got it, what did it do?

see_also.title: Average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?

see_also.title: Average treatment effect on the controls
see_also.one_liner: For people who didn't get it, what would it have done?

see_also.title: Average treatment effect on the overlap population
see_also.one_liner: For the people where treated and untreated genuinely overlap, what did it do?

see_also.title: Conditional average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: How does the effect vary from person to person, or place to place?

see_also.title: Group average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: How does the effect vary across pre-specified groups?

see_also.title: Average dose-response function
see_also.one_liner: If we changed the dose, how would the outcome change?

see_also.title: Manski bounds
see_also.one_liner: Report the range the effect must lie in given only what the data can support, without assuming away the missing counterfactual.

see_also.title: Structure learning (causal discovery)
see_also.one_liner: Search for a graph consistent with the data. It does not recover the true causal structure from observational data without extra assumptions.

see_also.title: Interference and spillovers
see_also.one_liner: When one unit's treatment affects another's outcome, estimate the direct and spillover effects separately instead of pretending neither exists.

see_also.title: Honest causal forest
see_also.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

design:did.title: Policy rolled out over time
design:did.one_liner: Some places or groups got it earlier than others.
design:did.plain_language: Some units were treated and others were not, and you observe both before and after. The comparison is of changes, not levels.
design:did.in_more_depth: Comparing changes removes anything about a unit that is fixed over time -- you do not need to measure it, only to believe it is stable. That is a real gain, and it is bought with a different assumption: that without the policy the two groups would have moved the same way. When everyone adopts at the same date, this is a clean 2x2. When they adopt at different dates, two-way fixed effects stops estimating what you want: it averages comparisons that include already-treated units acting as controls, with weights that can go negative. The modern estimators fix that by only ever comparing a newly treated cohort with units not yet treated. Clustering matters here more than almost anywhere. Standard errors should be clustered at the level treatment was assigned.
design:did.how_the_board_reads: Rows are units, columns are periods. The cells light up when treatment turns on.

what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

assumption_notes: Parallel trends -- untestable, but the pre-period is evidence
No anticipation before treatment arrives
SUTVA -- treated units do not spill over onto controls

methods.one_liner: Learn what untreated life looks like from untreated cells only, then ask how far each treated cell landed from it.

methods.title: Callaway & Sant'Anna group-time effects
methods.one_liner: Estimate one clean before-and-after for every adoption cohort, then say out loud how you averaged them.

methods.title: de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille
methods.one_liner: An estimator built for panels where treatment switches on and off, which the imputation and cohort estimators assume never happens.

methods.title: Doubly robust DiD
methods.one_liner: One before-and-after with covariates, using an outcome model and a comparison-group model together so either one can carry it.

methods.title: Event study (leads and lags)
methods.one_liner: Plot the effect period by period around adoption, so you can see whether the gap opened when the policy arrived or long before it.

methods.title: Two-stage DiD (Gardner / Wooldridge-Mundlak)
methods.one_liner: Strip out unit and period effects using untreated cells only, then regress what is left on the policy.

methods.title: Goodman-Bacon decomposition
methods.one_liner: Open up a two-way fixed effects estimate and show every two-group comparison inside it, with the weight each one carries -- including the ones that use already-treated units as controls.

methods.title: Matched difference-in-differences
methods.one_liner: Match treated to comparison units on pre-period characteristics first, then difference.

methods.title: Sun & Abraham event study
methods.one_liner: Give every cohort its own event-study path, then average the paths by cohort size instead of letting the regression choose the weights.

methods.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences (synthdid)
methods.one_liner: Weight both units and periods, then take a difference-in-differences -- halfway between synthetic control and DiD.

methods.title: Triple differences
methods.one_liner: Compare the treated-versus-comparison difference for the group the policy could reach with the same difference for a group inside the same units that it could not.

methods.title: Two-way fixed effects
methods.one_liner: One regression with unit and period fixed effects. Familiar, fast, and not an average treatment effect when units adopt at different dates.

methods.title: Difference-in-differences (2x2)
methods.one_liner: Two groups, two periods: compare how much the treated group changed with how much the comparison group changed over the same window.

methods.title: Matrix completion
methods.one_liner: Treat the missing treated-period outcomes as holes in a panel and fill them in with a low-rank model of what the panel would have done.

methods.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences
methods.one_liner: Weight the comparison units and the pre-treatment periods, then run a difference in differences on the result - a level gap is allowed, a trend gap is not.

design:rd.title: A cutoff decided eligibility
design:rd.one_liner: Crossing a score, age, or border switched the programme on.
design:rd.plain_language: A rule assigned treatment on one side of a threshold. Right at the threshold, which side you land on is as good as random.
design:rd.in_more_depth: The credibility of this design is local and its estimate is local with it. You learn about units at the cutoff and nobody else, which is exactly right if the policy question is about moving the threshold, and a poor fit if it is about the programme overall. Two things can break it. If people could control their score precisely, they sorted across the line and the comparison is not as-good-as-random -- the density test looks for that. If the same threshold triggers other rules, the jump combines them and nothing separates them. The binned scatter is the design. If you cannot see the discontinuity, be suspicious of an estimator that reports one.
design:rd.how_the_board_reads: Type the threshold into the Cutoff box. The binned scatter appears before any estimator does.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

design:iv.title: Something else pushed people in
design:iv.one_liner: An instrument or encouragement changed treatment, not the outcome directly.
design:iv.plain_language: An instrument moved treatment without touching the outcome any other way. You learn the effect for the people it moved.
design:iv.in_more_depth: The instrument does the work randomisation would have done, but only for part of the population: the compliers, whose treatment status the instrument actually changed. It says nothing about people who would have been treated regardless, or never. The arrow you did not draw -- from instrument straight to outcome -- is the exclusion restriction, and it cannot be tested. A strong first stage tells you the instrument moves treatment; it is silent about other routes. Weak instruments are the practical trap. Below an effective F of about ten, the usual interval is not trustworthy and a weak-instrument-robust set is the honest report, even when it is unbounded.
design:iv.how_the_board_reads: The arrow from the instrument straight to the outcome is missing on purpose. That missing arrow is the exclusion restriction, and it is an assumption you are making.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

assumption_notes: Relevance -- testable, and the effective F is the number to read
Exclusion -- untestable
