what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

when_to_use: The question every trial faces: the effect was measured on volunteers in eight sites, and the policy is national.
when_not_to_use: Requires that the effect modifiers are measured in both populations and that the target population overlaps the study one. Where it does not, the transported estimate is extrapolation with extra steps.

probes.title: Subset stability
probes.one_liner: Re-estimate on random subsets. The answer should move about as much as losing that much data costs, and no more.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull

what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding

when_not_to_use: The confounder is simulated. The grid says how strong one would have to be, never whether one exists, and the answer depends on the shape assumed for it.

what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_to_use: It replaces the appendix table nobody reads with the picture that actually settles the argument: every defensible choice, sorted.
when_not_to_use: A grid chosen after seeing the answers is not a specification curve. Decide the grid first, and include the specifications you would not have chosen.

what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_to_use: Panel and synthetic-control results are often one unit's story. This is the check that finds out, and it reads as a forest anyone can follow.
when_not_to_use: With many small groups the probe drops almost nothing and always looks stable. The group has to be the level treatment was assigned at.
Individually randomised data with no clustering, where each group is one row

when_to_use: Coefficient stability gets claimed informally in almost every paper; this at least makes the claim quantitative and shows what it depends on.
when_not_to_use: Proportional selection is a strong and unverifiable assumption, and R_max is assumed rather than estimated. The bound moves a long way with both, which is why they are plotted together rather than reported as one number.

what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_to_use: The cheapest honest test there is: if the design finds an effect where none can exist, it will find one where none exists on the real outcome too.
when_not_to_use: A placebo that is not really a placebo. Anything the treatment can touch, however indirectly, makes a non-null result uninterpretable.

when_not_to_use: Shifting the date needs real pre-periods; with two periods there is nowhere to move it to. Permutation asks whether the labelling matters, not whether the design is confounded.

what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_to_use: A quick stability check on the adjustment: an estimate that moves when noise is added is fitting the sample.
when_not_to_use: It is a weak test. Passing it says nothing about unmeasured confounding, because the added variable is not a confounder -- it is noise.

what_it_assumes.title: Randomisation held
what_it_assumes.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

what_it_assumes.title: SUTVA / no interference
what_it_assumes.explains: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.

what_it_assumes.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
what_it_assumes.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

what_it_assumes.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

what_it_assumes.title: Positivity / overlap
what_it_assumes.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

what_it_assumes.title: Parallel trends
what_it_assumes.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

what_it_assumes.title: No anticipation
what_it_assumes.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

what_it_assumes.title: No manipulation of the running variable
what_it_assumes.explains: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

what_it_assumes.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
what_it_assumes.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

what_it_assumes.title: Instrument relevance
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

what_it_assumes.title: Exclusion restriction
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

what_it_assumes.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
what_it_assumes.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

what_it_assumes.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
what_it_assumes.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

what_it_assumes.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
what_it_assumes.explains: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: The treated unit is at an extreme of the donor distribution on the predictors, or the pre-period gap has a persistent level offset.

what_it_assumes.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
what_it_assumes.explains: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

what_it_assumes.title: Functional form of the counterfactual trend
what_it_assumes.explains: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Few pre-period points; residual autocorrelation that survives the model; the estimate flips when you add a seasonal term or a quadratic trend.

what_it_assumes.title: Sequential ignorability
what_it_assumes.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

what_it_assumes.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
what_it_assumes.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
what_it_assumes.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

when_to_use: It separates an answer that lives in the population from one that lives in a handful of rows, and it works for every method.
when_not_to_use: Some spread is precision, not fragility: dropping a fifth of the data widens the interval by about a tenth. The probe reports the expected spread alongside the observed one for exactly that reason.

when_to_use: Trimming is normally a silent default. This makes it a visible choice, shows what it costs in sample, and marks the variance-minimising threshold rather than inventing a universal one.

estimand:ATE.title: Average treatment effect
estimand:ATE.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?
estimand:ATE.plain_language: If everyone in the population had been treated, compared with nobody being treated, how would the average outcome differ?
estimand:ATE.in_more_depth: The most natural quantity and often the hardest to identify. It requires the comparison to be credible for every kind of unit, including those who would never realistically be treated, so it leans hardest on overlap. Where the treated and untreated groups barely resemble each other, the ATE is estimated partly by extrapolation, and an effect on the overlap population may be the more honest target.
estimand:ATE.common_mistake: Reporting an ATE from a design that only identifies the effect for the treated, or for compliers.

methods.title: Interference and spillovers
methods.one_liner: When one unit's treatment affects another's outcome, estimate the direct and spillover effects separately instead of pretending neither exists.

methods.title: Two-stage least squares
methods.one_liner: Use only the part of the treatment that the instrument moved, and see what happened to the outcome.

methods.title: Two-step GMM
methods.one_liner: Weight the instruments by how informative each one actually is, using a weight matrix estimated from the data.

methods.title: LIML (and Fuller)
methods.one_liner: The maximum-likelihood cousin of two-stage least squares, which stays much better behaved when the instruments are weak.

methods.title: Marginal treatment effects
methods.one_liner: Trace the effect as a function of how reluctant a unit is to be treated, instead of reporting one local average.

methods.title: Shift-share (Bartik) instruments
methods.one_liner: Combine national shocks with local exposure shares to build an instrument for local changes.

methods.title: G-estimation of structural nested models
methods.one_liner: Estimate the effect of a treatment regime by finding the parameter that removes the association between treatment and the blipped-down outcome.

methods.title: Parametric g-formula
methods.one_liner: Model each period in turn, then simulate the world where everyone followed the strategy you name.

methods.title: Longitudinal modified treatment policies (lmtp)
methods.one_liner: Estimate the effect of shifting a continuous or multi-valued treatment, rather than of setting everyone to one value.

methods.title: Sequential doubly robust (ICE g-formula with augmentation)
methods.one_liner: Regress backwards from the final outcome, then correct with the treatment probabilities: right if either set of models is right.

methods.title: Longitudinal TMLE for survival outcomes
methods.one_liner: Time-to-event outcomes with time-varying treatment and censoring, targeted at each time.

methods.title: Marginal structural model (time-varying weights)
methods.one_liner: Reweight each person-period so the treated and untreated histories look alike, then fit one simple model to the reweighted data.

methods.title: Interventional direct and indirect effects
methods.one_liner: Shift the mediator to the distribution it would have in the population, rather than to each person's own unobservable counterfactual.

methods.title: Natural direct and indirect effects
methods.one_liner: Split the total effect into the part that travelled through the mediator and the part that did not.

methods.title: Honest causal forest
methods.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

methods.title: Double ML (interactive)
methods.one_liner: A separate outcome model for each arm plus a treatment model, combined in a doubly robust score: right if either side is right.

methods.title: Double ML (partially linear)
methods.one_liner: Predict the outcome and the treatment from the confounders, then regress what is left of one on what is left of the other.

methods.title: Meta-learner (T, S, X, DR)
methods.one_liner: Build the per-unit effect out of ordinary prediction models, four different ways, on the same cross-fitting.

methods.title: Doubly robust (AIPW)
methods.one_liner: Use a treatment model and an outcome model together; it is right if either one is.

methods.title: Coarsened exact matching
methods.one_liner: Bin the covariates, then compare only inside bins that contain both arms.

methods.title: Genetic matching
methods.one_liner: Search over distance-metric weights until balance is as good as it can get, instead of trusting one metric.

methods.title: Optimal and full matching
methods.one_liner: Choose the whole set of matches at once to minimise total distance, rather than greedily one treated unit at a time.

methods.title: Multiple imputation compatible with the analysis
methods.one_liner: Impute the missing values several times, run the analysis in each, and combine -- instead of dropping every row with a gap.

methods.title: Outcome regression (g-computation)
methods.one_liner: Model the outcome, then ask what would have happened if everyone had been treated, and if nobody had.

methods.title: Super Learner nuisance models
methods.one_liner: Combine several candidate learners by cross-validated weights instead of betting on one.

methods.title: Targeted maximum likelihood (TMLE)
methods.one_liner: Fit the outcome model, then nudge it once in the direction the treatment model says it is wrong.

methods.title: Covariate balancing propensity score
methods.one_liner: Fit the treatment model so that it balances covariates, rather than fitting it to predict treatment and hoping balance follows.

methods.title: Propensity weighting
methods.one_liner: Reweight the sample so the treated and untreated groups look alike on the measured confounders.

methods.title: Boosted propensity scores (twang)
methods.one_liner: Grow a boosted model for the propensity score, stopping at the iteration that balances covariates best.

methods.title: Cluster-randomised trial
methods.one_liner: When whole schools, clinics or villages were assigned, the number of clusters is the sample size that matters.

methods.title: Difference in means

methods.one_liner: Re-run the randomisation thousands of times with the outcomes held fixed, and see how unusual what actually happened really is.

methods.title: Blocked or stratified experiment
methods.one_liner: Estimate inside the blocks the randomisation was run in, then average them the way your estimand says to.

methods.title: Local randomisation RD
methods.one_liner: Treat a narrow window around the cutoff as a small randomised experiment rather than fitting a curve through it.

methods.title: Transportability and generalisability
methods.one_liner: Take an effect estimated in one population and ask what it would be in another with a different mix of characteristics.

estimand:ATT.title: Average treatment effect on the treated
estimand:ATT.one_liner: For people who actually got it, what did it do?
estimand:ATT.plain_language: Among the units that actually got the programme, how much did it change their outcome compared with what would have happened without it?
estimand:ATT.in_more_depth: Usually the policy-relevant number for an existing programme: it describes the people the programme actually reached. It also asks less of the data than the ATE, because you only need comparison units that resemble the treated, not the other way round. It is the default for matching and for difference-in-differences, and it is what the sample flow is quietly protecting: if matching drops a fifth of the treated units, the ATT is now for the four fifths that remained, and that is a different population.
estimand:ATT.common_mistake: Assuming the ATT equals the ATE when treated units differ from untreated ones -- which is exactly why they needed adjusting.

methods.title: de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille

methods.one_liner: One before-and-after with covariates, using an outcome model and a comparison-group model together so either one can carry it.

methods.title: Event study (leads and lags)
methods.one_liner: Plot the effect period by period around adoption, so you can see whether the gap opened when the policy arrived or long before it.

methods.title: Two-stage DiD (Gardner / Wooldridge-Mundlak)
methods.one_liner: Strip out unit and period effects using untreated cells only, then regress what is left on the policy.

methods.title: Goodman-Bacon decomposition
methods.one_liner: Open up a two-way fixed effects estimate and show every two-group comparison inside it, with the weight each one carries -- including the ones that use already-treated units as controls.

methods.title: Matched difference-in-differences
methods.one_liner: Match treated to comparison units on pre-period characteristics first, then difference.

methods.title: Sun & Abraham event study
methods.one_liner: Give every cohort its own event-study path, then average the paths by cohort size instead of letting the regression choose the weights.

methods.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences (synthdid)
methods.one_liner: Weight both units and periods, then take a difference-in-differences -- halfway between synthetic control and DiD.

methods.title: Triple differences
methods.one_liner: Compare the treated-versus-comparison difference for the group the policy could reach with the same difference for a group inside the same units that it could not.

methods.title: Two-way fixed effects
methods.one_liner: One regression with unit and period fixed effects. Familiar, fast, and not an average treatment effect when units adopt at different dates.

methods.title: Difference-in-differences (2x2)
methods.one_liner: Two groups, two periods: compare how much the treated group changed with how much the comparison group changed over the same window.

methods.title: Interference and spillovers

methods.title: ARIMA with an intervention
methods.one_liner: Model the memory in the series itself, then ask how big a step, pulse or ramp the data need at the intervention date.

methods.title: Bayesian structural time series (CausalImpact)
methods.one_liner: Model the counterfactual series with a structural time-series model and control series, and report a posterior rather than an interval.

methods.title: Controlled ITS
methods.one_liner: The same interruption, measured against a series the intervention did not touch, so a shock that hit everybody is not booked as your effect.

methods.title: Segmented regression
methods.one_liner: Fit the trend before the interruption, project it forward, and measure the jump and the change of direction after it.

methods.title: Marginal treatment effects

methods.title: G-estimation of structural nested models
methods.one_liner: Estimate the effect of a treatment regime by finding the parameter that removes the association between treatment and the blipped-down outcome.

methods.title: Longitudinal TMLE for survival outcomes
methods.one_liner: Time-to-event outcomes with time-varying treatment and censoring, targeted at each time.

methods.title: Honest causal forest
methods.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

methods.title: Double ML (interactive)
methods.one_liner: A separate outcome model for each arm plus a treatment model, combined in a doubly robust score: right if either side is right.

methods.title: Meta-learner (T, S, X, DR)
methods.one_liner: Build the per-unit effect out of ordinary prediction models, four different ways, on the same cross-fitting.

methods.title: Doubly robust (AIPW)
methods.one_liner: Use a treatment model and an outcome model together; it is right if either one is.

methods.title: Coarsened exact matching
methods.one_liner: Bin the covariates, then compare only inside bins that contain both arms.

methods.title: Genetic matching
methods.one_liner: Search over distance-metric weights until balance is as good as it can get, instead of trusting one metric.

methods.title: Nearest-neighbour matching
methods.one_liner: Pair each treated unit with the most similar untreated unit, then compare within pairs.

methods.title: Optimal and full matching
methods.one_liner: Choose the whole set of matches at once to minimise total distance, rather than greedily one treated unit at a time.

methods.title: Multiple imputation compatible with the analysis
methods.one_liner: Impute the missing values several times, run the analysis in each, and combine -- instead of dropping every row with a gap.

methods.title: Outcome regression (g-computation)
methods.one_liner: Model the outcome, then ask what would have happened if everyone had been treated, and if nobody had.

methods.title: Super Learner nuisance models
methods.one_liner: Combine several candidate learners by cross-validated weights instead of betting on one.

methods.title: Targeted maximum likelihood (TMLE)
methods.one_liner: Fit the outcome model, then nudge it once in the direction the treatment model says it is wrong.

methods.title: Covariate balancing propensity score
methods.one_liner: Fit the treatment model so that it balances covariates, rather than fitting it to predict treatment and hoping balance follows.

methods.title: Entropy balancing
methods.one_liner: Find the weights closest to equal that make the covariate means match exactly.

methods.title: Propensity weighting
methods.one_liner: Reweight the sample so the treated and untreated groups look alike on the measured confounders.

methods.title: Boosted propensity scores (twang)
methods.one_liner: Grow a boosted model for the propensity score, stopping at the iteration that balances covariates best.

methods.title: Synthetic control
methods.one_liner: Build a weighted copy of the treated place out of untreated places that looked like it beforehand, then watch the two lines separate.

methods.title: Augmented synthetic control
methods.one_liner: When no weighted average of the donors can match the treated place, correct the leftover bias with a ridge model and show the size of the correction.

methods.title: Matrix completion
methods.one_liner: Treat the missing treated-period outcomes as holes in a panel and fill them in with a low-rank model of what the panel would have done.

methods.title: Microsynth (many treated units)
methods.one_liner: Synthetic control when the treated unit is a neighbourhood or a small area and there are many of them.

methods.title: Prediction intervals for synthetic control (scpi)
methods.one_liner: Confidence intervals for a synthetic control that come from a model of the prediction error rather than from permutation.

methods.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences
methods.one_liner: Weight the comparison units and the pre-treatment periods, then run a difference in differences on the result - a level gap is allowed, a trend gap is not.

estimand:ATC.title: Average treatment effect on the controls
estimand:ATC.one_liner: For people who didn't get it, what would it have done?
estimand:ATC.plain_language: For the units that did not get the programme, what would it have done to them?
estimand:ATC.in_more_depth: This is the expansion question: if you extended an existing programme to the people currently outside it, what could you expect? It requires the comparison to be credible in the opposite direction -- treated units that resemble the untreated -- which is often the thinner side of the overlap.
estimand:ATC.common_mistake: Extrapolating to untreated units that look nothing like any treated unit.

estimand:ATO.title: Average treatment effect on the overlap population
estimand:ATO.one_liner: For the people where treated and untreated genuinely overlap, what did it do?
estimand:ATO.plain_language: The effect for the units where treated and untreated genuinely overlap, weighted so that the comparison is as stable as it can be.
estimand:ATO.in_more_depth: Overlap weights put most weight where the probability of treatment is near a half -- the units for whom the comparison is best supported -- and almost none where treatment was nearly certain either way. The result has the smallest variance among weighted estimators and never has an exploding weight. The price is that the population is defined by the data rather than by policy. It is an excellent stability check and an awkward headline: "the effect among the people where comparison was possible" is honest, but it is not a group a minister can point at.
estimand:ATO.common_mistake: Reporting it as if it were the ATE for a policy-relevant population.
estimand:ATO.notation: weights: (1 - e) for treated, e for untreated

estimand:LATE.title: Local average treatment effect
estimand:LATE.one_liner: For people who only got it because of the instrument or the cutoff, what did it do?
estimand:LATE.plain_language: The effect for the units whose treatment status was actually changed by the instrument, or who sit at the cutoff. Not for everyone.
estimand:LATE.in_more_depth: In an instrumental-variables design the compliers are the people the instrument moved -- and you cannot identify who they are, only their average effect. In a regression discontinuity the analogous group is units at the threshold. Different instruments move different people and therefore identify different numbers. Two studies with different instruments can both be right and still disagree, which is a feature of the estimand rather than a contradiction.
estimand:LATE.common_mistake: Calling it "the" effect. Different instruments identify different compliers and so different numbers.

estimand:CACE.title: Complier average causal effect
estimand:CACE.one_liner: For the people who comply with what they were offered, what did it do?
estimand:CACE.plain_language: In a randomised encouragement design, the effect among the people who took the treatment because they were offered it.
estimand:CACE.in_more_depth: The LATE by another name, in the setting where the instrument is random assignment. It scales the intention-to-treat effect by the share of people whose behaviour the offer changed. Both numbers are correct and they answer different questions. If the policy you are evaluating can only make an offer, the ITT is the effect of the policy. The CACE is the effect of the treatment on the people who accept it, which is what a clinician wants to know.
estimand:CACE.common_mistake: Reporting the CACE when the policy question is about everyone offered the programme -- that is the ITT.

estimand:ITT.title: Intention to treat
estimand:ITT.one_liner: For everyone who was offered it, what did the offer do?
estimand:ITT.plain_language: The effect of being offered the programme, whether or not people took it up. Usually the number a policy can deliver.
estimand:ITT.in_more_depth: It preserves the randomisation exactly, so it is the estimate that needs no extra assumptions. It is also diluted by noncompliance: an effective treatment with 30% take-up shows a small ITT, and that small number is the correct description of the policy as implemented. Reporting both the ITT and the complier effect, and saying which question each answers, is almost always better than choosing one.
estimand:ITT.common_mistake: Treating a diluted ITT as evidence the programme does not work, when take-up was the problem.

estimand:cohort_ATT.title: Group-time average treatment effect
estimand:cohort_ATT.one_liner: For each group that adopted it, what did their own rollout do?
estimand:cohort_ATT.plain_language: One effect for each adopting cohort in each period, before any averaging.
estimand:cohort_ATT.in_more_depth: The building block of modern difference-in-differences. Instead of one coefficient, you get a matrix: what the 2014 adopters experienced in 2015, in 2016, and so on. Everything else -- an overall effect, an event study, a per-cohort summary -- is an explicit average of these with weights you can see. That explicitness is the point. Two-way fixed effects also produces a weighted average, but with weights nobody chose and which can be negative.
estimand:cohort_ATT.common_mistake: Averaging cohorts with weights that can go negative -- which is what plain two-way fixed effects does.

estimand:CATE.title: Conditional average treatment effect
estimand:CATE.one_liner: How does the effect vary from person to person, or place to place?
estimand:CATE.plain_language: The effect as a function of characteristics: who benefits, and by how much.
estimand:CATE.in_more_depth: The most useful and most abused quantity in the catalogue. A flexible model will always produce varying predictions, including from noise, so the question is never "is there heterogeneity" but "is this ranking real". Two checks make it credible. Calibration asks whether the units predicted to benefit most actually did. The rank-weighted effect asks whether treating in the model's recommended order beats treating at random, and gives a standard error for the answer. Honest splitting -- choosing where the subgroups are on different rows from the ones that estimate their effects -- is what stops the estimate being optimistic by construction.
estimand:CATE.common_mistake: Reading noise as heterogeneity. Honest splitting and calibration checks exist for this reason.

estimand:GATE.one_liner: How does the effect vary across pre-specified groups?

estimand:GATE.in_more_depth: Pre-specification is what separates a group effect from a fishing expedition. estimand:dose_response.title: Average dose-response function
estimand:dose_response.one_liner: If we changed the dose, how would the outcome change?
estimand:dose_response.plain_language: How the outcome changes as the level of a continuous treatment changes.
estimand:dose_response.in_more_depth: A single linear coefficient assumes the tenth unit of a dose does what the first did, which is rarely true: effects saturate, and sometimes reverse. A dose-response curve estimates the whole function, with the positivity requirement now applying at every dose level -- and it usually fails at the extremes, where few units received that much.
estimand:dose_response.common_mistake: Fitting a single linear coefficient to a dose that acts non-linearly.

assumption:exchangeability.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
assumption:exchangeability.one_liner: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
assumption:exchangeability.plain_language: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
assumption:exchangeability.in_more_depth: This is the assumption the whole selection-on-observables design rests on, and no diagnostic in this product can test it. Balance plots show that the variables you measured are now comparable; they say nothing about the ones you did not measure. A perfectly flat Love plot is consistent with total confounding by something you never recorded. What you can do instead: argue from how treatment was actually assigned, draw the graph and see whether your adjustment set closes the back doors, and then ask the sensitivity question -- how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be, compared with the ones you did measure, before the conclusion changes?
assumption:exchangeability.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.
assumption:exchangeability.common_mistake: Reading "balance achieved" as "confounding removed". Balance is about the covariates in the model; confounding is about the ones that are not.

assumption:positivity.title: Positivity / overlap
assumption:positivity.one_liner: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
assumption:positivity.plain_language: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
assumption:positivity.in_more_depth: Positivity is the assumption you actually can look at. Fit a treatment model, plot the predicted probabilities by arm, and see whether the two distributions overlap. Where treated units sit at probabilities no control unit reaches, the estimate for those units comes from extrapolating the outcome model, not from anything in the data. The effective sample size is the honest denominator: reweighting a comparison group to look like the treated group can leave you with a thousand rows worth a hundred observations. Structural violations (a rule that made some group ineligible) cannot be fixed by any estimator. Random violations (a small sample in a thin region) show up as unstable weights.
assumption:positivity.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.
assumption:positivity.common_mistake: Trimming to a default cutoff to make the plot look better. Trimming changes the population the estimate is about, so it belongs in the sample flow as a stated choice, and the Probe bench plots the estimate against the threshold rather than picking one for you.

assumption:sutva.title: SUTVA / no interference
assumption:sutva.one_liner: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
assumption:sutva.plain_language: One unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome, and "treated" means the same thing for everyone who got it.
assumption:sutva.in_more_depth: Two claims in one. No interference says your neighbour's vaccination does not change your infection risk, your rival firm's subsidy does not change your employment. One version of treatment says the programme delivered in one clinic is the same programme delivered in another. Neither is testable from the data in a standard design. Both are often false in exactly the settings policy analysts care about -- vaccination, job training in a local labour market, school choice.
assumption:sutva.worry_when: Units interact: they compete for the same jobs, infect each other, share a classroom or a market. Or the "programme" is really a family of programmes whose intensity varied a lot across sites.
assumption:sutva.common_mistake: Treating spillover as noise. If treatment helps the treated partly by hurting the untreated, the comparison overstates the total effect, and no amount of adjustment recovers it.

assumption:consistency.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
assumption:consistency.one_liner: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
assumption:consistency.plain_language: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
assumption:consistency.in_more_depth: Consistency is what makes "the effect of X" mean anything. It is comfortable for a drug at a stated dose and uncomfortable for "obesity", "education" or "democracy", where the intervention is not defined and different ways of changing the variable would have different effects. Target-trial thinking is the discipline here: write down the trial you would run, including who is eligible, when time zero is, and what exactly is assigned. If you cannot write it, the estimand is not yet a question.
assumption:consistency.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.
assumption:consistency.common_mistake: Estimating the effect of a variable nobody could assign, then discussing it as if a policy could change it.

assumption:randomisation.title: Randomisation held
assumption:randomisation.one_liner: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
assumption:randomisation.plain_language: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
assumption:randomisation.in_more_depth: In a clean experiment this is the assumption that does all the work, and it is the one you get for free. What is not free is what happened afterwards. Attrition that differs by arm, treatment received that differs from treatment assigned, and outcomes measured differently by arm all break the guarantee. A baseline balance table checks that nothing went wrong in the mechanics. It is not a test of randomisation: with enough covariates some will differ by chance, and a failed balance test on a genuinely randomised trial is a false alarm as often as a real signal.
assumption:randomisation.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.
assumption:randomisation.common_mistake: Running a battery of balance tests and adjusting for whatever came out significant. That is a garden of forking paths, not a fix.

assumption:parallel_trends.title: Parallel trends
assumption:parallel_trends.one_liner: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
assumption:parallel_trends.plain_language: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
assumption:parallel_trends.in_more_depth: This is the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences, and it is about a counterfactual path nobody observes. The pre-period is the closest thing to evidence: if the groups already moved differently before the policy, the assumption is in trouble. If they moved together, that is consistent with parallel trends and also consistent with them diverging afterwards for reasons unrelated to the policy. Parallel trends is also scale-dependent: trends parallel in levels are generally not parallel in logs. Choosing the scale is part of the assumption, not a presentation detail. When pre-trends are imperfect, honest DiD asks the useful question: how much could trends have drifted before the conclusion breaks?
assumption:parallel_trends.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.
assumption:parallel_trends.common_mistake: Reading a pre-trend test that fails to reject as confirmation. Low power makes that easy, and a wide pre-period confidence interval is not evidence of parallel paths.

assumption:no_anticipation.title: No anticipation
assumption:no_anticipation.one_liner: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
assumption:no_anticipation.plain_language: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
assumption:no_anticipation.in_more_depth: Announcement usually precedes implementation, and people respond to announcements. If they do, the "before" period is already partly treated, which biases the comparison and can make the pre-trend look wrong even when parallel trends holds. The pre-period coefficients of an event study are where anticipation shows up: a drift starting exactly at the announcement date is the signature. Interrupted-time-series designs let you mark announcement and implementation as two separate dates for this reason.
assumption:no_anticipation.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

assumption:exclusion.title: Exclusion restriction
assumption:exclusion.one_liner: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
assumption:exclusion.plain_language: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
assumption:exclusion.in_more_depth: Exclusion cannot be tested. A strong first stage tells you the instrument moves treatment; it tells you nothing about whether it also moves the outcome another way. Overidentification tests compare instruments against each other and are silent when all of them are invalid in the same direction. What you can do: argue from how the instrument was generated, and look for placebo outcomes the instrument should not affect. Finding an effect there is evidence against exclusion; finding none is weak comfort.
assumption:exclusion.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.
assumption:exclusion.common_mistake: Treating a passed overidentification test as evidence for exclusion. It tests whether your instruments agree, not whether they are right.

Monotonicity is what makes the estimate a local average treatment effect on compliers. It is not testable, though the implied complier share and the proportions of each response type give a sanity check: a negative implied share is evidence something is wrong.

assumption:relevance.title: Instrument relevance
assumption:relevance.one_liner: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
assumption:relevance.plain_language: The instrument actually moves treatment, and moves it enough that the resulting estimate is not mostly noise.
assumption:relevance.in_more_depth: This one is testable, and the test matters more than people expect. With a weak instrument, two-stage least squares is biased towards the ordinary least squares estimate and its confidence interval has far less than nominal coverage -- a 95% interval that covers the truth 60% of the time. Report the effective F statistic rather than the naive one when the errors are not homoskedastic, and when it is small, report a weak-instrument-robust confidence set instead of the usual interval. An unbounded set is sometimes the honest answer.
assumption:relevance.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.
assumption:relevance.common_mistake: Adding more instruments to raise the first-stage F. Many weak instruments make the bias worse, not better.

assumption:no_manipulation.title: No manipulation of the running variable
assumption:no_manipulation.one_liner: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
assumption:no_manipulation.plain_language: People could not precisely control which side of the cutoff they landed on.
assumption:no_manipulation.in_more_depth: Regression discontinuity works because, right at the cutoff, which side you fall on is as good as random. That fails if people can fine-tune their score: applicants who just miss a threshold and resubmit, firms that report just under a reporting limit, students whose marks get nudged over a pass line. The density test is the standard check: if there is a cliff in the number of units just either side of the cutoff, someone was sorting. A smooth density does not prove there was no manipulation, but a jump is strong evidence there was. Covariate balance at the cutoff is the second check: pre-determined characteristics should not jump.
assumption:no_manipulation.worry_when: A visible spike or gap in the density at the cutoff; covariates that jump; a cutoff that people knew about and had time to respond to.

assumption:continuity.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
assumption:continuity.one_liner: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
assumption:continuity.plain_language: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
assumption:continuity.in_more_depth: The cutoff has to be doing one job. If the same threshold also triggers a different programme, a tax band or an administrative category, the jump you measure is the combined effect of all of them, and nothing separates them. Continuity is why the estimate is local: it is identified at the cutoff and the extrapolation away from it is a modelling choice, not a finding.
assumption:continuity.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.
assumption:continuity.common_mistake: Presenting the discontinuity estimate as the average effect of the programme for everyone eligible.

assumption:donor_fit.title: Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
assumption:donor_fit.one_liner: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
assumption:donor_fit.plain_language: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
assumption:donor_fit.in_more_depth: A synthetic control that cannot track the treated unit before the intervention has no claim to track it after. Pre-period fit is the closest thing to a testable condition this design has, and it is a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one: a good pre-fit can still be a coincidence, especially with a short pre-period and many donors. Report the pre-period root-mean-square prediction error, and compare it with the same quantity for placebo units. A treated unit whose post/pre error ratio is unremarkable among the placebos has not shown an effect.
assumption:donor_fit.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

assumption:convex_hull.title: Treated unit inside the donor convex hull
assumption:convex_hull.one_liner: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
assumption:convex_hull.plain_language: The treated unit's characteristics can be written as a weighted average of the donors', with weights that do not go negative.
assumption:convex_hull.in_more_depth: Classic synthetic control restricts weights to be non-negative and to sum to one, which forbids extrapolation on purpose. The price is that if the treated unit is more extreme than every donor -- richer, larger, more urban -- no combination can reach it, and the synthetic unit is biased towards the middle of the pool. That bias then shows up as a permanent gap that looks like an effect. Augmented synthetic control corrects for that bias explicitly, and reports the size of the correction so you can see how much work it is doing.

assumption:no_cointerventions.title: No co-interventions at the interruption
assumption:no_cointerventions.one_liner: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
assumption:no_cointerventions.plain_language: Nothing else changed at the same moment that also moves the outcome.
assumption:no_cointerventions.in_more_depth: An interrupted time series attributes the whole break to the policy. Policy rarely arrives alone: a smoking ban lands with a media campaign, a lockdown with a benefits change, a guideline with a payment reform. Any of those would produce the same picture. A control series that should have been unaffected is the main defence. If the control breaks at the same moment, something broader happened.
assumption:no_cointerventions.worry_when: A busy policy period; a national event at the same date; a change in how the outcome was measured or coded at the same date.

assumption:model_form.one_liner: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
assumption:model_form.plain_language: The line you fit before the interruption is the line the outcome would have continued to follow.
assumption:model_form.in_more_depth: This is an assumption, not an estimate, and it is doing more work than any coefficient in the model. A linear pre-trend extrapolated over several years is a strong claim. Seasonality, mean reversion after an unusual year, and slow-moving demographics all bend the counterfactual. Autocorrelated residuals are the standard failure: ordinary standard errors then understate uncertainty badly, sometimes by a factor of two or three.
