assumption:sequential_ignorability.title: Sequential ignorability
assumption:sequential_ignorability.one_liner: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
assumption:sequential_ignorability.plain_language: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
assumption:sequential_ignorability.in_more_depth: Mediation asks for two exchangeability assumptions instead of one, and the second is usually much harder: whatever determines how much of the mediator a person gets is rarely unrelated to their outcome. Randomising treatment does not randomise the mediator. Natural direct and indirect effects need a third, cross-world condition relating potential outcomes under treatment values that no single person can ever experience. No experiment, however large, can test it. That is why interventional (stochastic) effects are the better default in policy and health: they answer a slightly different question that a trial could in principle check.
assumption:sequential_ignorability.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.
assumption:sequential_ignorability.common_mistake: Reporting a product-of-coefficients decomposition as "the mechanism" without stating either assumption.

assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.one_liner: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.plain_language: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.in_more_depth: In longitudinal data the same variable is often a confounder for later treatment and a consequence of earlier treatment. Adjusting for it in an ordinary regression both blocks the path you want and opens a collider path; not adjusting for it leaves confounding. This is precisely the problem g-methods were invented for. Lag discipline is the practical form of this assumption: a covariate may adjust a treatment decision only if it was measured before that decision. The board draws arrows that cannot point into the future for this reason.
assumption:no_time_varying_confounding.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

diagnostic:adoption.title: Adoption pattern
diagnostic:adoption.one_liner: A grid of units by period, lit where treatment is on, sorted by when each unit adopted.
diagnostic:adoption.plain_language: A grid of units by period, lit where treatment is on, sorted by when each unit adopted.
diagnostic:adoption.in_more_depth: This is the picture that decides which difference-in-differences estimator you should be using. A single block of lit cells starting at one date is a 2x2. A staircase is staggered adoption, and two-way fixed effects is then averaging comparisons that include already-treated units used as controls. It also shows what you have to compare against: a row of never-treated units at the bottom, or nothing, in which case the comparison group has to be units not yet treated.
diagnostic:adoption.worry_when: No never-treated units; cohorts containing a single unit; treatment that switches back off, which the staggered estimators assume does not happen.

diagnostic:augmentation_gap.title: Augmentation gap
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.one_liner: The distance between the plain model-based estimate and the version with a correction term added.
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.plain_language: The distance between the plain model-based estimate and the version with a correction term added.
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.in_more_depth: Doubly robust methods combine a model of the outcome with a model of the treatment, and are consistent if either one is right. The correction term is the part that makes that guarantee work. Its size measures how much the two models disagree about the same data. A small gap means both models tell the same story and the guarantee is not being exercised. A large one means they do not, and the estimate is relying on the promise that at least one of them is right -- a promise that cannot be checked.
diagnostic:augmentation_gap.worry_when: A large gap: the outcome models and the treatment models disagree about the same data, and being right if either is right is doing real work.

diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.title: Goodman-Bacon decomposition
diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.one_liner: Every simple before-and-after comparison hidden inside a single fixed-effects coefficient, and how much weight each one carries.
diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.plain_language: Every simple before-and-after comparison hidden inside a single fixed-effects coefficient, and how much weight each one carries.
diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.in_more_depth: When units adopt a policy at different dates, a two-way fixed-effects regression is not one comparison; it is an average of many two-group, two-period comparisons. Some of them are the ones you would want: a group that adopts against a group that never does. Others compare a late adopter against an early adopter who is already treated -- using treated units as the control group. Those latter comparisons subtract the early group's ongoing effect, so if effects grow over time they can push the average in the wrong direction, and the weight attached to them can even be negative. This decomposition shows how much of your number comes from each kind, which is the evidence for whether a modern estimator is needed.
diagnostic:bacon_decomposition.worry_when: A large share of the estimate coming from comparisons that use already-treated units as controls, especially when their average differs from the clean comparisons.

diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.title: Bandwidth sensitivity path
diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.one_liner: The estimate recomputed using progressively wider and narrower windows around the cutoff.
diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.plain_language: The estimate recomputed using progressively wider and narrower windows around the cutoff.
diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.in_more_depth: Every discontinuity estimate is a choice about how far from the threshold to look. Narrow windows use only the most comparable units and are noisy; wide ones are precise and rely on the fitted curve to describe a longer stretch of the relationship. Automatic selectors trade the two off, and reasonable selectors disagree with each other. A finding that persists across a range of windows is much stronger than one that appears at the selected width and disappears either side. This path is how you tell which you have.
diagnostic:bandwidth_sensitivity.worry_when: An estimate that changes sign or size sharply between neighbouring windows; a result that exists only at the widest windows, where the local approximation is weakest.

speaks_to.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
speaks_to.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

diagnostic:baseline_balance.title: Baseline balance
diagnostic:baseline_balance.one_liner: In a randomised design, a check that the arms look alike on characteristics measured before assignment.
diagnostic:baseline_balance.plain_language: In a randomised design, a check that the arms look alike on characteristics measured before assignment.
diagnostic:baseline_balance.in_more_depth: Randomisation makes the arms comparable in expectation, not in every sample. The balance table is a check on the mechanics: that the randomiser worked, that nobody was reassigned, that the data was not merged wrongly. It is not a test of whether randomisation "worked" in a deeper sense. With many covariates some will differ by chance, and adjusting for whichever ones came out significant is a forking path, not a repair. Pre-specified covariate adjustment for precision is a different and better idea.
diagnostic:baseline_balance.worry_when: A large imbalance on a strong predictor of the outcome; imbalance that correlates with the order of enrolment; differential dropout after assignment.

diagnostic:bias_correction.title: Bias correction and robust interval
diagnostic:bias_correction.one_liner: Fitting a curve over a window leaves a predictable error at the edge. This shows how much correcting for it moves the estimate and widens the interval.
diagnostic:bias_correction.plain_language: Fitting a curve over a window leaves a predictable error at the edge. This shows how much correcting for it moves the estimate and widens the interval.
diagnostic:bias_correction.in_more_depth: The window width that gives the most accurate estimate is deliberately a little too wide -- it accepts some bias in exchange for a lot less noise. That trade means the leftover bias is about the same size as the standard error, so an interval computed as though there were none is too narrow and sits slightly off-centre. The remedy is to estimate the bias with a more flexible fit, subtract it, and widen the interval to account for having estimated it. The corrected interval is wider on purpose. It is the honest one at a window chosen for accuracy.
diagnostic:bias_correction.worry_when: A correction larger than one standard error, which means the fitted curve is doing real work inside the window and the answer depends on the shape you assumed.

diagnostic:block_structure.title: Block structure
diagnostic:block_structure.one_liner: When randomisation was done separately inside strata -- clinics, schools, waves -- this shows how big each block is and what share of it was treated.
diagnostic:block_structure.plain_language: When randomisation was done separately inside strata -- clinics, schools, waves -- this shows how big each block is and what share of it was treated.
diagnostic:block_structure.in_more_depth: A blocked trial is many small trials stacked together, and the analysis has to respect that: comparisons are made inside blocks and then averaged. This table is how you check the stacking is sound. Blocks that hold only treated units, or only untreated ones, contain no comparison and are dropped, and the table says how many were lost that way. Block sizes also decide how the interval is computed. With two units in a block there is no spread to measure inside it, so the calculation falls back on pooling across blocks, which assumes the blocks behave alike. That is a real assumption and it is worth knowing when you are leaning on it.
diagnostic:block_structure.worry_when: Most blocks hold a single treated and a single control unit, or a handful of large blocks carry the whole estimate; the interval then rests on the pooled fallback rather than on anything measured inside the blocks.

diagnostic:block_weighting.title: Block weights
diagnostic:block_weighting.one_liner: Two ways of combining blocked results give two different numbers, and the difference is a difference in the question, not in the arithmetic.
diagnostic:block_weighting.plain_language: Two ways of combining blocked results give two different numbers, and the difference is a difference in the question, not in the arithmetic.
diagnostic:block_weighting.in_more_depth: Averaging the block-level effects with each block weighted by how many units it holds gives the average effect across everyone in the study. Putting an indicator variable in for each block instead gives a precision-weighted average: it leans on the blocks where the treated share is nearest a half, because those blocks carry the most information. The two agree only when the treated share is the same in every block. Neither is wrong. But if you asked for the average effect on this population, the size-weighted number is the one that answers it, and the regression coefficient is quietly answering a different question under the same name.
diagnostic:block_weighting.worry_when: The two numbers disagree while the treated share moves across blocks; the choice of estimator is then a choice of estimand, not a choice of standard error.

diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.title: Bootstrap spread
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.one_liner: The whole estimate recomputed on many resamples of the data, and whether those resamples behaved themselves.
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.plain_language: The whole estimate recomputed on many resamples of the data, and whether those resamples behaved themselves.
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.in_more_depth: Resampling the data with replacement and repeating the entire fit -- models and all -- gives a picture of how much the answer would move if you had drawn a different sample from the same population. It is the fallback when no formula for the standard error is trustworthy, which is often the case once weights have been estimated rather than known. Two things are worth reading here rather than just the interval. First, how many resamples failed: a fit that breaks on some draws is telling you the model is fragile. Second, the shape: two humps mean the models are not fitting the same way on every resample, and an average of two behaviours is not a summary of either.
diagnostic:bootstrap_spread.worry_when: Resamples that fail to produce an estimate; a distribution with two humps; a bootstrap spread far above what the formula-based standard error claimed.

diagnostic:cate_calibration.title: CATE calibration
diagnostic:cate_calibration.one_liner: Sort units by predicted effect, then check whether the groups you predicted would benefit most actually did.
diagnostic:cate_calibration.plain_language: Sort units by predicted effect, then check whether the groups you predicted would benefit most actually did.
diagnostic:cate_calibration.in_more_depth: A model will always produce varying predictions, including from pure noise. Calibration asks whether the ranking means anything: regress the realised effect on the predicted one, and see whether the slope is near one. A slope near zero says the heterogeneity is a model artefact. This is the check that separates "we found who benefits" from "we fitted a forest".
diagnostic:cate_calibration.worry_when: A calibration slope far from one, or a confidence interval on it that comfortably includes zero.

diagnostic:cate_distribution.title: CATE distribution
diagnostic:cate_distribution.one_liner: The spread of the per-person effect estimates: how different the model thinks people are.
diagnostic:cate_distribution.plain_language: The spread of the per-person effect estimates: how different the model thinks people are.
diagnostic:cate_distribution.in_more_depth: A model that predicts one effect per person will always produce a spread, because estimation error alone produces one. So this picture is a description of the predictions, not evidence that the underlying effects differ. Read it together with the calibration check: if the ranking cannot be shown to mean anything, the width here is mostly noise. A spread of essentially zero is a finding rather than a failure. It says the learner looked for differences between people and did not find any that the data supports, which is a perfectly good answer to the question.
diagnostic:cate_distribution.worry_when: A wide spread while the calibration check says the ranking carries no information; you are then looking at estimation error, not heterogeneity.

diagnostic:cde_path.title: Controlled direct effect across mediator levels
diagnostic:cde_path.one_liner: The direct effect computed with the mediator held at each of several values. There is one number per value, not one number.
diagnostic:cde_path.plain_language: The direct effect computed with the mediator held at each of several values. There is one number per value, not one number.
diagnostic:cde_path.in_more_depth: A controlled direct effect asks what the treatment would do if the mediator were fixed, by intervention, at a particular level for everybody. That is a well-defined and checkable question -- unlike the natural decomposition, it does not require imagining a world nobody could live in -- but the answer depends on which level you fix. When the path across levels is flat, quoting one number is harmless. When it slopes, the path is the answer, and the level chosen must be one that a policy could actually impose.
diagnostic:cde_path.worry_when: A steep path reported as "the direct effect"; the honest answer is then the path itself.

diagnostic:cell_means.title: Cell means
diagnostic:cell_means.one_liner: The four averages -- treated and comparison, before and after -- that the headline difference is built from.
diagnostic:cell_means.plain_language: The four averages -- treated and comparison, before and after -- that the headline difference is built from.
diagnostic:cell_means.in_more_depth: A two-group, two-period difference-in-differences is arithmetic on four numbers: the change in the treated group minus the change in the comparison group. Seeing the four makes the estimate legible, and it makes obvious things that a coefficient hides, such as a comparison group that moved a long way on its own. When a third dimension is involved -- a group inside the treated units that the policy could not have affected -- the same table shows the extra subtraction, and whether the thing being subtracted really looks like a common shock.
diagnostic:cell_means.worry_when: One cell holding very few observations; a comparison group whose change is large in its own right, so the estimate is a difference between two moving things.

diagnostic:cem_strata.title: Coarsened strata and common support
diagnostic:cem_strata.one_liner: How many of the coarsened cells contain both treated and untreated units, and how many treated units had no comparable cell at all.
diagnostic:cem_strata.plain_language: How many of the coarsened cells contain both treated and untreated units, and how many treated units had no comparable cell at all.
diagnostic:cem_strata.in_more_depth: Coarsened exact matching guarantees balance by refusing to compare across cells. The price is pruning: with several covariates, most cells contain only one arm, and the treated units in those cells leave the analysis. That pruning is information. It tells you exactly where the data cannot answer the question, which a smooth propensity model hides.
diagnostic:cem_strata.worry_when: A large share of treated units pruned; the estimand quietly becoming the effect for an unusual subset.

diagnostic:censoring_weights.title: Censoring weights
diagnostic:censoring_weights.one_liner: How people who left the study before the end are accounted for.
diagnostic:censoring_weights.plain_language: How people who left the study before the end are accounted for.
diagnostic:censoring_weights.in_more_depth: People drop out, and if they drop out for reasons connected to their treatment or their outcome, the ones who remain are a selected group. The standard repair is to model who stays and then let each person who stayed stand in for the similar people who left. That works only if staying is predictable from what was measured. It also has the same failure mode as any weighting: when few people like someone remained, that person's weight becomes large and the estimate leans on them. The range of weights reported here is how you see it happening.
diagnostic:censoring_weights.worry_when: Large censoring weights, meaning a few people who stayed are standing in for many who left; or dropout that is clearly related to treatment.

speaks_to.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
speaks_to.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

diagnostic:cluster_structure.title: Cluster structure
diagnostic:cluster_structure.one_liner: How many groups treatment was assigned to, how big they are, and how much of the sample the largest one holds.
diagnostic:cluster_structure.plain_language: How many groups treatment was assigned to, how big they are, and how much of the sample the largest one holds.
diagnostic:cluster_structure.in_more_depth: When whole schools, villages or clinics were assigned together, the schools are the units that were randomised, not the pupils. The correction for that is a cluster-robust standard error, and its reliability grows with the number of clusters, not the number of rows: fifty thousand pupils in twelve schools carry twelve schools' worth of information about the policy. The table therefore reports the count, the spread of sizes and the share held by the largest cluster, because one or two dominant clusters behave like an even smaller study than the count suggests.
diagnostic:cluster_structure.worry_when: Fewer than about forty clusters, or one or two clusters holding much of the sample. The interval is then too narrow and the p-value too small.

diagnostic:cohort_att.title: Cohort effects
diagnostic:cohort_att.one_liner: One effect per group of units that adopted at the same date, instead of one number for all of them.
diagnostic:cohort_att.plain_language: One effect per group of units that adopted at the same date, instead of one number for all of them.
diagnostic:cohort_att.in_more_depth: Units that adopted in 2015 and units that adopted in 2019 may have had very different experiences: different circumstances, different versions of the policy, different lengths of exposure. Estimating each cohort separately shows that variation instead of averaging it away, and the overall figure is then an explicit average of these with weights you can see. Cohorts built from very few units produce noisy estimates, so read the spread together with the intervals rather than as a set of firm findings.
diagnostic:cohort_att.worry_when: Cohorts that disagree in sign or size, which means a single average hides which rollout actually worked; or a cohort resting on one or two units.

diagnostic:comparison_group.title: Comparison group used
diagnostic:comparison_group.one_liner: Which units are standing in for what would have happened without the policy, and how many of them there are.
diagnostic:comparison_group.plain_language: Which units are standing in for what would have happened without the policy, and how many of them there are.
diagnostic:comparison_group.in_more_depth: A staggered design can draw its comparison from units that never adopt, or from units that have not adopted yet, or from both. Never-treated units are the cleanest comparison and are sometimes unusual for the very reason they never adopted. Not-yet-treated units are more similar but stop being available as the panel fills up with adopters. This row says which pool was used and how thin it is. A handful of never-treated units, or cohorts of one, can do most of the work while the confidence interval gives no hint of how much rests on them.
diagnostic:comparison_group.worry_when: A very small comparison pool, or one built entirely from units that are unlike the adopters in obvious ways.

diagnostic:compliance.title: Compliance with assignment
diagnostic:compliance.one_liner: How many people in each arm actually took the treatment, and what that implies about who the estimate is about.
diagnostic:compliance.plain_language: How many people in each arm actually took the treatment, and what that implies about who the estimate is about.
diagnostic:compliance.in_more_depth: Offering a programme is not the same as delivering it. Some people offered it decline; some people not offered it find it anyway. The gap in take-up between the arms is what the analysis divides by when it converts the effect of the offer into the effect of the treatment, so a small gap means dividing by a small number, and the interval widens fast. That same gap defines who the number describes. Provided the offer never pushed anybody away from treatment, the people whose take-up the offer actually changed are the compliers, and the estimate is their effect -- not the effect for the people who would have taken it up regardless, nor for those who never would, nor for the population as a whole.
diagnostic:compliance.worry_when: Take-up in the control arm is high, or the take-up gap is small; the group the estimate describes is then a small and unusual slice of the sample.

speaks_to.title: Monotonicity / no defiers
speaks_to.explains: The instrument pushes everyone the same way, or not at all. Nobody takes the treatment only because they were discouraged from it.
speaks_to.worry_when: The instrument is an incentive that could plausibly backfire for some people, or it is a judge or examiner whose leniency ordering differs across case types.

diagnostic:compliers.title: Complier share
diagnostic:compliers.one_liner: An instrument only moves some people. The estimate describes those people, and this says roughly who and how many they are.
diagnostic:compliers.plain_language: An instrument only moves some people. The estimate describes those people, and this says roughly who and how many they are.
diagnostic:compliers.in_more_depth: Divide the sample into three kinds. Some would take the treatment whatever happened. Some would never take it. The rest -- the ones the instrument actually moves -- are the only people the estimate describes. Their share can be worked out from the take-up rates in each group, provided the instrument never pushed anybody in the wrong direction. A small share is not a flaw in the arithmetic, but it does limit the claim. An estimate for eight per cent of the sample is an estimate for eight per cent of the sample, and there is no statistical route from there to everybody else.
diagnostic:compliers.worry_when: A small share of movers, which makes the estimate about a sliver of the sample; or a negative share, which means the encouragement pushed some people the other way and the required assumption is in trouble.

diagnostic:constant_effect.title: Constant-effect assumption
diagnostic:constant_effect.one_liner: Some estimators assume the treatment does the same thing to everybody. This says what that assumption buys and what it costs.
diagnostic:constant_effect.plain_language: Some estimators assume the treatment does the same thing to everybody. This says what that assumption buys and what it costs.
diagnostic:constant_effect.in_more_depth: The partially linear model writes the outcome as one effect multiplied by the treatment, plus a flexible function of the confounders. The flexibility is all on the confounding side; the effect itself is a single number by construction. That restriction makes the estimator efficient and simple. When effects really do differ between people, the number it returns is a weighted average that leans towards the units whose treatment was hardest to predict. That is not the average treatment effect, though it is often close. If the heterogeneity checks find real differences, use the estimator that targets the average directly instead.
diagnostic:constant_effect.worry_when: The calibration diagnostic finds real heterogeneity, in which case this restriction is doing work that the data does not support.

diagnostic:covariate_balance.title: Covariate balance
diagnostic:covariate_balance.one_liner: Run the same estimate on variables the programme cannot have changed. They should show no jump.
diagnostic:covariate_balance.plain_language: Run the same estimate on variables the programme cannot have changed. They should show no jump.
diagnostic:covariate_balance.in_more_depth: Age, sex, anything recorded before the threshold was applied: none of these can be affected by crossing the line, so any apparent jump in them is a jump the design has manufactured. It usually means something else changes at the same threshold -- another programme, an administrative boundary, a different data source either side. This is one of the few checks that can catch the continuity assumption failing. A clean result does not establish it: the variables you did not measure could still jump.
diagnostic:covariate_balance.worry_when: A variable the programme cannot have changed jumping at the cutoff; or no covariates supplied at all, in which case nothing has been checked.

speaks_to.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
speaks_to.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
speaks_to.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

diagnostic:differential_attrition.title: Differential attrition
diagnostic:differential_attrition.one_liner: Whether the treated arm and the control arm lost rows at the same rate on the way from assignment to analysis.
diagnostic:differential_attrition.plain_language: Whether the treated arm and the control arm lost rows at the same rate on the way from assignment to analysis.
diagnostic:differential_attrition.in_more_depth: Randomisation makes the arms comparable at the moment of assignment. It says nothing about who is still in the file at the end. If the people offered the programme are more likely to answer the follow-up survey -- or less likely -- then the sample being compared has been selected by something that happened after assignment, and the protection randomisation bought you is gone. Adjusting for baseline characteristics does not repair this, because the selection happened downstream of the treatment rather than before it. What helps is bounding the answer under best and worst cases for the missing rows, and reporting the loss plainly.
diagnostic:differential_attrition.worry_when: The two arms lose rows at visibly different rates, or the reasons for leaving differ by arm.

diagnostic:ebal_convergence.title: Moment balance
diagnostic:ebal_convergence.one_liner: Whether the weighting actually achieved the balance it was asked for, and how far short it fell.
diagnostic:ebal_convergence.plain_language: Whether the weighting actually achieved the balance it was asked for, and how far short it fell.
diagnostic:ebal_convergence.in_more_depth: Entropy balancing does not fit a model of treatment and hope for balance; it solves directly for weights that make named summaries of the covariates -- means, and optionally spreads -- match between the groups exactly. When a solution exists, the remaining gaps are zero by construction and this table is a receipt. When no solution exists, the gaps are not zero, and that is informative: it means the treated group's profile is outside anything a reweighting of the available comparison units can reproduce. That is a data problem, not a solver problem, and no amount of tuning fixes it.
diagnostic:ebal_convergence.worry_when: Non-zero gaps after the solve, which say the treated profile is outside what reweighting the comparison group can reach.

diagnostic:endogeneity.one_liner: The plain regression estimate next to the instrumented one, and what their difference does and does not tell you.
diagnostic:endogeneity.plain_language: The plain regression estimate next to the instrumented one, and what their difference does and does not tell you.
diagnostic:endogeneity.in_more_depth: The two numbers are not competing estimates of the same thing. The plain regression describes an association across everybody; the instrumented figure is a causal effect for the people the instrument moves. They can differ because of confounding, because those people are unusual, or both. A formal test of whether the plain regression would have been enough exists and is reported, but it is only meaningful if the instrument is valid and strong. When the instrument is weak, a large gap between the two numbers is exactly what weak-instrument bias produces, so the gap is not evidence of confounding.
diagnostic:endogeneity.worry_when: An instrumented estimate several times the size of the plain one alongside a weak first stage; weak instruments, a small violation of the exclusion restriction, and a genuinely different group of movers all look like that.

diagnostic:ess.title: Effective sample size
diagnostic:ess.one_liner: How many observations the weighted comparison is really worth, and how much of the total weight the single largest unit carries.
diagnostic:ess.plain_language: How many observations the weighted comparison is really worth, and how much of the total weight the single largest unit carries.
diagnostic:ess.in_more_depth: Weighting concentrates the analysis on the units that resemble the other arm. Kish's effective sample size turns that concentration into a count you can compare with the nominal one. The weight histogram is the same information as a picture: a long right tail means a handful of rows are carrying the estimate, and their idiosyncrasies now show up in your confidence interval as precision you do not have.
diagnostic:ess.worry_when: An effective sample below about 40% of the nominal one; a single weight above about a fifth of the total; a histogram with a visible tail of extreme weights.

speaks_to.title: Positivity / overlap
speaks_to.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
speaks_to.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

produced_by.title: Genetic matching

produced_by.title: Nearest-neighbour matching
produced_by.one_liner: Pair each treated unit with the most similar untreated unit, then compare within pairs.

produced_by.title: Optimal and full matching
produced_by.one_liner: Choose the whole set of matches at once to minimise total distance, rather than greedily one treated unit at a time.

produced_by.title: Covariate balancing propensity score
produced_by.one_liner: Fit the treatment model so that it balances covariates, rather than fitting it to predict treatment and hoping balance follows.

produced_by.title: Entropy balancing

produced_by.title: Propensity weighting

diagnostic:evalue.title: E-value
diagnostic:evalue.one_liner: The smallest strength of association -- with the treatment and with the outcome -- that an unmeasured variable would need to explain away the result.
diagnostic:evalue.plain_language: The smallest strength of association -- with the treatment and with the outcome -- that an unmeasured variable would need to explain away the result.
diagnostic:evalue.in_more_depth: An E-value of 2.5 means a hidden variable would have to be associated with both the treatment and the outcome by a risk ratio of at least 2.5, above and beyond the covariates already in the model, before the finding could be attributed to it entirely. The same calculation applied to the end of the confidence interval says what it would take to move the result to the edge of statistical significance rather than to nothing. It is a convenient summary and it is not a test. It says nothing about whether such a variable exists, and it assumes a single confounder acting simply. Its value comes from the comparison with the associations your measured covariates actually show.
diagnostic:evalue.worry_when: An E-value near 1, meaning a very ordinary unmeasured variable would be enough; or an E-value smaller than the associations your measured covariates display.

speaks_to.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

diagnostic:evalue_scale.title: E-value scale
diagnostic:evalue_scale.one_liner: The E-value is defined for ratios of risks, so anything measured on another scale has to be converted first -- and the conversion is an approximation.
diagnostic:evalue_scale.plain_language: The E-value is defined for ratios of risks, so anything measured on another scale has to be converted first -- and the conversion is an approximation.
diagnostic:evalue_scale.in_more_depth: A difference in means, an odds ratio, a hazard ratio: each needs a different bridge to the risk-ratio scale the E-value formula expects, and each bridge carries its own conditions. Converting an odds ratio assumes the outcome is rare. Converting a standardised mean difference assumes the outcome is roughly bell-shaped. Where those conditions fail, the E-value inherits the failure. This row records which conversion was used, so that a reader can judge it rather than take the resulting number at face value.
diagnostic:evalue_scale.worry_when: The conversion's own conditions fail -- a common outcome treated as rare, or a mean difference on an outcome that is far from bell-shaped.

diagnostic:event_study.title: Event study
diagnostic:event_study.one_liner: One coefficient per period relative to treatment, with the period before treatment set to zero.
diagnostic:event_study.plain_language: One coefficient per period relative to treatment, with the period before treatment set to zero.
diagnostic:event_study.in_more_depth: The post-period coefficients trace out how the effect develops -- immediate, growing, fading. The pre-period coefficients are the closest thing to evidence about parallel trends: if the groups were already diverging, the design is in trouble. Read the pre-period as a picture rather than as a test. A wide, flat pre-period with large standard errors is not evidence of parallel trends; it is evidence you cannot tell.
diagnostic:event_study.worry_when: Pre-period coefficients drifting away from zero, especially starting at the announcement date; effects that appear entirely in the first period and vanish; wildly different dynamics across cohorts.

speaks_to.title: Parallel trends
speaks_to.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
speaks_to.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

diagnostic:extreme_confounder.title: Confounder strength needed to explain the estimate
diagnostic:extreme_confounder.one_liner: Suppose a hidden variable explained everything left unexplained about who was treated. How much of the outcome would it still need to explain?
diagnostic:extreme_confounder.plain_language: Suppose a hidden variable explained everything left unexplained about who was treated. How much of the outcome would it still need to explain?
diagnostic:extreme_confounder.in_more_depth: This is the worst case for one half of the problem and therefore a useful bound. By granting the hidden variable complete command of the treatment assignment, the question reduces to a single quantity: how strongly it would have to relate to the outcome to move the estimate to zero. If that remaining requirement is large, the finding survives even the most adverse assumption about selection into treatment. If it is small, then even a mild relationship with the outcome would suffice, and the estimate should be described as fragile.
diagnostic:extreme_confounder.worry_when: The share required is small enough that an ordinary unmeasured variable could reach it.

diagnostic:first_stage.title: First stage
diagnostic:first_stage.one_liner: How much the instrument actually moves the treatment, shown as a picture and as an F statistic.
diagnostic:first_stage.plain_language: How much the instrument actually moves the treatment, shown as a picture and as an F statistic.
diagnostic:first_stage.in_more_depth: A significant first stage is not the same as a strong one. What matters for the reliability of the second stage is the effective F statistic, which accounts for heteroskedasticity and clustering; the naive F can be comfortably large while the effective F is not. Below roughly ten, two-stage least squares is biased towards ordinary least squares and its confidence interval undercovers badly. The honest report there is a weak-instrument-robust confidence set.
diagnostic:first_stage.worry_when: An effective F below about ten; a first-stage effect that is statistically significant but substantively negligible; many instruments each doing very little.

speaks_to.worry_when: An effective F below about 10; a first-stage coefficient that is substantively tiny even if statistically significant; many instruments.

diagnostic:fold_stability.title: Stability across folds
diagnostic:fold_stability.one_liner: The estimate computed within each cross-fitting fold. They should scatter around the overall estimate by roughly its standard error.

diagnostic:forest_honesty.title: Honest splitting scheme
diagnostic:forest_honesty.one_liner: Confirmation that each tree used one set of rows to decide where the subgroups are and a different set to estimate the effect inside them.
diagnostic:forest_honesty.plain_language: Confirmation that each tree used one set of rows to decide where the subgroups are and a different set to estimate the effect inside them.
diagnostic:forest_honesty.in_more_depth: If the same rows both choose a split and estimate the effect on either side of it, the effect will look large -- the split was chosen because it looked large. Honest forests avoid that by dividing each tree's sample in two: one half draws the boundaries, the other half fills in the numbers, and no unit contributes to both jobs in the same tree. Each unit's own predicted effect then comes only from trees that never saw it. The cost is sample size, and this panel reports what that cost was: leaves too sparse to estimate, and units with few trees to average over, both push the per-person predictions back towards the overall average.
diagnostic:forest_honesty.worry_when: A large share of leaves falling back to the overall estimate, or units with very few trees that never saw them; the per-person effects are then mostly the average wearing a disguise.

diagnostic:group_time_att.title: Group-time effects
diagnostic:group_time_att.one_liner: One effect for each adoption cohort in each period, which is the building block every modern staggered estimator aggregates.
diagnostic:group_time_att.plain_language: One effect for each adoption cohort in each period, which is the building block every modern staggered estimator aggregates.
diagnostic:group_time_att.in_more_depth: Rather than fitting one coefficient to everything, these estimators compute a separate comparison for each cohort and each period, always against units that are not treated in either of the two periods being compared. Every headline number -- overall, by cohort, by time since adoption -- is then an average of these blocks with stated weights. The advantage is that no already-treated unit is ever used as a control, so the negative-weight problem cannot arise. The cost is that some blocks rest on very little data, and the table lets you see which.
diagnostic:group_time_att.worry_when: A block resting on one or two treated units, or on a very small comparison group; the average inherits that fragility without showing it.

diagnostic:honest_did.title: Honest DiD breakdown value
diagnostic:honest_did.one_liner: Rather than testing whether trends were parallel, this asks how far from parallel they could have been before your conclusion changes.
diagnostic:honest_did.plain_language: Rather than testing whether trends were parallel, this asks how far from parallel they could have been before your conclusion changes.
diagnostic:honest_did.in_more_depth: A pre-trend test that fails to reject is weak evidence, because such tests have little power exactly when a violation would matter. The alternative is to allow the trends to differ by some amount after treatment, widen the interval accordingly, and report the largest violation the conclusion can absorb. That number is called a breakdown value. Expressed in relative terms, it says how big a post-treatment violation would have to be compared with the wobbles already visible before treatment. It is a much more useful summary than a yes-or-no test, and it is still an assumption -- about the class of violations considered, not about their absence.
diagnostic:honest_did.worry_when: A breakdown value below one, which means the conclusion needs the post-treatment violation to be smaller than the ones you can already see in the pre-period.

diagnostic:icc_design_effect.title: Intra-cluster correlation and design effect
diagnostic:icc_design_effect.one_liner: How alike people are inside the same cluster, and how many independent observations your rows are really worth once that similarity is counted.
diagnostic:icc_design_effect.plain_language: How alike people are inside the same cluster, and how many independent observations your rows are really worth once that similarity is counted.
diagnostic:icc_design_effect.in_more_depth: Two pupils in one school resemble each other more than two pupils picked at random from the country, and the intracluster correlation puts a number between zero and one on that resemblance. Combine it with the cluster sizes and you get the design effect: the factor by which the sample behaves smaller than it looks. A design effect of four means a thousand rows carry about two hundred and fifty observations' worth of information. This is not a fault to be repaired. It is the price of assigning treatment to groups, and it should have been in the sample-size calculation before the study ran.
diagnostic:icc_design_effect.worry_when: A design effect well above two, or an effective sample close to the number of clusters; in the latter case analyse the cluster averages and say so.

diagnostic:imputation_fit.title: Untreated-cell model fit
diagnostic:imputation_fit.one_liner: How well the model of untreated behaviour describes the periods where nobody was treated, since everything else is built on it.
diagnostic:imputation_fit.plain_language: How well the model of untreated behaviour describes the periods where nobody was treated, since everything else is built on it.
diagnostic:imputation_fit.in_more_depth: Imputation estimators work by fitting a model of what units do when untreated -- unit differences plus period differences -- on the untreated observations only, then predicting what each treated unit would have done and subtracting. The effect is the average of those differences. That makes the fit of the comparison model the load-bearing element. If the untreated cells are not well described by unit and period effects alone, the predicted counterfactual carries error that lands entirely in the estimate.
diagnostic:imputation_fit.worry_when: A residual spread that is large next to the effect you are estimating; the imputed counterfactual then carries most of the uncertainty.

diagnostic:influence_spread.title: Influence-function spread
diagnostic:influence_spread.one_liner: Each unit's contribution to the estimate, and how much of the total the largest single contribution is.
diagnostic:influence_spread.plain_language: Each unit's contribution to the estimate, and how much of the total the largest single contribution is.
diagnostic:influence_spread.in_more_depth: Most modern estimators can be written as an average of one number per unit, and the standard error is the spread of those numbers divided by the sample size. That makes the contributions readable: you can see whether the answer is an average over many people or a handful of unusual rows with everybody else along for the ride. A single dominant contribution is an extreme weight wearing different clothes, and it has the same consequence -- the confidence interval assumes an averaging that did not really happen.
diagnostic:influence_spread.worry_when: One unit carrying a large share of the total contribution; removing it would visibly move the estimate.

diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.title: Residual autocorrelation
diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.one_liner: Whether the residuals of the segmented regression are still correlated over time. If they are, ordinary standard errors are far too small.
diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.plain_language: Whether the residuals of the segmented regression are still correlated over time. If they are, ordinary standard errors are far too small.
diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.in_more_depth: Monthly and quarterly series are almost always autocorrelated: a busy month is followed by a busy month. Ignoring it does not bias the estimate much but it shrinks the standard error, sometimes by a factor of two or three, which turns noise into a finding. The autocorrelation function of the residuals and a Ljung-Box test are the standard checks. When they fire, use a HAC standard error or model the error process explicitly, and say which in the report.
diagnostic:its_autocorrelation.worry_when: Large residual autocorrelation at lag one, or at the seasonal lag, that survives the fitted model.

diagnostic:its_control_shock.title: Control series at the interruption
diagnostic:its_control_shock.one_liner: A second series that the policy did not touch, to see whether the change happened everywhere.
diagnostic:its_control_shock.plain_language: A second series that the policy did not touch, to see whether the change happened everywhere.
diagnostic:its_control_shock.in_more_depth: The weakness of a single interrupted series is that anything else happening at the same time is indistinguishable from the policy. A control series -- a neighbouring region, an unaffected condition, an untargeted product -- turns that from an assumption into something partly checkable. If the control jumps at the same date in the same direction, the change was not the policy. If the two series were already drifting apart beforehand, the control was not a good stand-in to begin with, and the comparison inherits the drift.
diagnostic:its_control_shock.worry_when: The control jumping at the interruption in the same direction as the treated series, or the two series diverging before the interruption.

diagnostic:its_counterfactual.title: Counterfactual projection
diagnostic:its_counterfactual.one_liner: The line the series would have followed if the earlier pattern had simply continued, with a band around it.
diagnostic:its_counterfactual.plain_language: The line the series would have followed if the earlier pattern had simply continued, with a band around it.
diagnostic:its_counterfactual.in_more_depth: The effect is the distance between what happened and this projected line, so the projection deserves as much scrutiny as the estimate. Reading it is mostly a matter of plausibility: does the line stay inside the range the series has ever occupied, and does the fitted pattern describe the pre-period well enough to be worth extending? The band widens the further out it goes, and it prices in only the uncertainty in the fitted line. It does not price in the risk that the shape itself is wrong, which is usually the larger risk.
diagnostic:its_counterfactual.worry_when: A projection that leaves the range the series has ever occupied; a band so wide that any conclusion fits inside it; a pre-period fit that already misses systematically.

diagnostic:its_model_choice.title: Model choice
diagnostic:its_model_choice.one_liner: Which time-series model was fitted, what it was chosen against, and how close the runners-up were.
diagnostic:its_model_choice.plain_language: Which time-series model was fitted, what it was chosen against, and how close the runners-up were.
diagnostic:its_model_choice.in_more_depth: Time-series models differ in how they treat the series' memory -- whether today's value depends on yesterday's, on the surprise in yesterday's, or on the trend needing removal before either. Automatic selection picks the model that scores best on a fit criterion, and often several candidates score almost the same. When they do, the choice is close to arbitrary and it can matter for the estimate. The honest report says which was picked, what the alternatives were, and whether the conclusion holds under them too.
diagnostic:its_model_choice.worry_when: Two very different models scoring almost the same; a chosen model that still leaves correlation in the residuals; differencing forced rather than tested.

diagnostic:its_pre_period.title: Pre-period length
diagnostic:its_pre_period.one_liner: How many periods there are before the change, and whether they are enough to establish what was going to happen anyway.
diagnostic:its_pre_period.plain_language: How many periods there are before the change, and whether they are enough to establish what was going to happen anyway.
diagnostic:its_pre_period.in_more_depth: The counterfactual in this design is the continuation of the earlier trend, so the earlier trend has to be estimable. With six monthly points, one unusual month tilts the whole projected line, and the projection is what the effect is measured against. There is no fixed minimum, but eight to twelve points is a common floor and more is better -- particularly when the series has seasonality, which needs whole cycles rather than points to identify.
diagnostic:its_pre_period.worry_when: Fewer than about eight to twelve pre-period points; or a pre-period so short that a single unusual value tilts the projected line.

diagnostic:its_seasonality.title: Seasonality
diagnostic:its_seasonality.one_liner: Whether a repeating annual or weekly cycle remains in the series after the model has done its work.
diagnostic:its_seasonality.plain_language: Whether a repeating annual or weekly cycle remains in the series after the model has done its work.
diagnostic:its_seasonality.in_more_depth: Admissions rise in winter, sales rise in December, and a policy introduced in January will look effective if the season is not accounted for. The check looks for a cycle left over in what the model could not explain, and it matters most when the interruption falls near a seasonal peak or trough. Over-fitting seasonality has its own cost: terms for twelve months in a short series consume the degrees of freedom the effect needs. The aim is terms the data can actually support.
diagnostic:its_seasonality.worry_when: A cycle surviving in the residuals, particularly one whose peak sits near the interruption; or seasonal terms fitted that the data cannot support.

diagnostic:its_series.title: The series and the interruption
diagnostic:its_series.one_liner: The outcome plotted over time with a line at the date of the change. Read this before anything else.
diagnostic:its_series.plain_language: The outcome plotted over time with a line at the date of the change. Read this before anything else.
diagnostic:its_series.in_more_depth: An interrupted time series has one group and no comparison, so the entire argument is that the series was going one way and then changed. Whether that is visible here decides how much the modelling can be trusted; a model can always fit a step, and this is where you find out whether there is one to fit. Three things are worth checking. That the visible change sits at the marked date rather than before or after it. That the series had not already turned. And that the step is larger than the ordinary period-to-period movement of the series.
diagnostic:its_series.worry_when: The visible jump is at a different date from the marker; the series already turned before the interruption; the level shift is the size of the ordinary month-to-month wobble.

diagnostic:leave_one_out.title: Leave one unit out
diagnostic:leave_one_out.one_liner: Drop one unit -- or one cluster, or one donor -- at a time, refit, and see how far the estimate travels.
diagnostic:leave_one_out.plain_language: Drop one unit -- or one cluster, or one donor -- at a time, refit, and see how far the estimate travels.
diagnostic:leave_one_out.in_more_depth: An estimate that survives dropping any single unit is about a population. An estimate that collapses when one row leaves is about that row. This check does not need a model of anything; it just re-runs the analysis with each unit held out and plots where the answers land. It matters most when the number of units doing the work is small: a synthetic control built from a handful of donors, a panel with few clusters, or a matched analysis where one comparison unit was reused many times.
diagnostic:leave_one_out.worry_when: One omission that changes the answer materially. The estimate is then about that unit, not about the population it claims to describe.

diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.title: Level jump at a kink
diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.one_liner: A kink design assumes the rule changes the slope and not the level. This fits a step at the same threshold to check.
diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.plain_language: A kink design assumes the rule changes the slope and not the level. This fits a step at the same threshold to check.
diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.in_more_depth: Where a benefit formula changes its rate at a threshold, the design reads the change in slope as the effect. That reading requires the level itself to be continuous: if crossing the threshold also delivers a lump sum, or switches on some other entitlement, then a step and a bend are both present and attributing everything to the bend is wrong. The test fits a step in the same window. Finding one does not invalidate the data; it means the threshold does two things, and both should be estimated.
diagnostic:level_jump_at_kink.worry_when: A clear step at the threshold. The rule then changes the level as well as the slope, and the slope change alone is not the whole story.

speaks_to.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff

speaks_to.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

diagnostic:linear_form.title: Linearity of the outcome model
diagnostic:linear_form.one_liner: Whether the answer is being read off the data or produced by the shape the model was told to assume.
diagnostic:linear_form.plain_language: Whether the answer is being read off the data or produced by the shape the model was told to assume.
diagnostic:linear_form.in_more_depth: A marginal structural model reports the parameter of a model you chose -- commonly, that each additional period of treatment adds the same amount. If that is right, the model is a compact and efficient summary. If it is wrong, the number is the parameter of a wrong model rather than the contrast you wanted, and it will not agree with methods that make no such assumption. Refitting with a separate term for each treatment level is the direct check. When the two disagree, the linear form is carrying the estimate rather than describing the data.
diagnostic:linear_form.worry_when: A gap between the model-based number and the version that assumes no shape; or a suspicion that several confounders act together in ways a simple model cannot express.

diagnostic:love.title: Covariate balance (Love plot)
diagnostic:love.one_liner: Absolute standardised differences for every covariate, before and after adjustment, on one axis.
diagnostic:love.plain_language: Absolute standardised differences for every covariate, before and after adjustment, on one axis.
diagnostic:love.in_more_depth: Named after Thomas Love. Each covariate contributes one point before adjustment and one after, so you can see at a glance whether matching or weighting achieved what it promised. The dashed line at 0.1 is a convention. What matters is whether a residual imbalance sits on a variable that strongly predicts the outcome; a large remaining difference on an irrelevant covariate is harmless, and a small one on a powerful predictor is not. Variance ratios are reported alongside: two groups can have the same mean and very different spread, and matching on means alone will not show it.
diagnostic:love.worry_when: Any covariate still far from zero after adjustment; a variance ratio far from one; balance achieved only by discarding much of the sample.

diagnostic:manipulation.title: Density at the cutoff
diagnostic:manipulation.one_liner: Count how many units sit just below the threshold and just above it. A cliff between the two means somebody was steering.
diagnostic:manipulation.plain_language: Count how many units sit just below the threshold and just above it. A cliff between the two means somebody was steering.
diagnostic:manipulation.in_more_depth: The design works because units just either side of the threshold are otherwise alike -- an accident of a decimal place decided who got the programme. That stops being true if people could see the threshold and move themselves across it, because the ones who managed it are precisely those who wanted the treatment most or had the resources to arrange it. The check is a comparison of how densely packed the units are on each side. A smooth transition does not prove nobody manipulated anything; a visible cliff is strong evidence that somebody did.
diagnostic:manipulation.worry_when: Many more units just on the winning side of the cutoff than just below it; scores that pile up on round numbers; a threshold that was public and easy to game.

diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.title: Total = direct + indirect
diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.one_liner: The total effect split into the part that runs through the mediator and the part that does not.
diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.plain_language: The total effect split into the part that runs through the mediator and the part that does not.
diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.in_more_depth: The split is arithmetic: the two parts add to the total by construction, so their adding up is not evidence that either is right. Both pieces rest on the assumption that nothing unmeasured confounds the mediator and the outcome, which is usually harder to defend than the assumption about the treatment itself -- randomising a programme does not randomise how much of it people take up. The proportion mediated is the most-quoted and least-reliable summary here. It is a ratio of two estimates, it is unstable when the total effect is small, and it is not a share of anything at all when the two parts have opposite signs.
diagnostic:mediation_decomposition.worry_when: A proportion mediated quoted on its own; a total effect close to zero; two components with opposite signs.

diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.title: Plug-in bias of the meta-learner
diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.one_liner: Averaging a machine-learning model's per-person predictions gives a different number from the headline estimate, and the headline is the one with an honest interval.
diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.plain_language: Averaging a machine-learning model's per-person predictions gives a different number from the headline estimate, and the headline is the one with an honest interval.
diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.in_more_depth: Flexible learners are deliberately cautious: they pull predictions towards the middle to avoid fitting noise. That shrinkage is what makes them good at ranking people, and it is exactly what makes their average a poor estimate of the average effect -- the bias does not cancel out when you average, and no standard error is available for it. So the two numbers do different jobs. Use the per-person predictions to decide who to prioritise; use the headline, which is built to have a valid interval, to say how large the effect is.
diagnostic:metalearner_plug_in.worry_when: The two numbers are far apart, which measures how much the learner shrank its predictions; quoting the plug-in average as a magnitude would then be wrong.

The number it returns for a treated unit with no comparable control is the model's opinion, and nothing in the coefficient table marks it as such. That is why this product pairs outcome regression with the overlap plot rather than presenting it alone.

diagnostic:multiple_mediators.title: Multiple mediators
diagnostic:multiple_mediators.one_liner: With more than one mediator, the separate pathway effects do not add up to the total, and the shortfall is meaningful.
diagnostic:multiple_mediators.plain_language: With more than one mediator, the separate pathway effects do not add up to the total, and the shortfall is meaningful.
diagnostic:multiple_mediators.in_more_depth: Shifting each mediator on its own and then shifting them together gives three numbers, and the single-mediator effects will generally not sum to the joint one. The difference is what the mediators do jointly -- through interacting with each other, or because one causes another -- and it cannot be assigned to either of them. Pathway effects therefore partition the total only when the mediators neither interact nor cause one another, which is a strong condition and rarely stated when such tables are published.
diagnostic:multiple_mediators.worry_when: Path-specific effects presented as if they partitioned the total; a large difference between the sum of the separate effects and the joint one.

diagnostic:n_matched.title: Match quality
diagnostic:n_matched.one_liner: How many treated units found a partner, how many comparison units were used, and how often the same one was reused.
diagnostic:n_matched.plain_language: How many treated units found a partner, how many comparison units were used, and how often the same one was reused.
diagnostic:n_matched.in_more_depth: Matching without replacement forces bad pairs when the comparison pool is thin; matching with replacement fixes that and concentrates the estimate on a few units, which the effective sample size then reveals. Treated units that found no partner within the caliper leave the analysis, and that changes the estimand: it is now the effect for the treated units that could be matched.
diagnostic:n_matched.worry_when: Many unmatched treated units; one comparison unit reused a large number of times; matches that are close on the score but far apart on the covariates.

diagnostic:natural_course.title: Natural-course calibration
diagnostic:natural_course.one_liner: Simulate the world as it actually was and check that the simulation reproduces the data it was built from.
diagnostic:natural_course.plain_language: Simulate the world as it actually was and check that the simulation reproduces the data it was built from.
diagnostic:natural_course.in_more_depth: Simulation-based methods answer questions by generating fictional worlds from fitted models -- everybody treated, nobody treated, treated under some rule. The one world that can be checked is the one that already happened: let the simulation draw treatment from the fitted model instead of setting it by hand, and the result should look like the observed data. This is the only check on the models these methods depend on. Passing it does not make the intervened worlds correct, since those extrapolate beyond what was observed, but failing it means the machinery is misdescribing even the world it was fitted to.
diagnostic:natural_course.worry_when: A simulated natural course that does not resemble the data it came from. Nothing else checks these models.

diagnostic:negative_control.title: Negative control
diagnostic:negative_control.one_liner: An outcome the treatment cannot possibly have affected. Any effect found there is a measurement of your own bias.
diagnostic:negative_control.plain_language: An outcome the treatment cannot possibly have affected. Any effect found there is a measurement of your own bias.
diagnostic:negative_control.in_more_depth: Choose something that shares the same confounding as your real outcome but that the treatment could not touch -- an event before treatment began, or an unrelated condition. If people who took the treatment also do better on that, the difference cannot be the treatment, so it is whatever else separates the groups. This is more useful than any balance table, because it puts a number on the confounding rather than asserting its absence. A clean negative control is reassuring but not decisive: it rules out one route to a false positive, not all of them.
diagnostic:negative_control.worry_when: A negative control that is not null. The bias it reveals is not confined to the control -- it is a property of the comparison you are making.

diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.title: Nuisance models by fold
diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.one_liner: How well the treatment and outcome models predicted on data they did not see, fold by fold.
diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.plain_language: How well the treatment and outcome models predicted on data they did not see, fold by fold.
diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.in_more_depth: Double machine learning is only as good as its cross-fitting. These numbers tell you whether the nuisance models are learning anything, and whether they are stable: an out-of-fold error that swings wildly means the answer depends on which rows landed where. They are not model-selection criteria. A better-predicting nuisance model does not automatically give a better causal estimate; orthogonality is what protects the estimate, and these diagnostics tell you whether the machinery behind it is behaving.
diagnostic:nuisance_rmse.worry_when: Error or discrimination that varies a lot across folds; a treatment model that predicts treatment almost perfectly, which is a positivity problem in disguise.

diagnostic:oster_assumptions.title: Oster's assumptions
diagnostic:oster_assumptions.one_liner: The two assumptions behind the delta figure, stated plainly, because the number is meaningless without them.
diagnostic:oster_assumptions.plain_language: The two assumptions behind the delta figure, stated plainly, because the number is meaningless without them.
diagnostic:oster_assumptions.in_more_depth: The first is proportional selection: the variables you did not measure are related to the treatment in the same proportion as the ones you did. That would be true if your controls were a random draw from all possible confounders, and they almost never are -- researchers measure what they suspect matters. The second is a value for how well a regression including everything would fit the outcome. It is assumed rather than estimated, usually as a multiple of the fit you achieved, and the bound is sensitive to the choice. Both assumptions are reported here so the bound can be read as the conditional statement it is.
diagnostic:oster_assumptions.worry_when: Controls that were chosen precisely because they were thought to matter, which is exactly when proportional selection is least plausible.

diagnostic:oster_delta.title: Oster delta
diagnostic:oster_delta.one_liner: How much more important the things you did not measure would have to be than the things you did, to explain the result away.
diagnostic:oster_delta.plain_language: How much more important the things you did not measure would have to be than the things you did, to explain the result away.
diagnostic:oster_delta.in_more_depth: The idea starts from something you can watch: how far the estimate moves when you add your control variables, and how much better the model fits once they are in. If adding controls barely moves the estimate but greatly improves the fit, the controls were informative and yet unimportant to the answer -- which is mild evidence that further controls would behave the same way. Delta turns that reasoning into a number. Read it with care. The calculation needs an assumption about how well a regression on absolutely everything would fit, and nothing in your data pins that down; the bound moves a long way as you change it.
diagnostic:oster_delta.worry_when: A delta below 1, which means the conclusion needs the unmeasured variables to matter less than the ones you happened to collect; or a bound that swings as the assumed maximum fit is varied.

diagnostic:outcome_distribution.title: Outcome distribution
diagnostic:outcome_distribution.one_liner: The shape of the outcome in each arm, before any model is fitted.
diagnostic:outcome_distribution.plain_language: The shape of the outcome in each arm, before any model is fitted.
diagnostic:outcome_distribution.in_more_depth: A difference in means is a summary, and summaries hide things. An outcome piled up at zero, a count with a long tail, or a scale where almost everybody gives the same answer will each produce a mean difference, and in each case the mean difference is a poor description of what the treatment did. Look at the shape first. It tells you whether a straight-line model is a reasonable working description, whether the effect might sit at one end of the distribution rather than in the middle, and whether a transformation would change the question you are answering rather than just the units it is answered in.
diagnostic:outcome_distribution.worry_when: A heavy tail; a floor or ceiling that a large share of the sample sits on; two arms with the same mean and visibly different spread.

diagnostic:overid.title: Overidentification test
diagnostic:overid.one_liner: With more instruments than endogenous regressors, a check that they agree with each other.
diagnostic:overid.plain_language: With more instruments than endogenous regressors, a check that they agree with each other.
diagnostic:overid.in_more_depth: Sargan under homoskedasticity, Hansen's J with robust errors. Rejection says at least one instrument is invalid, or that effects are heterogeneous so different instruments identify different local effects. Failing to reject says the instruments agree. If they are all invalid in the same direction, they will agree perfectly, which is why this test is not evidence for the exclusion restriction.
diagnostic:overid.worry_when: A rejection; or a comfortable pass being described as validating exclusion.

diagnostic:overlap.title: Overlap between the arms
diagnostic:overlap.one_liner: The distribution of the estimated probability of treatment, drawn separately for the treated and the untreated. Where they do not overlap, there is no comparison to make.
diagnostic:overlap.plain_language: The distribution of the estimated probability of treatment, drawn separately for the treated and the untreated. Where they do not overlap, there is no comparison to make.
diagnostic:overlap.in_more_depth: Fit a model for the probability of being treated given the covariates, then plot the fitted probabilities by arm. If treated units sit at values no control unit reaches, the estimate for those units is produced by extrapolating the outcome model rather than by comparing anything. The summary reports the share of units outside the common support and how many effective control observations survive reweighting. Both matter: a picture can look reasonable while the effective sample has collapsed.
diagnostic:overlap.worry_when: A long stretch where only one arm appears; a treatment model that separates the groups almost perfectly; an effective control sample far below the nominal one.

speaks_to.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

diagnostic:pair_quality.title: Matched-pair quality
diagnostic:pair_quality.one_liner: How the matched pairs behind a sensitivity analysis were formed, and whether they are the same pairs the headline estimate used.
diagnostic:pair_quality.plain_language: How the matched pairs behind a sensitivity analysis were formed, and whether they are the same pairs the headline estimate used.
diagnostic:pair_quality.in_more_depth: Some sensitivity analyses -- the ones that ask how strong hidden bias would have to be -- are defined on matched pairs. When the main analysis matched differently, with replacement or one treated unit to several controls, the probe has to build its own pairs first, and the number it reports then describes those pairs rather than the estimate on the screen. That is not a bug, but it is a caveat worth carrying into the write-up: the sensitivity statement applies to the paired comparison shown here.
diagnostic:pair_quality.worry_when: The main analysis used a different matching rule from the probe, so the sensitivity number describes pairs the headline never used.

diagnostic:panel_balance.title: Panel balance
diagnostic:panel_balance.one_liner: Whether the same units are present in every period, and when the ones that come and go do so.
diagnostic:panel_balance.plain_language: Whether the same units are present in every period, and when the ones that come and go do so.
diagnostic:panel_balance.in_more_depth: Fixed effects compare a unit with itself over time, which works when the unit is there throughout. Units that appear or disappear mid-panel change the composition of the average, and if they do so around the time treatment arrives, the change in the average is partly a change in who is being averaged. That is selection, not bookkeeping, and no fixed effect removes it. The honest responses are to restrict to a balanced set of units and see whether the answer moves, or to model the entry and exit explicitly.
diagnostic:panel_balance.worry_when: Units entering or leaving the panel around the time they adopt; the composition, rather than the policy, then moves the outcome.
