diagnostic:permutation_distribution.title: Randomisation distribution
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.one_liner: Reshuffle the treatment labels the way the study actually assigned them, thousands of times, and see how unusual the real result looks.
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.plain_language: Reshuffle the treatment labels the way the study actually assigned them, thousands of times, and see how unusual the real result looks.
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.in_more_depth: This is inference that borrows nothing from the bell curve. If the treatment did nothing at all to anybody, then any relabelling of who was treated was equally likely, and the estimate you got should look like a typical draw from the reshuffled ones. The p-value is the share of reshuffles that came out at least as extreme as the real result. The reshuffling has to imitate the real assignment -- inside blocks, whole clusters at a time -- or it is answering a question about a study that was never run. Note also what is being tested: the sharp null that treatment changed nothing for anyone, which is a stronger statement than the usual null that the average effect is zero.
diagnostic:permutation_distribution.worry_when: The reshuffled distribution is not centred near zero, which means the scheme being simulated is not the scheme that produced the data; or so few distinct assignments exist that no small p-value is attainable at all.

speaks_to.title: Randomisation held
speaks_to.explains: Assignment really was by chance, and nothing after assignment broke the comparison -- no differential dropout, no crossover you have not modelled.
speaks_to.worry_when: Dropout differs across arms; take-up is far from assignment; the randomiser was a person with discretion.

diagnostic:person_time.title: Person-time and switching
diagnostic:person_time.one_liner: How many people, over how many periods, following how many distinct treatment histories.
diagnostic:person_time.plain_language: How many people, over how many periods, following how many distinct treatment histories.
diagnostic:person_time.in_more_depth: Methods for treatment that changes over time learn from people whose treatment changes. If almost everybody is either always treated or never treated, there is very little switching to learn from, and the machinery built for time-varying treatment has nothing much to work with. The count of distinct histories is the honest measure of that. It is also the reason these analyses need more data than they appear to: the effective sample is the number of people whose history differs, not the number of person-period rows.
diagnostic:person_time.worry_when: Almost everybody following one of two patterns; there is then little for a time-varying method to learn.

speaks_to.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
speaks_to.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
speaks_to.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

diagnostic:placebo_outcome.title: Placebo outcome
diagnostic:placebo_outcome.one_liner: Run the same analysis on an outcome the treatment should not move. Finding an effect means the design manufactures them.
diagnostic:placebo_outcome.plain_language: Run the same analysis on an outcome the treatment should not move. Finding an effect means the design manufactures them.
diagnostic:placebo_outcome.in_more_depth: The logic is the same as a negative control and the emphasis is different: here the point is to test the design as a whole -- the comparison group, the timing, the adjustment -- rather than to measure confounding specifically. A placebo effect of the same size and sign as the headline is a serious problem, because whatever produced it is presumably also present in the real outcome. A null placebo is worth reporting and is weak evidence: it shows the design did not fail in this particular way.
diagnostic:placebo_outcome.worry_when: A placebo effect of the same size and sign as the headline. The design cannot tell the two apart.

speaks_to.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
speaks_to.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
speaks_to.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.title: Placebo reduced form
diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.one_liner: Check whether the instrument moves outcomes it has no business moving.
diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.plain_language: Check whether the instrument moves outcomes it has no business moving.
diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.in_more_depth: The design requires the instrument to reach the outcome only through the treatment. That cannot be proved, but it can be caught failing: pick outcomes the treatment could not plausibly affect, and see whether the instrument moves them. If it does, there is a second route out of the instrument, and the exclusion restriction is not holding. Nothing moving is worth reporting and is not proof. It narrows the space of violations rather than closing it.
diagnostic:placebo_reduced_form.worry_when: Any placebo outcome the instrument does move. Exclusion cannot be established, but it can be caught failing.

speaks_to.title: Exclusion restriction
speaks_to.explains: The instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment. On the board, that is the arrow you did not draw.
speaks_to.worry_when: The instrument is a policy that changed several things at once; it is correlated with geography, time or institutions that have their own effects; it was chosen because it predicted the outcome.

diagnostic:placebo_treatment.title: Placebo treatment
diagnostic:placebo_treatment.one_liner: Pretend the treatment happened to someone else, or at a date when nothing happened, and see whether the method still finds an effect.
diagnostic:placebo_treatment.plain_language: Pretend the treatment happened to someone else, or at a date when nothing happened, and see whether the method still finds an effect.
diagnostic:placebo_treatment.in_more_depth: A fake treatment has no effect by construction, so anything the analysis reports for it is coming from somewhere else: a trend the design does not handle, a comparison group that was never comparable, or a model flexible enough to fit noise. This is one of the few checks that can demonstrate a problem rather than merely fail to find one, which makes a dirty result here far more informative than a clean one.
diagnostic:placebo_treatment.worry_when: A fake treatment that reproduces the headline effect. Whatever the design is picking up, it is not the policy.

diagnostic:policy_value.title: Honest policy value
diagnostic:policy_value.one_liner: How much better off you would be following the model's recommendation about who to treat, valued on data the model never saw.
diagnostic:policy_value.plain_language: How much better off you would be following the model's recommendation about who to treat, valued on data the model never saw.
diagnostic:policy_value.in_more_depth: A rule learned from data always looks good on that same data. The only honest valuation holds part of the sample back, applies the finished rule to it, and scores what it would have achieved there. That is the number to quote. The comparison that matters is not against treating nobody but against treating everybody, since blanket treatment is usually simpler to run and easier to defend. If the gain over treating everybody has an interval that includes zero, targeting has not been shown to be worth its complexity. Note the interval holds the fitted models fixed, so it is slightly narrower than the truth.
diagnostic:policy_value.worry_when: The held-out value falling well below the in-sample one, which means the rule fitted noise; or a gain over treating everybody whose interval includes zero.

diagnostic:positivity_by_period.title: Positivity by period
diagnostic:positivity_by_period.one_liner: Whether, at every time point, people of every kind had a real chance of both receiving and not receiving the treatment.
diagnostic:positivity_by_period.plain_language: Whether, at every time point, people of every kind had a real chance of both receiving and not receiving the treatment.
diagnostic:positivity_by_period.in_more_depth: Overlap is harder over time than at a single point, because it has to hold at each period and for each history. Once a patient has been on a drug for three periods, almost everybody like them stays on it, and the analysis is then asking what would have happened had they stopped -- a question the data contains no example of. This panel reports the worst period rather than the average, because positivity has to hold everywhere. A single period where treatment is nearly certain contaminates every quantity computed across the whole follow-up.
diagnostic:positivity_by_period.worry_when: A period where nearly everybody is certain to be treated, or certain not to be; the weights and simulated histories there are extrapolation rather than comparison.

speaks_to.title: Positivity / overlap
speaks_to.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
speaks_to.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

diagnostic:pre_trend_size.title: Size of the pre-trend
diagnostic:pre_trend_size.one_liner: The size of the movements in the pre-treatment period, which is the yardstick the robustness bounds are measured against.
diagnostic:pre_trend_size.plain_language: The size of the movements in the pre-treatment period, which is the yardstick the robustness bounds are measured against.
diagnostic:pre_trend_size.in_more_depth: Instead of testing whether the pre-period is flat, the honest approach asks how far trends could have differed after treatment before the conclusion changes -- and expresses that as a multiple of the differences you can see before treatment. This row reports the yardstick: the largest one-period movement in the pre-treatment coefficients, and how large it could plausibly be given the noise in estimating it. Everything reported in units of "relative magnitudes" is measured against this number, so a misleadingly small yardstick makes the robustness bounds look better than they are.
diagnostic:pre_trend_size.worry_when: A pre-period that is flat only because it is imprecisely estimated; a tiny measured wobble with wide intervals makes the bounds look reassuring when they are not.

speaks_to.title: Parallel trends
speaks_to.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
speaks_to.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

diagnostic:pre_trends.title: Pre-trend test
diagnostic:pre_trends.one_liner: A joint test that the pre-treatment coefficients are all zero. Useful, and much weaker evidence than it looks.
diagnostic:pre_trends.plain_language: A joint test that the pre-treatment coefficients are all zero. Useful, and much weaker evidence than it looks.
diagnostic:pre_trends.in_more_depth: Failing to reject is not confirmation. Pre-trend tests often have low power precisely in the situations where a violation would matter, and conditioning the analysis on having passed one distorts the estimates that follow. The better question is the one honest DiD asks: given what the pre-period shows, how far could trends have differed before the conclusion stops holding? That produces a breakdown value rather than a verdict.
diagnostic:pre_trends.worry_when: A test that passes only because the pre-period intervals are enormous; a visible trend that the joint test does not reject.

diagnostic:probe_runs.title: Probe runs
diagnostic:probe_runs.one_liner: How many of the re-runs a probe needed actually produced a number, and why the rest stopped.
diagnostic:probe_runs.plain_language: How many of the re-runs a probe needed actually produced a number, and why the rest stopped.
diagnostic:probe_runs.in_more_depth: A probe such as a placebo test or a specification curve works by running the whole analysis again under changed conditions. Some of those runs fail: a model does not converge, a subsample has nobody in one arm, a bandwidth leaves too few observations. Failures are not neutral and they are not noise. The specifications that could not be estimated are often the demanding ones, so a probe that only reports its successes is quietly reporting the easy half. This row exists so the count is visible next to the conclusion drawn from it.
diagnostic:probe_runs.worry_when: A large share of re-runs failing, especially when the failures cluster in one part of the grid.

diagnostic:propensity_clipping.title: Propensity clipping
diagnostic:propensity_clipping.one_liner: How many units had an estimated chance of treatment so close to zero or one that the analysis had to trim it back before dividing by it.
diagnostic:propensity_clipping.plain_language: How many units had an estimated chance of treatment so close to zero or one that the analysis had to trim it back before dividing by it.
diagnostic:propensity_clipping.in_more_depth: Inverse-probability weighting divides by the estimated chance of getting the treatment you actually got. When that chance is 0.001 the weight is a thousand, and one row swamps everything. The standard defence is clipping: pull extreme probabilities back to a floor and a ceiling before the division. Clipping stabilises the arithmetic and quietly changes the question. The units at the clip are the ones with no counterpart in the other arm, so keeping them at a fictitious probability is a modelling choice, not a measurement. Whichever way you go, the honest report says how many units were clipped and where the boundaries were set.
diagnostic:propensity_clipping.worry_when: More than a few per cent of units sitting at the clip, or one arm reaching probabilities the other never approaches; the estimate is then carried by extrapolation rather than by comparable units.

speaks_to.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

diagnostic:ps_calibration.title: Treatment-model calibration
diagnostic:ps_calibration.one_liner: Within bands of predicted treatment probability, does the share actually treated match the prediction?
diagnostic:ps_calibration.plain_language: Within bands of predicted treatment probability, does the share actually treated match the prediction?
diagnostic:ps_calibration.in_more_depth: A propensity score is only useful if it is a probability. Sorting units into deciles of the predicted probability and comparing with the realised treatment share is the simplest check that the model is not badly misspecified. A badly calibrated treatment model makes every weight derived from it suspect, and a doubly robust estimator loses one of its two chances.
diagnostic:ps_calibration.worry_when: Deciles where the predicted and realised shares are far apart, especially at the extremes where the weights are largest.

diagnostic:random_common_cause.title: Random common cause
diagnostic:random_common_cause.one_liner: Add a variable that is pure noise to the adjustment set. A well-behaved estimate should not move.
diagnostic:random_common_cause.plain_language: Add a variable that is pure noise to the adjustment set. A well-behaved estimate should not move.
diagnostic:random_common_cause.in_more_depth: This is a check on the machinery rather than on the design. A variable generated at random causes nothing and is caused by nothing, so including it should leave the estimate essentially where it was, give or take a little sampling noise. When the estimate does move, the adjustment is unstable -- typically because the model is straining against thin overlap, or has more parameters than the data can support. Passing this check is reassuring about the arithmetic and says nothing whatever about unmeasured confounding.
diagnostic:random_common_cause.worry_when: An estimate that shifts when a variable known to cause nothing is added. That is instability in the adjustment, not evidence about the effect.

speaks_to.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
speaks_to.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

diagnostic:rate.title: Rank-weighted average treatment effect
diagnostic:rate.one_liner: A single number for how much better you would do by treating people in the order the model recommends, rather than at random.
diagnostic:rate.plain_language: A single number for how much better you would do by treating people in the order the model recommends, rather than at random.
diagnostic:rate.in_more_depth: It summarises the curve traced out as you treat progressively more of the population in predicted-benefit order. A RATE indistinguishable from zero means the model's ranking is not usable for targeting, whatever its predictions look like. It has a standard error, which matters: comparing two targeting rules by eye is how people convince themselves of heterogeneity that is not there.

diagnostic:raw_means.title: Raw means by cohort and period
diagnostic:raw_means.one_liner: The average outcome for each group in each period, before any model is fitted.
diagnostic:raw_means.plain_language: The average outcome for each group in each period, before any model is fitted.
diagnostic:raw_means.in_more_depth: This is the picture the whole design argues about. Difference-in-differences claims that, absent the policy, the treated group's line would have continued parallel to the comparison group's. You cannot check that claim after treatment, but you can look at the lines before it, and you can see whether they were the same shape. Everything the estimator does afterwards is a subtraction on these averages. If the lines look wrong here -- crossing, diverging, one of them jumping in a period when nothing happened to it -- no fixed effect further down the pipeline will repair that.
diagnostic:raw_means.worry_when: Lines that already diverge before anyone adopts; a group whose line is a different shape entirely; a jump in a period when nothing happened.

speaks_to.title: Parallel trends
speaks_to.explains: Without the policy, treated and comparison groups would have moved the same way. Not that they were at the same level -- that their paths would have been parallel.
speaks_to.worry_when: Pre-period event-study coefficients drift away from zero; the policy was adopted because outcomes were already moving; the groups differ in composition in ways that interact with time.

diagnostic:rd_plot.title: Binned scatter at the cutoff
diagnostic:rd_plot.one_liner: Average outcomes in narrow bands of the score, either side of the threshold, with the fitted curve drawn through them.
diagnostic:rd_plot.plain_language: Average outcomes in narrow bands of the score, either side of the threshold, with the fitted curve drawn through them.
diagnostic:rd_plot.in_more_depth: This plot is the design. Before any technical choice has been made, it shows whether something happens at the threshold and whether the relationship away from the threshold is smooth enough for a local fit to be believable. The step you can see in the fitted curve at the cutoff is the estimate; nothing else in the analysis adds a jump that is not visible here. In a kink design, where the rule changes the rate rather than the level, you are looking for a bend rather than a step, and the estimate is the change in slope.
diagnostic:rd_plot.worry_when: The binned averages wander in ways the fitted line does not follow; the step at the cutoff is smaller than the wobble in the bands away from it; or very few observations sit in the bands nearest the threshold.

speaks_to.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
speaks_to.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
speaks_to.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

diagnostic:reduced_form.title: Reduced form
diagnostic:reduced_form.one_liner: The direct relationship between the instrument and the outcome, before any division. It is the part of the design that rests on the least.
diagnostic:reduced_form.plain_language: The direct relationship between the instrument and the outcome, before any division. It is the part of the design that rests on the least.
diagnostic:reduced_form.in_more_depth: If the instrument was well assigned, its relationship with the outcome is itself a credible causal effect -- of the encouragement, not of the treatment. That makes it the sturdiest number in an instrumental-variables analysis: no division, no weak-instrument problem, no reliance on how many people the instrument moved. A flat reduced form is decisive in a way the ratio is not. If the encouragement did not move the outcome at all, then either the treatment does nothing or the encouragement did not move treatment, and the ratio of two small numbers will not settle which.
diagnostic:reduced_form.worry_when: A flat reduced form combined with a weak first stage, in which case the ratio can land anywhere; or a reduced form that appears only once a particular control is added.

diagnostic:regime_support.title: Support for the intervention regime
diagnostic:regime_support.one_liner: How many people actually followed the treatment strategy you are asking about.
diagnostic:regime_support.plain_language: How many people actually followed the treatment strategy you are asking about.
diagnostic:regime_support.in_more_depth: A question such as "what if everybody had stayed on treatment for five years" is answerable to the extent that somebody did. If almost nobody in the data followed that path, the estimate is the model's opinion about a history it never saw, and the correction terms that are meant to protect against a wrong model are dividing by a very small probability. A low share is not a reason to abandon the question. It is a reason to say plainly that the answer rests on the model rather than on comparable people.
diagnostic:regime_support.worry_when: Almost nobody following the strategy being asked about; the estimate is then largely the outcome model's extrapolation.

diagnostic:robustness_value.title: Robustness value
diagnostic:robustness_value.one_liner: A single number for how strongly an unmeasured variable would have to be related to both the treatment and the outcome to explain the result away.
diagnostic:robustness_value.plain_language: A single number for how strongly an unmeasured variable would have to be related to both the treatment and the outcome to explain the result away.
diagnostic:robustness_value.in_more_depth: The robustness value is expressed as a share of the variation left over after your controls: a value of 0.05 means a hidden variable explaining five per cent of the remaining variation in treatment and five per cent of the remaining variation in the outcome would be enough to erase the estimate. Its usefulness comes from the benchmark. The same quantity can be computed for the covariates you did measure, so you can say "an unmeasured variable would have to be twice as informative as household income" instead of quoting an abstract number. Note the calculation assumes the hidden variable enters linearly and on its own, so it is a guide, not a guarantee.
diagnostic:robustness_value.worry_when: The strength required is no more than a covariate you already measured. If a variable you happened to collect is that informative, one you did not collect plausibly is too.

diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.title: Rosenbaum bounds
diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.one_liner: For matched pairs: how unequal two apparently identical units' chances of treatment would have to be before the conclusion stops holding.
diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.plain_language: For matched pairs: how unequal two apparently identical units' chances of treatment would have to be before the conclusion stops holding.
diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.in_more_depth: Matching pairs units that look alike on the variables you measured. If something you did not measure still made one of them more likely to be treated, the pair is not the fair comparison it appears to be. The bound asks how large that hidden difference in the odds of treatment would have to be -- a factor of 1.2, of 2, of 5 -- before the result could be explained by it. The number is often called Gamma. It is a statement about a comparison, not a discovery about the world: it does not say a hidden variable exists, only what one would have to do. Note too that it assumes the hidden variable affects treatment but is otherwise summarised by that single factor.
diagnostic:rosenbaum_bounds.worry_when: A breakdown value close to 1. A value of 1.1 means a hidden variable that shifted the odds of treatment by a tenth would suffice, and unmeasured variables routinely do more than that.

speaks_to.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
speaks_to.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
speaks_to.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

designs.title: Adjust for background differences
designs.one_liner: Treatment was not random; we can measure the things that made people get it.

diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.title: Discreteness of the running variable
diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.one_liner: How many distinct values the score actually takes close to the threshold. A handful means this is a comparison of a few groups.
diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.plain_language: How many distinct values the score actually takes close to the threshold. A handful means this is a comparison of a few groups.
diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.in_more_depth: The usual analysis treats the score as continuous, so that units get arbitrarily close to the threshold from both sides. Scores that take only whole numbers, or only a few values, break that picture: there is a nearest value below and a nearest value above, and nothing in between. When that happens the honest treatment is different. Standard errors should allow for units sharing a value, and an analysis that treats the units at the two adjacent values as if they had been randomised fits the situation better than a curve fitted through a handful of points.
diagnostic:running_variable_discreteness.worry_when: Only a few distinct values either side of the threshold inside the window, or a large number of units sitting exactly on the cutoff.

speaks_to.title: Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff
speaks_to.explains: Everything else that affects the outcome changes smoothly through the cutoff, so the only thing that jumps is the treatment.
speaks_to.worry_when: Several rules share the threshold; the running variable is coarse, so "at the cutoff" is really a wide band; the estimate depends heavily on the bandwidth.

designs.title: A cutoff decided eligibility
designs.one_liner: Crossing a score, age, or border switched the programme on.

produced_by.title: Do the covariates jump at the cutoff too?
produced_by.one_liner: Run the same estimator on variables the programme cannot have changed; they should not step at the threshold.

produced_by.title: Did people sort across the cutoff?
produced_by.one_liner: Compare how many units sit just below the threshold with how many sit just above.

produced_by.title: Fuzzy RD (crossing the cutoff only nudged people in)
produced_by.one_liner: Divide the jump in the outcome by the jump in take-up: the effect for the people the cutoff actually moved.

produced_by.title: Regression kink (the rule bends, it does not switch)
produced_by.one_liner: Where a formula changes slope rather than switching on, measure the change in slope of the outcome.

produced_by.title: Sharp RD at the cutoff
produced_by.one_liner: Fit a line either side of the threshold and measure the step between them.

references: Kolesar & Rothe (2018), Inference in regression discontinuity designs with a discrete running variable

diagnostic:sc_augmentation.title: Size of the augmentation correction
diagnostic:sc_augmentation.one_liner: How far the correction for imperfect pre-treatment fit moved the answer.
diagnostic:sc_augmentation.plain_language: How far the correction for imperfect pre-treatment fit moved the answer.
diagnostic:sc_augmentation.in_more_depth: When no blend of comparison places can match the treated place, the augmented method estimates the leftover imbalance and corrects for it, using a fitted model to bridge the gap. This is a deliberate, well-motivated extrapolation, and its size tells you how much of the final answer comes from the model rather than from the comparison. A small correction means the donors were nearly good enough and the correction is a refinement. A large one means the pool was inadequate and the answer is substantially a model's prediction.
diagnostic:sc_augmentation.worry_when: A correction larger than the original estimate; the donors were then far from the treated unit and the outcome model, not the donor pool, is doing the work.

diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.title: Treated unit inside the donor hull
diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.one_liner: Whether any blend of the comparison places could actually reproduce the treated place, or whether it sits outside their range entirely.
diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.plain_language: Whether any blend of the comparison places could actually reproduce the treated place, or whether it sits outside their range entirely.
diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.in_more_depth: A blend with non-negative weights can only land somewhere between the units being blended. If the treated place is more extreme than every comparison place on some characteristic -- richer than all of them, larger than all of them -- then no blend can match it, and the fit will be systematically off in a direction the weights cannot fix. Classic synthetic control refuses to extrapolate and simply fits as best it can. Methods that add a correction term extrapolate deliberately, which is a reasonable response provided the correction is reported and read, not buried.
diagnostic:sc_convex_hull.worry_when: The treated unit sitting outside the range of the donors on characteristics that matter; better optimisation cannot repair that.

diagnostic:sc_gap.title: Treated minus synthetic gap
diagnostic:sc_gap.one_liner: The distance between the treated place and its synthetic twin, period by period. After the intervention, that distance is the estimate.
diagnostic:sc_gap.plain_language: The distance between the treated place and its synthetic twin, period by period. After the intervention, that distance is the estimate.
diagnostic:sc_gap.in_more_depth: Before the intervention the gap should hover near zero -- that is what the weights were chosen to achieve. Afterwards it is free to move, and the movement is the estimated effect. Reading it as a picture rather than as a single number tells you whether the effect arrived suddenly, built up, or faded. The most informative part is often the last stretch before the intervention. A gap that has already started drifting in the direction of the effect indicates anticipation, a mis-dated intervention, or a fit that was never good, and each of those undermines what follows.
diagnostic:sc_gap.worry_when: A gap that is already moving in the direction of the effect before the intervention date.

diagnostic:sc_loo.title: Leave one donor out
diagnostic:sc_loo.one_liner: Drop each contributing comparison place in turn and refit. The estimate should not depend on any single one.
diagnostic:sc_loo.plain_language: Drop each contributing comparison place in turn and refit. The estimate should not depend on any single one.
diagnostic:sc_loo.in_more_depth: Synthetic controls often rest on a few places carrying most of the weight, and those places have their own histories -- a local recession, a different policy, a data revision. Dropping each in turn and refitting shows how much of the estimate is really about the treated unit and how much is about one of its stand-ins. Some movement is expected, since the blend has to be rebuilt each time. What matters is the size of the movement relative to the effect being claimed.
diagnostic:sc_loo.worry_when: Dropping one donor moving the estimate by a large share of the effect itself; the result then rests on one comparison unit rather than on a synthetic one.

diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.title: Matrix-completion rank
diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.one_liner: How flexible the fitted model of untreated behaviour was allowed to be.
diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.plain_language: How flexible the fitted model of untreated behaviour was allowed to be.
diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.in_more_depth: Matrix completion fills in the outcomes that would have been observed if nobody had been treated, by assuming the panel is driven by a small number of underlying patterns shared across units and periods. The rank is how many such patterns were used, and the penalty is what stopped it using more. A higher rank fits the observed data more closely, including its noise. That is why the pre-treatment fit here is not evidence of anything on its own -- the model was fitted on those very periods. The placebo-in-time check is the honest fit test for this family of methods.
diagnostic:sc_mc_rank.worry_when: A high rank, which means the model was flexible enough to fit noise; read the placebo-in-time panel rather than the pre-period fit.

diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.title: Placebo in space
diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.one_liner: Re-run the whole method pretending each comparison place was the treated one. If many of them show a gap as large, the real one is unremarkable.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.plain_language: Re-run the whole method pretending each comparison place was the treated one. If many of them show a gap as large, the real one is unremarkable.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.in_more_depth: With a single treated unit there is no sampling distribution to appeal to, so the yardstick has to be built by pretending. Each comparison place takes a turn as the treated unit and gets its own gap; the real one is then ranked among them. The statistic is usually the post-intervention gap relative to the pre-intervention fit error, because a place that was fitted badly to begin with will show a large gap afterwards for no interesting reason. Note the arithmetic limit: with seventeen comparison places the smallest attainable p-value is about one in eighteen, which is a property of the design and not a shortcoming of the software.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_space.worry_when: Several comparison places showing ratios as large as the treated unit's; or a pool so small that no small p-value is attainable however large the effect.

diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.title: Placebo in time
diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.one_liner: Move the intervention to an earlier date when nothing happened, refit on the earlier data only, and see whether the method finds an effect anyway.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.plain_language: Move the intervention to an earlier date when nothing happened, refit on the earlier data only, and see whether the method finds an effect anyway.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.in_more_depth: This is the cleanest test of whether the method manufactures breaks. Only data from before the real intervention is used, so any apparent effect at the fake date is produced by the fitting rather than by a policy. A large pseudo-effect means either that the pre-period fit is unstable or that the outcome contains breaks of this size routinely, in which case the real one is not distinguishable from them. It needs enough pre-treatment history to be possible at all, which is why it is sometimes unavailable.
diagnostic:sc_placebo_time.worry_when: A sizeable effect at a date when nothing happened; or too little pre-treatment history for the check to run, leaving nothing that rules this out.

diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.title: Pre-treatment fit
diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.one_liner: How closely the weighted combination of comparison places tracked the treated place before the intervention. This is the whole basis of the method.
diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.plain_language: How closely the weighted combination of comparison places tracked the treated place before the intervention. This is the whole basis of the method.
diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.in_more_depth: A synthetic control is a made-up comparison unit: a weighted blend of other places chosen so that the blend follows the treated place through the years before anything happened. If the blend does that well, it is reasonable to let it stand in for what would have happened afterwards. If it does not, there is no argument left. The fit is reported as the typical distance between the two lines before treatment, compared against how much the treated place's own outcome moves about. When that distance is a large share of the outcome's ordinary variation, much of the gap you see afterwards could simply be the same fit error continuing.
diagnostic:sc_pre_fit.worry_when: A pre-treatment fit error that is a large share of the treated unit's own variation; a synthetic that cannot reproduce the pre-period is not a counterfactual.

diagnostic:sc_time_weights.one_liner: Which pre-treatment periods the fit was asked to match most closely.
diagnostic:sc_time_weights.plain_language: Which pre-treatment periods the fit was asked to match most closely.
diagnostic:sc_time_weights.in_more_depth: Some variants of the method weight the earlier periods rather than treating them all alike, concentrating the match on the stretch of history most informative about the years that follow. That is often sensible, and it has a consequence worth seeing: if nearly all the weight sits on one or two periods, the comparison rests on that slice of history. The fitted level difference reported alongside is the other half of the story. Donors can reproduce the shape of the treated unit's path while sitting systematically above or below it, and some methods allow for that explicitly.
diagnostic:sc_time_weights.worry_when: Nearly all the weight on one or two periods; or a large level shift, meaning the donors match the shape but not the level of the treated unit.

diagnostic:sc_weights.title: Donor weights
diagnostic:sc_weights.one_liner: Which comparison places make up the synthetic twin, and how much of it each one is.
diagnostic:sc_weights.plain_language: Which comparison places make up the synthetic twin, and how much of it each one is.
diagnostic:sc_weights.in_more_depth: The method chooses a weighted average of the available comparison units, usually with the weights adding to one and none of them negative, so that the result is a genuine blend rather than an extrapolation. Reading the weights is how you sanity-check the comparison: a synthetic California made mostly of two states is a two-state comparison, and those two states' histories are now your identifying assumption. Sparse weights are normal and not by themselves a problem. Concentration is the thing to notice, because it decides how much of the answer rests on one place's particular circumstances.
diagnostic:sc_weights.worry_when: One donor carrying more than about half the weight; the analysis is then a two-unit comparison in synthetic-control costume, and that donor's own history around the intervention deserves reading.

diagnostic:seed_stability.title: Stability across seeds
diagnostic:seed_stability.one_liner: Repeat the whole procedure with different random splits and see whether the answer stays put.
diagnostic:seed_stability.plain_language: Repeat the whole procedure with different random splits and see whether the answer stays put.
diagnostic:seed_stability.in_more_depth: Cross-fitting divides the data into folds at random, and the division is an arbitrary choice made by a random number generator. If the estimate changes materially when that choice changes, then the reported precision is describing sampling variation while ignoring a second source of variation that is just as real. The remedy when it fires is to average over several splits and to widen the interval accordingly, or to use a simpler learner that is less sensitive to which rows it trained on.
diagnostic:seed_stability.worry_when: A spread across seeds comparable to the standard error, or a sign that changes; the split is arbitrary and the answer should not depend on it.

diagnostic:spec_curve.title: Specification curve
diagnostic:spec_curve.one_liner: Every defensible version of this analysis, sorted from smallest estimate to largest, with the one on your board marked.
diagnostic:spec_curve.plain_language: Every defensible version of this analysis, sorted from smallest estimate to largest, with the one on your board marked.
diagnostic:spec_curve.in_more_depth: Reporting three robustness checks is a sample of size three from a space the analyst chose. Running the grid -- covariate sets, calipers, bandwidths, trimming rules -- and drawing all of the answers puts the whole space on one picture, so a reader can see how much of it supports the conclusion. A finding that holds across most of the curve is stronger than one that holds for three hand-picked variants. A curve that crosses zero says the finding is a specification rather than a result. Where the marked specification sits in the ordering is itself worth reading.
diagnostic:spec_curve.worry_when: A curve that crosses zero; or the specification on the board sitting at one end of the curve rather than in the middle of it.

diagnostic:strategy_paths.title: Treatment strategies compared
diagnostic:strategy_paths.one_liner: The simulated outcome path under each strategy being compared, so you can see when and how they diverge.
diagnostic:strategy_paths.plain_language: The simulated outcome path under each strategy being compared, so you can see when and how they diverge.
diagnostic:strategy_paths.in_more_depth: The headline is a difference at the end of follow-up; the paths show how it got there. A gap that widens steadily is a plausible cumulative effect. A gap that is fully present in the first period, before the treatment could have acted, is a sign the models are picking up differences between the people following each strategy rather than the strategies themselves. Both paths come from the same fitted models, so the difference between them is exactly as good as those models are.
diagnostic:strategy_paths.worry_when: A gap that appears in the first period, before the treatment has had time to act.

diagnostic:subgroups.title: Pre-specified subgroups
diagnostic:subgroups.one_liner: Effects estimated inside named groups, with a reminder of how easily one of them looks impressive by chance.
diagnostic:subgroups.plain_language: Effects estimated inside named groups, with a reminder of how easily one of them looks impressive by chance.
diagnostic:subgroups.in_more_depth: Each subgroup contrast is estimated the same way as the headline, so individually they are sound. The difficulty is collective: with twenty contrasts and no real differences at all, you expect one to cross the conventional threshold by luck, and it is that one that tends to get written up. The defence is to say in advance which subgroups you would examine, and to label everything else as exploration. Where a stricter threshold is appropriate, this panel reports what it would be for the number of contrasts actually run.
diagnostic:subgroups.worry_when: Any of these groups was chosen after seeing the data, or a single significant subgroup is reported without the others beside it.

diagnostic:subset_stability.title: Stability on random subsets
diagnostic:subset_stability.one_liner: Refit the analysis on random parts of the data and see whether the answer stays put.
diagnostic:subset_stability.plain_language: Refit the analysis on random parts of the data and see whether the answer stays put.
diagnostic:subset_stability.in_more_depth: Half the data gives a noisier estimate, and that is expected: the interval should widen by roughly the square root of two. What is not expected is draws that contradict each other, or a spread far wider than the loss of precision explains. That pattern means the estimate depends on which rows happened to be included, which is a different and worse problem than ordinary sampling noise. This is a blunt check and a useful one, because it needs no assumptions beyond the ones the analysis already makes.
diagnostic:subset_stability.worry_when: A spread much wider than the loss of precision explains, or subsets that flip sign while the headline interval excludes zero.

diagnostic:temporal_ordering.title: Temporal ordering of covariates
diagnostic:temporal_ordering.one_liner: A check that every variable used to adjust a decision was measured before that decision was taken.
diagnostic:temporal_ordering.plain_language: A check that every variable used to adjust a decision was measured before that decision was taken.
diagnostic:temporal_ordering.in_more_depth: A variable cannot confound a choice that had already been made. If a measurement was taken after treatment started, adjusting for it does not remove bias; it removes part of the effect, because some of what the treatment did shows up in that measurement. In longitudinal data this is easy to get wrong, because the same variable appears at many time points and only some of them are eligible. The rule is simple to state and worth restating: a covariate may adjust a treatment decision only if it was recorded before that decision.
diagnostic:temporal_ordering.worry_when: A covariate measured after the treatment it is adjusting for.

diagnostic:tmle_targeting.title: Targeting step
diagnostic:tmle_targeting.one_liner: How far the final correction moved the estimate away from the plain outcome model's answer, and whether the correction converged.
diagnostic:tmle_targeting.plain_language: How far the final correction moved the estimate away from the plain outcome model's answer, and whether the correction converged.
diagnostic:tmle_targeting.in_more_depth: Targeted learning starts from an outcome model's prediction and then applies one small correction designed to remove the bias that a prediction-focused model leaves behind. That correction is driven by the treatment probabilities, so its size tells you two things at once: how far off the initial outcome model was, and how extreme the weights are. A small, cleanly converged correction is the healthy case. A large one is not automatically wrong, but it means the answer is coming from the correction rather than from the model it corrected, and the overlap diagnostics are then the ones to read.
diagnostic:tmle_targeting.worry_when: A large correction, or an equation the step failed to solve; both point back to extreme treatment probabilities.

diagnostic:treatment_mediator_interactio.title: Treatment-mediator interaction
diagnostic:treatment_mediator_interactio.one_liner: Whether the mediator does the same work whether or not the treatment is on.
diagnostic:treatment_mediator_interactio.plain_language: Whether the mediator does the same work whether or not the treatment is on.
diagnostic:treatment_mediator_interactio.in_more_depth: If it does, the decomposition into direct and indirect effects is unambiguous. If it does not -- if the treatment changes how much the mediator matters -- then there are two mirror-image ways of splitting the total, they disagree, and neither is more correct than the other. Which one gets reported becomes an unstated choice. A model fitted without an interaction term assumes the question away rather than answering it, which is why the term is tested rather than omitted.
diagnostic:treatment_mediator_interactio.worry_when: A strong interaction reported as a single direct effect; or a real interaction forced to zero, so the decomposition depends on which mirror you happened to report.

diagnostic:trim_cost.title: What trimming costs
diagnostic:trim_cost.one_liner: How many units a proposed trimming rule would drop, and who they are.
diagnostic:trim_cost.plain_language: How many units a proposed trimming rule would drop, and who they are.
diagnostic:trim_cost.in_more_depth: Trimming discards units whose estimated chance of treatment is too extreme for a stable comparison. It is a defensible response to poor overlap, and it is not free: the units dropped are not a random sample, they are precisely the ones least like anybody in the other arm. After trimming, the estimate refers to the units that remain. If a fifth of the treated group has gone, "the effect of the programme on participants" is no longer what the number means, and the sample flow records the change so the report can say so.
diagnostic:trim_cost.worry_when: A threshold that drops a large share of the treated units, which has quietly redefined who the answer is about.

speaks_to.title: Positivity / overlap
speaks_to.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.

diagnostic:trim_stability.title: Stability across trimming thresholds
diagnostic:trim_stability.one_liner: The estimate recomputed at a range of trimming thresholds, so you can see whether the units in the tails are deciding it.
diagnostic:trim_stability.plain_language: The estimate recomputed at a range of trimming thresholds, so you can see whether the units in the tails are deciding it.
diagnostic:trim_stability.in_more_depth: If the estimate barely moves as you trim more aggressively, the tails were not doing much and the finding is about the bulk of the data. If it walks steadily in one direction, the answer is being set by the units with the least comparable counterparts -- the ones the model had to extrapolate for. There is no threshold that is correct in general. The point of the curve is to make the choice visible rather than to make it for you, and to let a reader see whether the headline sits in the middle of the range or at one end of it.
diagnostic:trim_stability.worry_when: The estimate walks steadily as you trim, or changes sign anywhere along the path.

diagnostic:unobserved_confounder.title: Simulated unobserved confounder
diagnostic:unobserved_confounder.one_liner: Nobody can prove there is no missing common cause. This asks the answerable question instead: how strong would one have to be to overturn the finding?
diagnostic:unobserved_confounder.plain_language: Nobody can prove there is no missing common cause. This asks the answerable question instead: how strong would one have to be to overturn the finding?
diagnostic:unobserved_confounder.in_more_depth: Every adjustment in an observational design rests on having measured the things that pushed people towards treatment and also move the outcome. That assumption cannot be checked against the data, because the variables in question are precisely the ones you do not have. What can be done is to imagine one and see what it would need to look like. If a variable would have to be more strongly related to both the treatment and the outcome than anything you actually measured, the finding is fairly robust. If an ordinary, unremarkable variable would be enough, it is not. That comparison -- against the covariates you did collect -- is what makes the exercise informative rather than decorative.
diagnostic:unobserved_confounder.worry_when: A confounder weaker than the ones you did measure would be enough to take the estimate to zero.

diagnostic:weak_iv_set.title: Weak-instrument-robust set
diagnostic:weak_iv_set.one_liner: A confidence set built by inverting a test that stays valid however weak the instrument is. It can be an interval, several intervals, or the whole line.
diagnostic:weak_iv_set.plain_language: A confidence set built by inverting a test that stays valid however weak the instrument is. It can be an interval, several intervals, or the whole line.
diagnostic:weak_iv_set.in_more_depth: The usual two-stage least squares interval assumes the instrument is strong. When it is not, that interval is simply wrong -- too narrow, and centred in the wrong place. The Anderson-Rubin set makes no such assumption. An unbounded set is not a failure of the method: it is the correct statement that the data cannot pin the parameter down, and reporting a tidy interval instead would be the failure.
diagnostic:weak_iv_set.worry_when: The robust set is much wider than the Wald interval, or unbounded, while the Wald interval looks precise.

diagnostic:weighted_balance.title: Balance after weighting
diagnostic:weighted_balance.one_liner: Whether, after weighting, the treated and untreated person-periods look alike on the variables the weights were built from.
diagnostic:weighted_balance.plain_language: Whether, after weighting, the treated and untreated person-periods look alike on the variables the weights were built from.
diagnostic:weighted_balance.in_more_depth: Weighting for time-varying treatment is meant to create a pseudo-population in which the treatment decision at each period is unrelated to everything measured up to that point. This table is the check on whether it did: every covariate at every period, compared between the person-periods where treatment was given and those where it was not, after the weights are applied. The check deliberately uses the raw rather than the stabilised weights, because it is the raw ones that define the pseudo-population balance is supposed to hold in. Residual imbalance means the treatment model has not removed the confounding it was there to remove -- which is a modelling failure, and separate from the untestable assumption that everything relevant was measured at all.
diagnostic:weighted_balance.worry_when: Covariates still far apart after weighting, especially ones that strongly predict the outcome.

diagnostic:weights_by_period.title: Weights by period
diagnostic:weights_by_period.one_liner: How much of the sample survives, in effective terms, as the weights accumulate across periods.
diagnostic:weights_by_period.plain_language: How much of the sample survives, in effective terms, as the weights accumulate across periods.
diagnostic:weights_by_period.in_more_depth: Weighting for time-varying treatment multiplies one weight per period together, so the product grows more extreme the longer the follow-up. A history that was mildly unusual at each of eight time points can end up with an enormous cumulative weight, and the estimate then rests on a handful of people. Watching the effective sample fall period by period is the clearest early warning this design gives. The point estimate will not show it, and neither will the standard error, which assumes the weighting worked.
diagnostic:weights_by_period.worry_when: The effective sample collapsing as more periods are multiplied in, or one history carrying a large share of the weight.

concept:concept.about.title: About Causal Capybara
concept:concept.about.one_liner: A desktop studio for applied causal inference. Serious causal inference, casual to use.
concept:concept.about.plain_language: A desktop studio for applied causal inference. Serious causal inference, casual to use.
concept:concept.about.in_more_depth: The object of work here is a causal question, not an equation. You state the question in ordinary language, complete a picture of the research design, look at the diagnostics that design depends on, and then estimate -- usually with several methods at once, because the disagreement between them is part of what you learned. Everything runs locally. Your data does not leave this machine unless you export it, and there is no telemetry. The engines are the R and Python packages the field already publishes with; this application orchestrates them, records what was assumed, and refuses to present an estimate as causal because of the estimator's name. concept:concept.caliper.title: Caliper
concept:concept.caliper.one_liner: The largest difference you are willing to tolerate inside a matched pair. Beyond it the treated unit is left unmatched rather than paired with somebody unlike them.
concept:concept.caliper.plain_language: The largest difference you are willing to tolerate inside a matched pair. Beyond it the treated unit is left unmatched rather than paired with somebody unlike them.
concept:concept.caliper.in_more_depth: Matching pairs each treated unit with the most similar untreated one available -- but "the most similar available" can still be very dissimilar when the comparison pool is thin. A caliper puts a bound on the gap, usually stated as a fraction of the spread of the estimated treatment probability, and refuses the pair when nothing falls inside it. The trade is explicit. A tight caliper gives better-matched pairs and drops more treated units; a loose one keeps everybody and admits worse comparisons. The dropping is not just a loss of precision: the question changes with it, because the answer now describes the treated units that could be matched rather than all of them. That is why the count of unmatched treated units belongs beside the estimate rather than in a footnote.

concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.title: Cluster-robust standard errors
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.one_liner: A way of computing uncertainty that treats each group -- a school, a village, a clinic -- as one group's worth of independent evidence, rather than counting every row inside it separately.
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.plain_language: A way of computing uncertainty that treats each group -- a school, a village, a clinic -- as one group's worth of independent evidence, rather than counting every row inside it separately.
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.in_more_depth: If a whole school was assigned to the programme together, its pupils do not each carry separate evidence about whether the programme works: they share a headteacher, a catchment and a year. An interval computed as though the pupils were independent counts the same information over and over and comes out far too narrow, so an effect looks settled when it is not. The cluster-robust version allows rows within a group to be related in any way at all, and assumes only that different groups are independent of each other. What it needs in return is enough groups. Its accuracy grows with the number of clusters, not the number of rows, and with only a couple of dozen it becomes optimistic again -- which is the point at which a small-sample correction, or reshuffling whole clusters at a time, is the safer route.
concept:concept.cluster_robust_se.common_mistake: Clustering at the wrong level -- on the individual when assignment was by school, or on the year when the policy varied by state. The rule is to cluster at the level treatment was assigned.

see_also.title: Clustering
see_also.one_liner: When treatment was assigned to whole groups -- states, schools, clinics -- the number of independent observations is closer to the number of groups than the number of rows.

see_also.title: Cluster-randomised trial
see_also.one_liner: When whole schools, clinics or villages were assigned, the number of clusters is the sample size that matters.

concept:concept.clustering.title: Clustering
concept:concept.clustering.one_liner: When treatment was assigned to whole groups -- states, schools, clinics -- the number of independent observations is closer to the number of groups than the number of rows.
concept:concept.clustering.plain_language: When treatment was assigned to whole groups -- states, schools, clinics -- the number of independent observations is closer to the number of groups than the number of rows.
concept:concept.clustering.in_more_depth: Standard errors that ignore the group structure can be several times too small, which turns a null result into a finding. The rule of thumb is to cluster at the level treatment was assigned at, which is usually coarser than the level the data is stored at. With few clusters -- under about forty -- the usual cluster-robust correction is itself unreliable, and the honest move is a small-sample correction, a t distribution with the number of clusters minus one, or a cluster bootstrap. This product states which one it used on every result.
concept:concept.clustering.worry_when: Fewer than about forty clusters; very unequal cluster sizes; clustering at a finer level than treatment was assigned.
references: Cameron & Miller (2015), A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference

concept:concept.collider.title: Colliders and why adjusting can hurt
concept:concept.collider.one_liner: A variable that two arrows point into. Conditioning on it creates an association between its causes that was not there before.
concept:concept.collider.plain_language: A variable that two arrows point into. Conditioning on it creates an association between its causes that was not there before.
concept:concept.collider.in_more_depth: Suppose talent and looks both help an actor get hired, and are unrelated in the population. Among people who were hired, the two become negatively related: if someone got in without much talent, they probably had looks. Nothing caused that association except your decision to look only at the hired. The same thing happens whenever you adjust for a variable that treatment and outcome both influence, or condition on a sample selected on such a variable. It is bias you added.
concept:concept.collider.common_mistake: Treating "adjust for more covariates" as always safer. Colliders and post-treatment variables make it worse.
references: Elwert & Winship (2014), Endogenous selection bias

concept:concept.complete_case.title: Complete-case analysis
concept:concept.complete_case.one_liner: Dropping every row that is missing any value the analysis needs and computing on what is left. Most software does this silently.
concept:concept.complete_case.plain_language: Dropping every row that is missing any value the analysis needs and computing on what is left. Most software does this silently.
concept:concept.complete_case.in_more_depth: The rows that survive are not a random sample of the rows you started with. If the people doing badly were also the ones more likely to skip the follow-up, the surviving sample is healthier than the population it is meant to describe, and every number computed on it inherits that. The bias can run in either direction, and how large it is cannot be read off the rows that remain. It is not always wrong. If whatever drove the missingness is unrelated to the outcome once you account for the variables you kept, complete cases are unbiased and merely less precise. The honest minimum is to report how many rows went, and whether they went from the treated and untreated groups at the same rate.
concept:concept.complete_case.common_mistake: Reporting the analysis sample size without the starting one, so a third of the data can disappear without anybody noticing.

concept:concept.confounding.title: Confounding
concept:concept.confounding.one_liner: A common cause of both the treatment and the outcome makes the two look related even when the treatment does nothing.
concept:concept.confounding.plain_language: A common cause of both the treatment and the outcome makes the two look related even when the treatment does nothing.
concept:concept.confounding.in_more_depth: If healthier people are both more likely to take a drug and more likely to survive, the drug looks effective whether or not it is. Adjusting means comparing treated and untreated units that match on the common cause, so that the remaining difference cannot be explained by it. The hard part is not the arithmetic; it is knowing what the common causes are. Adjustment can only handle the ones you measured, which is why the exchangeability assumption stays untested no matter how good the balance plot looks.
concept:concept.confounding.common_mistake: Adjusting for everything available. Some variables -- descendants of the treatment, and colliders -- introduce bias when you condition on them.

concept:concept.consort.one_liner: A step-by-step record of how the imported rows became the analysis sample, with a reason for every row that left.
concept:concept.consort.plain_language: A step-by-step record of how the imported rows became the analysis sample, with a reason for every row that left.
concept:concept.consort.in_more_depth: Borrowed from the CONSORT diagrams of clinical trials. Complete-case drops, caliper failures, trimming, bandwidth truncation and donor restrictions all appear as explicit steps. The rule behind it is that no estimator in this product is allowed to silently change the population an estimate refers to. If matching could not find a partner for a fifth of the treated units, the estimand is now the effect for the other four fifths, and the flow says so.

concept:concept.cross_fitting.title: Cross-fitting
concept:concept.cross_fitting.one_liner: Fit the nuisance models on one part of the data and apply them to another, so a flexible learner cannot fit its own noise into the effect estimate.
concept:concept.cross_fitting.plain_language: Fit the nuisance models on one part of the data and apply them to another, so a flexible learner cannot fit its own noise into the effect estimate.
concept:concept.cross_fitting.in_more_depth: Machine-learning models for the treatment and outcome overfit, and if the same rows fit the model and enter the score, the overfitting shows up as bias in the estimate and as a confidence interval that is too narrow. Splitting into folds, fitting on the complement and predicting on the held- out fold removes that route, at the price of a little variance. It is what makes double machine learning honest, and it is why the fold diagnostics are mandatory whenever a learner is used: if the estimate swings wildly across folds, the answer depends on the split.
references: Chernozhukov et al. (2018), Double/debiased machine learning

see_also.title: Honest splitting
see_also.one_liner: Use one half of the data to decide where the subgroups are and the other half to estimate their effects.

concept:concept.cross_world.title: Cross-world assumptions
concept:concept.cross_world.one_liner: A condition relating outcomes under treatment and mediator values that no single person could ever experience together. Not testable, even in principle.
concept:concept.cross_world.plain_language: A condition relating outcomes under treatment and mediator values that no single person could ever experience together. Not testable, even in principle.
concept:concept.cross_world.in_more_depth: Natural direct and indirect effects need you to compare what would happen if a person were treated but their mediator took the value it would have taken untreated. No experiment can create that world for anyone, so no experiment can check the assumption. This is why interventional (stochastic) direct and indirect effects are preferred in policy and health settings: they replace the impossible comparison with one where the mediator is drawn from a distribution, which a trial could in principle implement.
references: Robins & Richardson (2010)
VanderWeele, Vansteelandt & Robins (2014)

see_also.title: Sequential ignorability
see_also.explains: No unmeasured confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship, and none of the mediator-outcome relationship either, even after conditioning on treatment.
see_also.worry_when: There is a variable affected by treatment that also confounds the mediator-outcome relationship. Under that structure the natural effects are not identified at all.

see_also.title: Interventional direct and indirect effects
see_also.one_liner: Shift the mediator to the distribution it would have in the population, rather than to each person's own unobservable counterfactual.

concept:concept.donor_pool.title: The donor pool
concept:concept.donor_pool.one_liner: The set of untreated places a synthetic comparison is allowed to be built from. Choosing it is a research decision, not a technical one.
concept:concept.donor_pool.plain_language: The set of untreated places a synthetic comparison is allowed to be built from. Choosing it is a research decision, not a technical one.
concept:concept.donor_pool.in_more_depth: A synthetic control builds its stand-in by blending other units, and it can only blend the ones you put in front of it. Include somewhere that got its own version of the policy and the comparison is contaminated by it. Include somewhere with nothing in common with the treated place and it will simply receive a weight of zero -- harmless, but it makes the pool look larger than it really is. Leave out the one place that would have matched well and the fit suffers for a reason nothing in the output will name. The pool also fixes how strong the placebo evidence can be. The treated unit's gap is judged against the gaps you get by pretending each donor was treated instead, so five donors give five comparisons, and "more extreme than all of them" is a one-in-six statement. No amount of computing makes it a stronger one.
concept:concept.donor_pool.common_mistake: Treating the pool as given because it arrived with the dataset. Write down why each unit is in it and why the excluded ones are out; that list is part of the design and belongs in the write-up.

see_also.title: Synthetic control
see_also.one_liner: Build a weighted copy of the treated place out of untreated places that looked like it beforehand, then watch the two lines separate.

see_also.title: Treated unit inside the donor hull
Pre-treatment fit from the donor pool
see_also.explains: The weighted combination of untreated units reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path closely enough to stand in for it afterwards.
see_also.worry_when: Visible pre-period gaps; a short pre-period relative to the number of donors; one donor carrying most of the weight.

concept:concept.effective_sample_size.title: Effective sample size
concept:concept.effective_sample_size.one_liner: How many observations your weighted comparison is really worth. Almost always smaller than the number of rows, sometimes dramatically.
concept:concept.effective_sample_size.plain_language: How many observations your weighted comparison is really worth. Almost always smaller than the number of rows, sometimes dramatically.
concept:concept.effective_sample_size.in_more_depth: Weighting a comparison group to resemble the treated group concentrates the analysis on the few comparison units that actually resemble them. Kish's effective sample size expresses that concentration as a count: a thousand rows with wildly unequal weights can be worth eighty observations. It is the honest denominator. When it collapses, the confidence interval is narrower than the evidence, and the estimate rests on a handful of units whose individual peculiarities now matter.
concept:concept.effective_sample_size.worry_when: The effective sample is below about 40% of the nominal one, or a single weight carries more than a fifth of the total.

see_also.title: Positivity / overlap
see_also.explains: Every kind of unit had some chance of being treated and some chance of not being treated. Where that fails, there is no comparison to make and the model is inventing one.
see_also.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

see_also.title: Average treatment effect on the overlap population
see_also.one_liner: For the people where treated and untreated genuinely overlap, what did it do?

concept:concept.estimand_first.title: Estimand first, estimator second
concept:concept.estimand_first.one_liner: Decide what number you want before deciding how to compute it. The estimator does not define the question; the question restricts the estimators.
concept:concept.estimand_first.plain_language: Decide what number you want before deciding how to compute it. The estimator does not define the question; the question restricts the estimators.
concept:concept.estimand_first.in_more_depth: "The effect of the programme" is not yet a quantity. For whom -- everyone, the people who took it up, the people at the eligibility cutoff, the people an encouragement moved? Against what -- no programme, the old programme, the programme at a different dose? Different designs identify different estimands, and this is why the app shows unavailable estimands greyed rather than hiding them: it is telling you what your design cannot answer, which is usually more useful than what it can.

see_also.title: Average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: If everyone got the programme, how would the average outcome change?

see_also.title: Average treatment effect on the treated
see_also.one_liner: For people who actually got it, what did it do?

see_also.title: Local average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: For people who only got it because of the instrument or the cutoff, what did it do?

see_also.title: I already know the method

concept:concept.forest_plot.title: The forest plot, and why there is no headline number
concept:concept.forest_plot.one_liner: One row per method, each with its interval. When several methods ran, the forest is the result -- not a single number chosen from it.
concept:concept.forest_plot.plain_language: One row per method, each with its interval. When several methods ran, the forest is the result -- not a single number chosen from it.
concept:concept.forest_plot.in_more_depth: Picking the estimate you liked best after seeing them all is how honest people produce dishonest research. This product therefore shows a headline number only when exactly one method ran; otherwise the range across defensible methods is the finding, and the generated prose describes the range. You can nominate a preferred estimate for a report. It is stored as a choice and displayed as a choice, not as a conclusion.

see_also.title: Specification curve

see_also.title: Provisional results

concept:concept.honest_splitting.title: Honest splitting
concept:concept.honest_splitting.one_liner: Use one half of the data to decide where the subgroups are and the other half to estimate their effects.
concept:concept.honest_splitting.plain_language: Use one half of the data to decide where the subgroups are and the other half to estimate their effects.
concept:concept.honest_splitting.in_more_depth: If the same rows choose the split and estimate the effect inside it, the estimate is biased upwards by construction: the split was chosen because the effect looked large there. Honest trees and honest forests avoid it by separating the two jobs inside every tree. The price is variance -- half the rows for each job -- which is why honest methods need more data than they first appear to. The reward is a heterogeneity estimate you can believe.
references: Athey & Imbens (2016), Recursive partitioning for heterogeneous causal effects

see_also.title: Honest causal forest
see_also.one_liner: Grow trees that look for units whose effect differs, keeping the rows that chose each split away from the rows that estimate it.

see_also.title: Conditional average treatment effect
see_also.one_liner: How does the effect vary from person to person, or place to place?

see_also.title: Subgroups and multiplicity
see_also.one_liner: Look at enough subgroups and one will look impressive. Pre-specify them, or report that you did not.

concept:concept.multiplicity.title: Subgroups and multiplicity
concept:concept.multiplicity.one_liner: Look at enough subgroups and one will look impressive. Pre-specify them, or report that you did not.
concept:concept.multiplicity.plain_language: Look at enough subgroups and one will look impressive. Pre-specify them, or report that you did not.
concept:concept.multiplicity.in_more_depth: With twenty subgroups and no real heterogeneity, you expect one significant result at the 5% level. The problem is not the arithmetic, it is that the subgroup gets written up as a finding and the other nineteen do not appear. Causal Capybara marks subgroup estimates as a separate group in the results and attaches a multiplicity caution rather than presenting them as a table of independent findings. For discovered rather than pre-specified heterogeneity, the calibration test and the rank-weighted effect are the honest summaries.
