concept:concept.negative_control.title: Negative controls
concept:concept.negative_control.one_liner: A variable that shares your suspected confounding but cannot be affected by the treatment. An effect there is a measurement of your bias.
concept:concept.negative_control.plain_language: A variable that shares your suspected confounding but cannot be affected by the treatment. An effect there is a measurement of your bias.
concept:concept.negative_control.in_more_depth: If a vaccine appears to prevent injuries as well as influenza, the apparent influenza effect is at least partly healthy-user bias. That is more useful than any test of balance, because it puts a number on the confounding rather than asserting its absence. Negative-control exposures work the same way in reverse: something that could not cause the outcome but shares its confounders.
references: Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen & Cohen (2010), Negative controls

see_also.title: Negative control
see_also.one_liner: Estimate something that shares the confounding but not the causal path. A non-zero answer is bias you can see.

see_also.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
see_also.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
see_also.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

concept:concept.not_yet_treated.title: Not-yet-treated comparisons
concept:concept.not_yet_treated.one_liner: Units that do adopt the policy, but later. While they are still waiting they can serve as the comparison group for units that adopted earlier.
concept:concept.not_yet_treated.plain_language: Units that do adopt the policy, but later. While they are still waiting they can serve as the comparison group for units that adopted earlier.
concept:concept.not_yet_treated.in_more_depth: The obvious comparison group in a staggered design is the units that never adopt. Sometimes there are very few of them, and they are often unusual for the very reason they never adopted. The alternative is to borrow from the future: in 2006 a state that adopts in 2011 is untreated, and it probably resembles a 2007 adopter more closely than a permanent hold-out does. Two costs come with it. The pool thins as the panel runs on and more units switch on, so the later periods rest on fewer comparisons than the early ones. And it assumes those waiting units are not already reacting to a policy they can see coming, which is the no-anticipation assumption doing real work rather than sitting decoratively in the ledger.

see_also.title: Staggered adoption
see_also.one_liner: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.

see_also.title: No anticipation
see_also.explains: Units did not change behaviour before treatment arrived because they knew it was coming.
see_also.worry_when: There was a public announcement well before the policy started, or the pre-period coefficients move in the period immediately before adoption.

gaps: no citation

concept:concept.placebo.title: Placebo tests
concept:concept.placebo.one_liner: Run the same analysis somewhere the effect cannot exist. If you find one, the design is producing effects that are not there.
concept:concept.placebo.plain_language: Run the same analysis somewhere the effect cannot exist. If you find one, the design is producing effects that are not there.
concept:concept.placebo.in_more_depth: A placebo outcome is one the treatment should not touch. A placebo treatment is a fake date or a permuted assignment. A placebo unit is a donor treated as though it had been intervened on. Each asks the same question: does this design manufacture findings? A clean placebo is reassuring and not decisive -- it rules out one route to a false positive, not all of them. A dirty placebo is much more informative, because it demonstrates a problem rather than failing to find one.

see_also.title: Placebo outcome
see_also.one_liner: Run the same analysis on something the treatment could not have changed. It should find nothing.

see_also.title: Placebo treatment
see_also.one_liner: Move the policy date earlier, reshuffle who was treated, or swap in a variable that cannot cause the outcome.

see_also.title: Synthetic control placebos
see_also.one_liner: Re-run the whole method pretending each donor was the treated unit. If many donors show a gap as large, the real one is unremarkable.

gaps: no citation

concept:concept.provisional.title: Provisional results
concept:concept.provisional.one_liner: A result the product does not think you should trust as it stands. It still computed it; it just will not let the flag disappear.
concept:concept.provisional.plain_language: A result the product does not think you should trust as it stands. It still computed it; it just will not let the flag disappear.
concept:concept.provisional.in_more_depth: A run is marked provisional when something specific happened: the core diagnostic for the design was never opened, the weights are degenerate, the instrument is weak, a staggered panel was estimated with two-way fixed effects, matching dropped part of the treated group, or a synthetic control could not reproduce the pre-period. The flag travels. It appears on the forest plot as a different marker, in the estimates table, in the navigator, in the status bar's count, and in the generated report. You can always proceed; you cannot quietly proceed.

see_also.worry_when: Any single weight carries a large share of the total; the effective sample is far below the nominal one; the propensity model separates the arms almost perfectly; treated units sit outside the control group's range.

concept:concept.selection_bias.title: Selection bias
concept:concept.selection_bias.one_liner: Who ends up in your analysis sample can create an association all by itself, quite apart from confounding.
concept:concept.selection_bias.plain_language: Who ends up in your analysis sample can create an association all by itself, quite apart from confounding.
concept:concept.selection_bias.in_more_depth: Dropout that differs by treatment arm, complete-case analysis when missingness depends on the outcome, and administrative samples that only record people who reached a certain stage all condition on a consequence of the very things you are studying. This is why every dropped row appears in the sample flow with a reason. The flow is not bookkeeping: it is the record of which selections you made, so that you and a reader can judge whether any of them was a collider.

see_also.title: Colliders and why adjusting can hurt
see_also.one_liner: A variable that two arrows point into. Conditioning on it creates an association between its causes that was not there before.

see_also.title: The sample flow
see_also.one_liner: A step-by-step record of how the imported rows became the analysis sample, with a reason for every row that left.

concept:concept.spec_curve.title: Specification curve
concept:concept.spec_curve.one_liner: Every defensible version of the analysis, sorted by estimate, so you can see the whole distribution instead of one draw from it.
concept:concept.spec_curve.plain_language: Every defensible version of the analysis, sorted by estimate, so you can see the whole distribution instead of one draw from it.
concept:concept.spec_curve.in_more_depth: A robustness check that reports three alternative specifications is a sample of size three from a space the analyst chose. A specification curve runs the grid -- covariate sets, calipers, bandwidths, trimming thresholds -- and plots all of them with the headline marked. A conclusion that survives most of the curve is stronger than one that survives three hand-picked variants. A curve that swings through zero tells you the finding is a specification, not a result.
references: Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson (2020), Specification curve analysis

see_also.title: Specification curve
see_also.one_liner: Run the grid of defensible specifications and sort the answers. The curve is the result, not the one you happened to run.

see_also.one_liner: One row per method, each with its interval. When several methods ran, the forest is the result -- not a single number chosen from it.

concept:concept.staggered_adoption.title: Staggered adoption
concept:concept.staggered_adoption.one_liner: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.
concept:concept.staggered_adoption.plain_language: Units switch the policy on at different dates rather than all at once. It is the ordinary case in policy data, and it breaks the simplest before-and-after arithmetic.
concept:concept.staggered_adoption.in_more_depth: With a single adoption date the comparison is easy to state: adopters against non-adopters, before against after. When states adopt in 2004, 2009 and 2013, one regression coefficient has to combine many overlapping comparisons, and some of them treat a unit that is already under the policy as though it were an untreated control. If the effect grows or fades after adoption, those comparisons subtract one real effect from another and can drag the average towards zero, or past it. Estimators built for staggered adoption avoid this by never using an already-treated unit as a control. They compute one effect for each adoption cohort in each period and then average those blocks with weights you can look at and argue with.

see_also.title: Two-way fixed effects
see_also.one_liner: A regression that gives every unit its own baseline level and every period its own shift, so only change within a unit over time is compared. It is the workhorse behind difference-in-differences, and it misbehaves when units adopt at different dates.

see_also.title: Not-yet-treated comparisons
see_also.one_liner: Units that do adopt the policy, but later. While they are still waiting they can serve as the comparison group for units that adopted earlier.

see_also.title: Callaway & Sant'Anna group-time effects
see_also.one_liner: Estimate one clean before-and-after for every adoption cohort, then say out loud how you averaged them.

concept:concept.standardised_difference.title: Standardised mean difference
concept:concept.standardised_difference.one_liner: The gap between groups on a covariate, divided by a pooled standard deviation, so covariates on different scales can be compared on one axis.
concept:concept.standardised_difference.plain_language: The gap between groups on a covariate, divided by a pooled standard deviation, so covariates on different scales can be compared on one axis.
concept:concept.standardised_difference.in_more_depth: It is the number a Love plot shows, before and after adjustment. The convention of worrying above 0.1 is a convention, not a law -- it comes from simulation studies, and what matters is whether a residual imbalance is on a variable that strongly predicts the outcome. Unlike a t-test of balance, it does not shrink as the sample grows, which is why balance is judged with it rather than with p-values.
references: Austin (2009), Balance diagnostics

see_also.title: Exchangeability / no unmeasured confounding
see_also.explains: Treated and untreated units are comparable once you condition on the confounders you measured. Everything that pushed people towards treatment and also moves the outcome is in your adjustment set.
see_also.worry_when: Treatment was chosen by people who knew something about the likely outcome that you do not observe. Clinical judgement, self-selection into a programme, and administrative triage are the classic cases.

concept:concept.target_trial.title: The target trial
concept:concept.target_trial.one_liner: Write down the randomised experiment you would run if you could, then ask what your data lets you emulate.
concept:concept.target_trial.plain_language: Write down the randomised experiment you would run if you could, then ask what your data lets you emulate.
concept:concept.target_trial.in_more_depth: Eligibility, time zero, the treatment strategies being compared, the follow-up, the outcome, and the causal contrast. Making each explicit catches most of the errors that produce implausible observational results: immortal time bias, prevalent-user bias, and outcomes that precede the exposure. It is also the fastest way to notice that a question has no well-defined intervention behind it, in which case the estimand needs rewriting before any estimator is chosen.
references: Hernán & Robins (2016), Using big data to emulate a target trial

see_also.title: Consistency / well-defined intervention
see_also.explains: The outcome you observe under the treatment a unit received is the same as the potential outcome under that treatment. In practice: the treatment has to be a thing someone could actually do.
see_also.worry_when: The treatment is a state of the world rather than an action, or it is coded from several very different real interventions.

see_also.title: Treatment that changes over time
see_also.one_liner: The same person is treated, untreated, treated again; confounders also move.

concept:concept.time_varying_confounding.title: Time-varying confounding
concept:concept.time_varying_confounding.one_liner: A variable that is both a consequence of past treatment and a cause of future treatment. Ordinary regression cannot handle it; g-methods can.
concept:concept.time_varying_confounding.plain_language: A variable that is both a consequence of past treatment and a cause of future treatment. Ordinary regression cannot handle it; g-methods can.
concept:concept.time_varying_confounding.in_more_depth: In a study of a blood-pressure drug, blood pressure is affected by earlier doses and drives later ones. Adjust for it and you block part of the drug's effect and open a collider path. Leave it out and confounding remains. Inverse-probability weighting for a marginal structural model, the parametric g-formula, and longitudinal targeted learning all solve the same problem in different ways: they model the treatment process over time rather than conditioning on its consequences.
references: Robins, Hernán & Brumback (2000)
Daniel et al. (2013), Methods for dealing with time-dependent confounding

see_also.title: No unmeasured time-varying confounding
see_also.explains: At every period, the things that drive the treatment decision and also affect the outcome are measured -- and measured before that decision.
see_also.worry_when: Clinical measurements taken after the dose was changed; employment status recorded at the end of a period used to explain treatment at its start.

see_also.title: Marginal structural model (time-varying weights)
see_also.one_liner: Reweight each person-period so the treated and untreated histories look alike, then fit one simple model to the reweighted data.

see_also.title: Parametric g-formula
see_also.one_liner: Model each period in turn, then simulate the world where everyone followed the strategy you name.

concept:concept.twfe.title: Two-way fixed effects
concept:concept.twfe.one_liner: A regression that gives every unit its own baseline level and every period its own shift, so only change within a unit over time is compared. It is the workhorse behind difference-in-differences, and it misbehaves when units adopt at different dates.
concept:concept.twfe.plain_language: A regression that gives every unit its own baseline level and every period its own shift, so only change within a unit over time is compared. It is the workhorse behind difference-in-differences, and it misbehaves when units adopt at different dates.
concept:concept.twfe.in_more_depth: "Fixed effect" here just means a separate intercept. One per unit absorbs everything about a state that never changes -- its size, its politics, its weather. One per period absorbs anything that hit everybody at once, like a recession. What is left to explain the outcome is the timing of the policy. With two groups and two periods this reproduces the difference-in-differences answer exactly. With many adoption dates it no longer does. The single coefficient becomes a weighted average of every two-group, two-period comparison the data allows, including ones that use an early adopter as the control for a later one. Those weights are decided by the arithmetic rather than by you, and some of them can be negative. The decomposition diagnostic shows what your particular number is made of.
concept:concept.twfe.common_mistake: Reading the coefficient as "the" effect. Under staggered adoption it is an average with weights nobody chose, and it is not guaranteed to lie between the smallest and the largest of the true effects it averages.

concept:guardrail.bad_control.title: Bad controls
concept:guardrail.bad_control.one_liner: Anything measured after treatment, or caused by it, does not belong in the adjustment set. Adjusting for it blocks part of the effect you are trying to measure.
concept:guardrail.bad_control.plain_language: Anything measured after treatment, or caused by it, does not belong in the adjustment set. Adjusting for it blocks part of the effect you are trying to measure.
concept:guardrail.bad_control.in_more_depth: If a training programme raises earnings partly by raising the chance of being employed, then adjusting for employment removes that pathway from the estimate. The number you get is not the effect of the programme; it is the effect holding fixed one of the ways the programme works. Causal Capybara flags variables that look post-treatment -- by name, and by timing when the design has a time variable -- and marks them on the board. It does not remove them for you: the guardrail explains, and you decide. If you genuinely want the effect that does not run through a mediator, that is a controlled direct effect, and it is a different estimand with its own assumptions.
concept:guardrail.bad_control.worry_when: A covariate is named like a follow-up measurement; a covariate is dated after the treatment decision; adjusting for it moves the estimate a lot.

example:lalonde.one_liner: why overlap comes before the estimate
example:lalonde.question: A training programme against a survey comparison group. The comparison group is nothing like the trainees, and the overlap plot says so before any estimator runs.
example:lalonde.teaches: why overlap comes before the estimate
example:lalonde.plain_language: A training programme against a survey comparison group. The comparison group is nothing like the trainees, and the overlap plot says so before any estimator runs.

provenance.data_origin: Independent deterministic simulation; no original study records.
provenance.rights: Generated locally by Causal Capybara from original simulation code. No rows, labels, or documentation from the cited study are redistributed.
provenance.truth: ATT is built in and reported in the project note.
provenance.simulated_note: Simulated data built to the shape of the original study, not the original data. The lesson is real; the numbers are not the published ones.

tour.title: This data is simulated
tour.body: Simulated data built to the shape of the original study, not the original data. The lesson is real; the numbers are not the published ones. After LaLonde (1986) and Dehejia & Wahba (1999). The built-in effect is recorded in the project so you can check what the estimators recover.

tour.title: Read the question
tour.body: The strip at the top is the whole analysis in one sentence: the effect of the training programme on 1978 earnings, for people eligible for it, against comparable people who did not take part.

tour.title: Look at the overlap before anything else
tour.body: The trainees and the comparison group are not alike. The propensity histogram shows most of the comparison group sitting where no trainee sits, and the effective sample size tells you how few of them are really being used.

tour.title: Notice what the app refuses to do
tour.body: Nothing was dropped to make the picture look better. Trimming is available on the Probe bench as a curve, so you can see what it costs rather than accept a package default.

tour.title: Estimate the recommended set
tour.body: Four methods, not one. Matching, weighting, outcome regression and the doubly robust estimator disagree here, and the disagreement is the finding.

tour.title: Read the forest, not a number
tour.body: There is no headline number when several methods ran. Outcome regression sits highest because it reaches furthest into the region where the two groups do not overlap at all. Propensity weighting sits far below zero, on the wrong side of no effect entirely, because it has almost nobody comparable to lean on. Matching, and the doubly robust method that fits both a model of who took part and a model of earnings so that either one being right is enough, land close to the built-in effect. The spread between the four is the finding, and it is a statement about this data rather than about the methods.

tour.title: Ask how wrong it could be
tour.body: Run the sensitivity probe. It answers a specific question: how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be, compared with the covariates you did measure, to explain the estimate away?
